threads.subject: implied status determination based on A70 work permit submission date -- REP-2020-1130
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Background: An applicant submits an A70 Open Work Permit application in conjunction with an In-Canada Spousal Sponsorship PR by Canada Post. The Canada Post receipt indicates submission date (e.g. December 20, 2019) prior to work permit expiry date (e.g. December 21, 2019). But the IRCC confirmation email received a few months after submission indicates an IRCC receipt date (e.g. December 23, 2019) after the work permit expiry date. The applicant has now been offered employment and employer wants confirmation that the applicant is authorized to work on implied status.
We acknowledge that PRs are considered "received" for purposes of an implied status determination on the IRCC receipt date. However, IRCC has previously advised that paper-based work permit submissions are considered “received" on the postage submission date rather than IRCC receipt date. There are currently no published guidelines for what implied status determination date applies in the context of a paper-based work permit submission in conjunction with a PR so we were hoping that such ambiguity would be interpreted in favour of the applicant.
Question: Does the postage submission date rule apply in the context of an A70 Open Work Permit application submitted concurrently with an In-Canada Spousal Sponsorship PR? I.e. is the applicant on implied status in the scenario outlined above?
Thank you kindly,
threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION: Does the postage submission date rule apply in the context of an A70 Open Work Permit application submitted concurrently with an In-Canada Spousal Sponsorship PR? I.e. is the applicant on implied status in the scenario outlined above?
RESPONSE: Please forgive the delay in responding. The postage submission date is no longer used for any temporary resident application (ie: visitor, student, or worker). For electronic applications, the Department uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) around the world to ensure that time is equal for all. Therefore, we do not base receipt date and time on time zones’ but rather that an application is submitted before midnight UTC on the day their status expires. If the application was received after midnight on the day of expiry, the applicant does not benefit from the extension of their status under R183(5). The date received for paper applications is the date physically received and stamped at the Case Processing Centre. If the date physically received is after the expiry date of the applicant's status, the officer will backdate the received date by seven days to account for any mail delivery delays.
If a temporary resident also applies for renewal of their work or study permit before the expiry of their existing permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) or section 189 of the IRPR authorized them to work or study without a permit under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal and only as long as the person remains in Canada.

threads.subject: Student-Non PGWP ELIGIBLE. -- REP-2020-1215
threads.question:
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Hi I have done an application for WP from within Canada for a student who has just graduated from a college ,the study of which is not eligible for PGWP. This applicant got an job offer and LMIA from an employer in Canada and on the basis of that I submitted IMM5710 FOR WORK PERMIT. At the time of application her study permit was valid. Does she qualify to work in Canada during the processing of her WP application ? Is she under implied status ?
Thanks and regards
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTioN: Does she qualify to work in Canada during the processing of her WP application ? Is she under implied status ?
RESPonSE: When a person applies for a work permit from within Canada they are using the form : Application to change conditions or extend my stay in Canada – Worker" application form [IMM 5710]. They are requesting to change their condition" in that they be authorized to work and to “extend their stay" in Canada. It is the “extend their stay" request under section R181 that triggers the extension of status under subsection R183(5). Therefore, the person who submits a work permit application in Canada (not using the outside of Canada process) will have their temporary resident status extended during the processing period (ie: until a decision is made) if they met the requirements of subsection R183(5).
Please note that the status is therefore not implied' but 'maintained'
In order to qualify to work while a work permit application is in process in Canada, the applicant must meet the requirements of paragraph 186 (u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. They must have submitted an application for renewal of a work permit under subsection 201(1). Since your example was a study permit holder and they are applying for their first work permit, they are not submitting under R201(1) but under R200. Therefore, they do not qualify to work without a permit.
186 A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date;

threads.subject: question about ability to work on implied status (R186 + R201) -- REP-2020-1436
threads.question:
Dear Immigration Representatives,
I am an immigration lawyer in Edmonton, and I work for
I would like to ask about IRCC's interpretation of R201(1)(b) in the context of continuing authorization to work without a WP as per R186(u)
We know that those with previously held WP can continue working without WPs pursuant to R1196(u):
(u) until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date;
L'information divulguée en vertu de la [oi sur l'accès à Finformatior
and R201(1): 201 (1) A foreign national may apply for the renewal of their work permit if
- (a) the application is made before their work permit expires; and
- (b) they have complied with all conditions imposed on their entry into Canada.
Questions:
1) What does the requirement in R201(1)(b) exactly mean and where are these conditions recorded or to be found?
2)In what instances a WP-holder would not benefit from R186(u) when they have applied for a new WP?
3) Example: how would a protected person in Canada who has applied for a new WP demonstrate that they complied with all conditions imposed on their entry into Canada?
Thank you in advance.
I am a full member in good standing with the Law Society of Alberta, member ID:
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuEsTioN: 1) What does the requirement in R201(1)(b) exactly mean and where are these conditions recorded or to be found? RESPoNSE: The conditions are listed on the work permit under the 'Conditions' section or in the printed Remarks on the bottom of the permit. The mandatory conditoins on all foreign nationals in Canada are specified in section 183 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and those that may be imposed by an officer are specified in section R185.
QuESTioN: 2)In what instances a WP-holder would not benefit from R186(u) when they have applied for a new WP? RESPoNSE: If the holder of a work permit that specified a single employer or a single occupation, changed their employer or changed their occupation without pre-approval then they would not meet the requirement of R201(1)(b).
QuESTioN: 3) Example: how would a protected person in Canada who has applied for a new WP demonstrate that they complied with all conditions imposed on their entry into Canada? RESPoNSE: For an officer to issue a work permit to an applicant under R201, the officer must be satisfied that the requirements of R200 continue to be met. R200(2) exempts those applying under the LMIA-exemptions of R206 or R207(c0 or
(d) from meeting the requirement that the foreign national will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay under Division 2 of Part 9.
A person who has been determined to be a convention refugee and therefore has protected person status in Canada, is usually exempt from the need to demonstrate that they have complied with conditions imposed on entry as they have usually already been reported for non-compliance with conditions.

threads.question:
Good afternoon
Thank you for the response However, the second answer is still not clear to me.
My RCIC friend sent me a copy of a response sent by this e-mail address saying that R186(w)(ii) was not exclusively for PGWP applicants. Now you mentioned R186(w) saying the person needs to meet the requirements for PGWP in order to be able to work under this same subsection.
You also said that any work that they complete during the time the recently graduated student would not count as eligible work experience under the HCCP/HS W. Still, would they be allowed to work? Even though it is not counting towards the HCCP
program requirements? Or are you saying this would be illegal work?
Today I have a client who will be graduating from a post-secondary program at a private institution (diploma). She is not eligible for a PGWP. She wants to apply for the HCCP program and needs to know if she can work after she sends her application for PR and WP through the HCCP even though she is not eligible for a PGWP and she will have just graduated from a private diploma.
I understand that since HCCP is a new program, there are many things that may not be clear yet. However, my client is in a complicated situation as she wishes to immigrate and will not have a PGWP, and for this reason I am reaching to you again for clarification.
Thank you.
On Wed, Oct 28, 2020 at 1:46 PM wrote:
Dear
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representative Mailbox. Please see below the responses to your questions.
1 - If a temporary resident in Canada, (visitor, student or worker) applies for this program, will this temporary resident be under implied status? I understand that the answer would be yes for students and workers but I’ve heard differently.
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, such as by submitting a work permit application together with their PR application, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made. Such a person is considered to have implied status as a temporary resident during that period. Please see here for more information.
2 - If a student applies for this program before his/her program of studies, which allows her to work off campus, finishes, can he/she begin working full-time once the program of studies ends?I thought that only PGWP applicants were allowed
to work in this situation but, again, I’ve heard differently from other consultants once again.
In order for any foreign national to work in Canada, they must have the proper authorisation to do so. Based on the scenario that you have described, the applicant has a valid study permit, has applied for the HCCP/HSW during their program of studies, and has graduated. In a situation where the student has graduated, and is awaiting a decision on their HCCP/HSW application, any work that they complete during that time would not count as eligible work experience under the HCCP/HSW. Individuals with valid study permits are permitted (with certain parameters) to work without a work permit off campus for up to 20 hours per week under R186(v). In addition, they can work without a work permit under subsection 186(w) if they have applied for a work permit before their study permit expires, and meet the requirements described here. However, eligible work experience under the HCCP/HSW must be acquired under a valid work permit.
It should be noted that eligible experience must not include any period during which the foreign national was engaged in
full-time study or was self-employed.
The applicant should only begin working once they receive the proper approval. Officers issue the occupation-restricted open work permit after stage 1 approval (positive permanent residence pre-assessment) of the APR. If a stage 1 negative decision is rendered, the work permit application is rejected and associated temporary residence fees are refunded. Please see here for more information.
3 - The website mentions a "Canadian Employer”. I just want to make sure that only Canadian citizens are allowed to be employers in this program. Students, workers and PRs, even though they have the business registration number with CRA could not be the employers.
If the non-resident is eligible to register with CRA for a business number and can meet other requirements for employers as per the offer of employment offer form, their status as a temporary resident (authorized to study or work) would not be a barrier to making the initial job offer. However, as with any job offer, an officer would need to review all information and circumstances in the application to support a thorough assessment of the eligibility criteria, including genuineness of
the employer/employee relationship.
The officer needs to be satisfied that the job offer is valid and genuine. Proof that a job offer is valid and genuine may include but is not limited to:
- a genuine need for a caregiver (for example, proof of a school-age child or a person with medical needs in the home)
- the fact that the wage specified in the job offer is aligned with the prevailing wage in the province where the work will be carried out
- the fact that the employer has the financial ability to pay the wages specified in the job offer
- in the case of a live-in arrangement, the fact that reasonable accommodations are provided (for example, a private room)

In a situation where the student has graduated, and is awaiting a decision on their HCCP/HSW application that includes a work permit application, they have the authorisation work, as per paragraph 186
(w) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations: Under R186(w), a foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit if they are or were the holder of a study permit who has completed their program of study and (i) they met the requirements set out in paragraph (v), and (ii) they applied for a work permit before the expiry of that study permit and a decision has not yet been made in respect of their application As referenced, they also need to meet the requirements under paragraph 186 (v) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations: if they are the holder of a study permit and (i) they are a full-time student enrolled at a designated learning institution as defined in section 211.1, (ii) the program in which they are enrolled is a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec, in each case, of a duration of six months or more that leads to a degree, diploma or certificate, and (iii) although they are permitted to engage in fulltime work during a regularly scheduled break between academic sessions, they work no more than 20 hours per week during a regular academic session. As mentioned in our previous response, in a situation where the student has graduated, and is awaiting a decision on their HCCP/HSW application, any work that they complete during that time would not count as eligible work experience under the HCCP/HSW. Individuals with valid study permits are permitted (with certain parameters) to work without a work permit off campus for up to 20 hours per week under paragraph R186(v). In addition, they can work without a work permit under paragraph 186(w) if they have applied for a work permit before their study permit expires, and meet the requirements described here. However, eligible work experience under the HCCP/HSW must be acquired under a valid work permit. threads.subject: Implied Status R. 183 and 186 - Authorization to Work -- REP-2020-2162
threads.question:
Dear Sirs/Mesdames,
I am an Immigration Lawyer practicing in British Columbia. Iam an active member in good standing of the Law Society of British Columbia-Member numbei
I hope you can provide some guidance on the issue of implied status, and ability to continue working under same, when an application for a Temporary Resident Permit from within Canada is filed as opposed to an application for a work permit extension from within Canada is filed.
Assume non-visa requiring foreign national had a two year, employer specific, LMiA based work permit that expired on September 1, 2020. Prior to that date, the applicant filed an application for a Temporary Resident Permit by mail from within Canada and included the correct fee payment of $200. In doing so the applicant applied using only the IMM 5708 (extension as a Visitor) and they did not specifically request work authorization as part of that TRP application, nor did they use the IMM 5710 (extension as a Worker), nor did they include application processing fees for the work authorization (although I understand that these can be waived as fee exempt).
- Question 1) Can you confirm if R. 183(5) permits them to stay in Canada during the processing of the TRP application? Question 2) Can you confirm if R. 183(6) permits them to continue working for the employer listed on the work permit that expired on September 1, 2020? Or does the implied status only permit them to remain in Canada as a Visitor during the processing of the TRP application? Question 3) Considering the applicant did not include an IMM 5710–Application to extend as a Worker, or make any request for consideration of work authorization in general, can they claim the ability to continue working per the conditions of the original work permit during the processing of the application under R. 186(u)?
Many thanks in advance any policy guidance you can share on the above matters.
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
Question 1) Can you confirm if R. 183(5) permits them to stay in Canada during the processing of the TRP application? Response 1)When a foreign national applies for a new Temporary Resident Permit (TRP), they are not renewing under section R181 but applying for a new TRP as per section A24. Therefore, they do not maintain their temporary resident status during the processing period.
Question 2) Can you confirm if R. 183(6) permits them to continue working for the employer listed on the work permit that expired on September 1, 2020? Or does the implied status only permit them to remain in Canada as a Visitor during the processing of the TRP application? Response 2) In your scenario where the person is applying for a TRP, they do not meet the requirements of R183(5) in that they have not submitted an application for extension of status under R181. Therefore, subsection R183(6) does not apply. Please note, that the authority to work while a work permit application is pending is provided in paragraph R186(u) not subsection R183(6).
Question 3) Considering the applicant did not include an IMM 5710–Application to extend as a Worker, or make any request for consideration of work authorization in general, can they claim the ability to continue working per the conditions of the
original work permit during the processing of the application under R. 186(u)?
Response 3) No, the authority to work without a permit under R186(u) is triggered by an application to renew a work permit under subsection R201(1). If the person did not hold a work permit and submit an application renew it prior to the expiry date, they do not meet the requirements of R201(1) and therefore do not benefit from the authority to work without a permit as per R186(u).

threads.subject: a-75 work permit -- REP-2020-2363
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
1. An FN holds an A-75 work permit that contains a remark that authorizes them to work across Canada
2. That person relocates from Quebec to Ontario.
3. That person's employment, which used to be based in Quebec, is now based in Ontario.
In this case, can the person still work and live in Ontario on the A-75 work permit, or must they obtain a new work permit?
Thank you,
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear
Question:
In this case, can the person still work and live in Ontario on the A-75 work permit, or must they obtain a new work permit?
Response:
It should be noted that there are two sets of conditions imposed under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) –conditions imposed on employers (R209.2) and conditions imposed on temporary foreign workers (R185).
“Location" is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the “same working conditions". The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMIA exemption requirement or justification (for instance, provincial nominees). In this situation, given that one of the requirement under the A75 work permit is for the applicant to reside in Quebec, the employer would be considered to be in non-compliance. It is recommended that the employer submit a voluntary disclosure and maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection.
As for the worker, if there is no location noted (including in the ADDITIONAL INFORMATION or REMARKS section) and no condition imposed regarding location noted on the work permit, then the worker may change locations, but only for the employer specified on the work permit. The person has to keep in mind that they will not be able to seek a work permit extension under the A75 CSQ holder exemption if they no longer reside in Quebec. This may also impact their permanent residence application.

threads.question:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Due to the impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic on our operations, we have experienced delays in providing a response. Visitor Record: If the applicant obtained a visitor record with an expiry date of 2 years, they can stay in Canada until the expiry date on the document. Parents and Grandparents Sponsorship: As there is no requirement that a sponsor must be a permanent resident or Canadian citizen for the 3 years immediately preceding the application in order to sponsor parents and grandparents, there is no requirement that the income must be obtained only after becoming a permanent resident. However, as a rule, financial resources must originate from Canadian sources. If income is received from foreign sources, it can be considered if it was declared by the sponsor to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and appears on the Notice of Assessment (NOA). Yes, a sponsor is allowed to submit more than one sponsorship application at the same time for different family class relatives (i.e. their parents and grandparents), provided that, where applicable, the necessary income requirements are met for the total number of persons involved. A spouse or common-law partner may co-sign an undertaking to help meet the necessary income requirements by pooling financial resources when sponsoring a parent or grandparent, however no other family member can co-sign. Note that co-signers are required to meet the same requirements as sponsors, regardless of how long they have been married to or living in a common-law relationship with the sponsor. This means, for parent and grandparent applications, co-signers must also provide proof from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) for the three taxation years immediately preceding the date of the application in order for their income to be included in the necessary income assessment.
We hope you find this information useful.

I am hoping you can help clarify the following situation:
- FW applies for a lmia based wp with a planned duration of2 years
- lmia expires while wp is in processing-WP is approved
- FW arrives in Canada but the wp is only issued for 10 months because the passport is only valid for 10 months.
Question:
Can the FW extend their passport and then apply to extend the WP for the remaining 14 months?

While there are specific circumstances that allow a post-graduate work permit or an IEC work permit to be extended I have not found or seen any specific references to lmia based work permits.
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your question.
Question: Can the FW extend their passport and then apply to extend the WP for the remaining 14 months?
Answer:
Yes they can.
In cases of passport expiry, provided the initial LMIA and WP application were received before the LMIA expiry date-which seems to be the case based on the information below, temporary foreign workers will be able to renew their existing WP at CPC-E, without seeking a new LMIA. That is, while the expiry date of the LMIA will have passed, the temporary foreign worker met the initial time frame for the application and can therefore be extended up until the end of the duration time
outlined in the initial LMIA, provided the passport has been renewed accordingly.

threads.subject: Change of passport before entering Canada with a work permit approval letter -- REP-2020-2582
threads.question:
Seasons greetings!
Question
Does a foreign worker need a new work permit approval letter if they use a new passport to enter Canada?
Specifically, a foreign national is issued a work permit approval letter by a visa office. Before they travel to Canada they apply
L'nmdon for and receive a new passport because the previous passport is expiring withing 6 months. Can they used the approval letter with the new passport or are they required to advise the visa office and request a new approval letter?
Thank you.
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTloN: Does a foreign worker need a new work permit approval letter if they use a new passport to enter Canada?
RESPoNSE: The work permit itself is not linked to the passport, so no new POE Letter of Introduction (work permit approval) letter is required. The foreign national should inform the border services officer on arrival that they have a new passport.
However, the electronic travel authorization (eTA) or the temporary resident visa (TRV) are linked to specific passport numbers. Therefore, in order for the eTA or TRV to be linked to the correct passport for travel, the applicant should obtain a new eTA or TRV.

threads.subject: Implied Status and Restoration Questions -- REP-2020-1289
threads.question:
# Hello,
I am writing today to request a response on the following questions:
1. Restoration Is it possible for an individual whose work permit has expired to file for restoration and request that their status be restored to that of a visitor? Or, is it that the individual could only qualify for restoration if they were requesting to be restored to their previous status (work permit holder)?
2. Implied Status Where an individual holds an open work permit (as a dependent to their spouse who is on a study permit), do they benefit from implied status if before their current open work permit expires, they apply for a new LMIA-based work permit? Where an individual holds an open work permit (as a dependent to their skilled worker spouse who is on a work permit), do they benefit from implied status if before their current open work permit expires, they apply for a new LMIA-based work permit?
Thank you kindly for your assistance.
Kind Regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTloN: Is it possible for an individual whose work permit has expired to file for restoration and request that their status be restored to that of a visitor? Or, is it that the individual could only qualify for restoration if they were requesting to be restored to their previous status (work permit holder)?
RESPoNSE: When a person is applying to restore their status, the status is temporary resident with authorization to study or work. Therefore, when restoring they may restore their status as temporary resident without requesting authorization to continue studying or working.
QUESTION: Where an individual holds an open work permit (as a dependent to their spouse who is on a study permit), do they benefit from implied status if before their current open work permit expires, they apply for a new LMIA-based work permit?
RESPoNSE: When a temporary resident submits an application for work permit renewal under R201 (ie: prior to expiry of existing WP) they are in essences submitting two applications in one. The first is for an extension of their status under R181 and the second for a renewal of their work permit under R201.
It is the application for an extension of status under R181 that triggers the extension of status during the processing period by operation of law under R183(5). This allows the person to remain in Canada while their application is being processed.
It is the application under R201 that triggers the authority to work without a permit under R186(u) as per the condition on their existing permit and so long as they remain in Canada.
QUESTloN: Where an individual holds an open work permit (as a dependent to their skilled worker spouse who is on a work permit), do they benefit from implied status if before their current open work permit expires, they apply for a new LMIA-based work permit?
RESPoNSE: It does not matter what type of work permit is held at the time of work permit renewal application for the status to be extended during the processing period.

threads.subject: the Location of work on LMIA-Exempt work permits -- REP-2020-2470
threads.question:
Dear IRCC,
My name is Ihave a question about the location of work on LMIA-Exempt work permits.
I have a potential client who came to work in Canada under the LMIA-exempt program as a in New Brunswick. Since his occupation/job duties and his employer has multiple branches in the Canada, he may be assigned to work in different locations, other than where the headquarter of his employer is located. However, on his work permit, the location of employment is specified (the city of the headquarter). He said when his employer checked with the provincial immigration office about that concern, and his employer was told not to worry about since New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have an agreement on the Business Incorporation Acts that there is not much difference between the provinces.
Firstly, is this true? And secondly, in this case, what should we do to make everything correct? Should the foreign worker apply to change the conditions imposed on his work permit? I checked the operational instructions and guidelines of temporary workers (the link is as below), it sounds like we can apply to ask an officer to remove such restrictions. If so, how to proceed? Please advise. Thank you very much.
[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/eligibility/eligibility-admissibility-conditions-including-validity-period.html
Sincerely,
threads.answer:
Hello,
The location identified in the location field is used for statistical purposes and taken from the work permit application submitted by the client. The client may work at any location specified in the LMlA-exempt work permit unless the following condition is imposed 'Not authorized to work in any other location'. If this condition is on the work permit, then a new work permit must be submitted along with a new offer of employment.

threads.subject: Can Spousal Open Work Permit and Study Permit Be Held At Same Time? -- REP-2020-2584
threads.question:
Good morning,
I am a lawyer in good standing with the Law Society of Ontario
Can an applicant for permanent residence under the in-Canada spouse class, who has a permanent resident application in process with an accompanying open work permit in process as well, apply for a study permit? If so, and if both the open work permit and study permit applications are approved, may they hold both the open work permit and study permit at the same time?
Thank you in advance for your assistance.

中 and Citizenship Caneda ot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuEsTioN: Can an applicant for ... an accompanying open work permit in process as well, apply for a study permit? If so, and if both the open work permit and study permit applications are approved, may they hold both the open
work permit and study permit at the same time?
RESPoNSE: Submitting an application for authorization to work does not preclude the applicant from also submitting an application for authorization to study. However, the requirements for the separate permits must be met. To be able to submit a work permit application from within Canada the applicant must fall into one of the paragraphs of section R199 and to apply for a study permit in Canada the requirements are found in section R215.
There is no legal bar to holding both a study and work permit as long as the applicant is able to comply with any conditions listed on both.

and Cizenship Canada
Lnmn Must a Migrant Worker be currently working for an employer to apply for the Open Work Permit for Vulnerable Worker? The eligibility requirement states migrant workers must have a valid work permit etc.

Eligibility requirements
Work authorization
At the time they apply, migrant workers must be in Canada and must either
- have a valid work permit that is LMIA-required (including work permits issued under the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program)
- have a valid work permit that is LMIA-exempt and employer-specific
- be authorized to work without a work permit under implied status as a result of applying for a renewal of one of these types of work permits [R186(u)]
Objectives of this provision
- to provide migrant workers who are experiencing abuse, or who are at risk of abuse, with a distinct means to leave their employer o This is done by opening the possibility of obtaining a work authorization for other employers.
- to mitigate the risk of migrant workers in Canada who are leaving their job and working irregularly (that is, without authorization) as a result of abusive situations
- to facilitate the participation of migrant workers who are experiencing abuse, or who are at risk of abuse, in any relevant inspection of their former employer, recruiter or both
- to help migrant workers in assisting authorities, if required (noting that this is not required for the issuance of the open work permit), by reducing the perceived risk and fear of work permit revocation and removal from Canada
Who may benefit from this measure?
- migrant workers in Canada who currently hold a valid LMIA-required work permit issued under subparagraph R200(1)(c)(iii) or a valid LMIA-exempt, employer-specific work permit issued under subparagraph R200(1)(c) (ii.1)
- migrant workers who have applied for a renewal of their employer-specific work permit under subsection R201(1) and who are currently authorized to work in Canada under paragraph R186(u) (implied status)

threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I hope that this email finds you and all of the team at Imm Reps well.
I am seeking your guidance with respect to the below guidance which can be located at [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-)
nmigration, Réfugiés
manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes/validity-suspension-duration-employment.html
Specifically, I am seeking guidance as to whether foreign nationals who qualify to renew their existing work permits without obtaining a new LMIA based on their passport expiry having resulted in the original LMIA-based work permit being issued for a shorter duration than that identified in the LMIA must apply inland for that renewal or if they could apply either at a port of entry (if eligible to do so) or to a visa office abroad (specifically in the case of an individual who needs a visa to enter Canada, and who needs to renew both the visa and the work permit pursuant to this policy, but based on timing and employment associated travel, cannot wait the 90+ days for an online work permit extension application processed inland followed by another 26+ days for the TRV renewal (based on current posted processing times). The below guidance is not clear on this point.
Passport expiry effect on duration of work
The expectation is that CIC or CBSA officers will issue a work permit for the duration of work indicated in the LMIA. However, in cases of passport expiry, a work permit may be issued for a shorter duration than identified in the LMIA. For example, if the LMIA work duration is two years but the temporary foreign worker's passport will expire in one year, the officer will issue a one-year work permit.
In cases of passport expiry only, provided the initial LMIA and work permit application were received before the assessment expiry date, temporary foreign workers will be able to renew their existing work permits without obtaining a new LMIA. That is, while the assessment expiry date of the LMIA has passed, the temporary foreign worker met the initial time frame for application and his work permit can therefore be extended for the duration outlined in the initial LMIA, provided the passport has been renewed accordingly. To assist officers processing the extension, CIC and CBSA officers are asked to record reasons in the GCMS Case Notes view tab when a work permit is issued for a shorter duration than is indicated in the LMIA.
Many thanks as always for your guidance.
Kind regards,

Hello :
QUESTION: In relation to your comments, can you kindly provide us with a definition and clarification as to what IRCC deems
to be 'employment'?
Specifically, will an employer who puts a foreign worker on a leave without pay (ie: foreign worker retains their employment status during the period that they're out of status, however does not physically work), still be considered to be compliant with IRPA 124(1)(c)?
RESPoNSE: In order to determine if the foreign national is 'working', please review section 2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
Work means an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that is in direct competition with the activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market.
An employer can offer a foreign national employment, hire them or have them on leave but it is when the foreign national engages in the ‘activity' of the employment that the foreign national must have authorization to do so. If the foreign national is not committing the activity (ie: work) then for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and Regulations, no authorization is required. The foreign national can start or resume the activity once they have received authorization to do so.

<RCC. - # # Hello,

RESPoNSE: There are two considerations in this situation. Therefore, an employer may 'offer' employment but they can not have the foreign national begin work until the foreign national is authorized to do so. If the foreign national had authorization to work and that authorization expires, the employer must stop the employment until such time as the foreign national is authorized to work
The choice of how to stop the employment is a decision between the employer and the foreign national. However, the employer must keep in mind what they stated in the initial Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMlA) or Offer of employment as it pertains to ending the employment.

threads.answer:

Dear Sir or Madam,
Can an application for an A75 LMIA-exempt work permit be made outside of Canada by a CSQ holder who is normally resident in Quebec but travelling abroad for a short period of time (ie. Vacation, business trip, etc)? It is unclear if an applicant
must be physically present in Quebec in order to satisfy the requirements of this LMIA
exemption: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/quebec-cases/labour-market-impact-assessment-exempt-work-permit-renewals- extensions-certain-quebec-selection-holders.html
I am Quebec lawyer Thank you in advance.
Best regards/Meilleures salutations,
Page 76
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTioN: Can an application for an A75 LMIA-exempt work permit be made outside of Canada by a CSQ holder who is normally resident in Quebec but travelling abroad for a short period of time (ie. Vacation, business trip, etc)?
RESPONSE: The eligibility for the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)-exempt work permit renewals and extensions for certain Quebec Selection Certificate (CSQ) holders currently in Quebec (exemption code A75) category requires that the individual 'reside' in Quebec. Residence is normally assessed as where an individual resided for the most time in a given calendar year. Therefore, a person who is outside of Quebec for a short period could apply for this category of work permit.
It should be noted that applications in this category must be submitted using the in-Canada application form IMM 5710.
To be eligible for a work permit under paragraph R205(a), foreign nationals must
- currently reside in Quebec
- have a valid work permit
- have an offer of employment submitted by the employer to IRCC
- hold a CSQ under the Quebec skilled worker class; the CSQ must indicate one ofthe following codes in section 9, Catégorie: o “IQ – Travailleurs qualifiés" o “IP – Travailleurs” o “IT — Travailleurs qualifiés" o “IZ – PEQ Travailleurs" 。“TY – PEQ Étudiants" o “I6 Travailleurs Art. 40"
- be in one of the following situations: o have a valid CSQ (within the 24- or 36-month validity period) at the time of their initial A75 work permit application if they have not yet submitted their permanent residence application o have submitted their permanent residence application before the expiry date of the CSQ, and the application is stil in process; the work permit (initial application or renewal) may be issued under the LMIA exemption code A75, even if the CSQ is expired
- fall under one of the following categories: o applicant seeking to extend their work permit for their current employer or renew it with a different employer in the province of Quebec o applicant seeking a work permit with a new employer in the province of Quebec o student who has obtained a post-graduation work permit that is still valid and who has an offer of employment in the province of Quebec o work permit holder through participation in one of the following categories under the International Experience
Canada (IEC) Program: Working Holiday
■ Young Professionals
■International Co-op (Internship)
Work permit renewals and extension requests under this exemption should be submitted directly to an IRCC case processing centre.

threads.subject: TFW Changing locations -- REP-2020-0565
threads.question:
Hello
My name is and my RCIC number is
Ihave two scenarios that need some information or clarity-
Scenario1 - TFW foreign worker is working at one employer location on a valid work permit approved based on LMIA. TFW foreign worker wants to work on a different location now which is owned by same employer, same company under same CRA business number. Is he required to apply for change of conditions of work permit as his current work permit is location specific. Will his employer need a new LMIA to get him transfer to a different location ?
Scenario 2- TFW is working on his valid WP approved based on LMIA. WP is location specific. Employer is planning to change his work location now. Does TFW need to apply to change conditions on WP ? Does his employer need to get another LMIA for new location or just communication to service Canada and IRCC is required.
This information will be very helpful. Thank you for your time in advance.
Page 1214
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuEsTioN: Scenario1 - TFW foreign worker is working at one employer location on a valid work permit approved based on LMIA. TFW foreign worker wants to work on a different location now which is owned by same employer, same company under same CRA business number. Is he required to apply for change of conditions of work permit as his current work permit is location specific. Will his employer need a new LMIA to get him transfer to a different location ?
Scenario 2- TFW is working on his valid WP approved based on LMIA. WP is location specific. Employer is planning to change his work location now. Does TFW need to apply to change conditions on WP ? Does his employer need to get another LMIA for new location or just communication to service Canada and IRCC is required.
RESPoNSE: There are two sets of conditions to consider in employment location -those imposed under section 185 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and those imposed on the employer under 209.3 of the IRPR. In the first scenario, if the location is imposed on the work permit, the worker must change their conditions to move locations. The same is true for the second scenario.
Worker conditions: The foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include "not authorized to work at any other location". If this condition is imposed and a location is specified, the worker will need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMlA-exempt work permit or new LMIA) in order to change locations.
Employer conditions: "Location" is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the "same working conditions". The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMlA exemption requirement or justification (for instance, provincial nominees). (IRCC) does not require proactive notification of changes, but the employer is required to maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at the time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the voluntary disclosure process.

threads.answer:

Question: Can Internationally Educated Health Professionals (IEHP)who are physically present in Ontario and are not Permanent Residents, work in Canada under supervision of a registered Healthcare worker to help Canadians?
If yes can you also consider foreign trained workers (nurses or doctors) who have the Temporary Resident Visa to travel however they are at present in their respective countries?
Lastly would you also process applications of Internationally Educated Health Professionals (IEHP) who are still abroad and would like to apply under Emergency Services Provider where essentially if they have TRV they can then travel to Canada and can work in hospitals/ health care facilities without work permit and without getting registered with College of Nursing.
All they need is "orders" to board plane from overseas to help Canadians in the frontline help.

Response: Please note that the current travel restrictions do not change the requirements of the temporary worker programs. To be authorized to work in Canada, foreign nationals must meet the eligibility criteria of the specific work permit (or authorization to work without a work permit under R186) category under which they've applied, including any provincial/territorial requirements. At this time, IRCC is prioritizing work permit applications under specific essential and critical occupations in the agriculture, agri-food, truck driving, and health care industries. Please see the program delivery instructions specific to Prioritizing work permit processing for essential occupations for a list of prioritized occupations.
Work permit-required foreign nationals are exempt to the travel restrictions as per the following:

Document to present to the air carrier: The status document [IMM 1442] (the actual valid work permit document).
2. Foreign nationals who received a positive decision from IRCC (documented by a letter of introduction) on a work permit application but whose work permit has not yet been issued. The foreign national's purpose of travel must not be discretionary or optional. Consult Determining whether entry of temporary workers will be for a discretionary or optional purpose. Document to present to the air carrier: A paper copy or e-version of the letter of introduction
Only specific work permit-exempt foreign nationals working in critical occupations are exempt from the travel restrictions at this time as per the Orders in Council -this includes providers of emergency services under paragraph R186(t) for the protection or preservation of life or property (includes firefighters and medical service providers). threads.subject: Question sur les stagiaires, les permis de travail et le statut d'étudiant ou non -- REP-2020-1955
threads.question:
Bonjour Nos excuses pour le délai dans notre réponse.
Questions :
1. j’ai des questions concernant les Boursiers postdoctoraux diplômés du doctorat en philosophie (Ph. D.) et titulaires d’une bourse de recherche [code dispense d’ElMT C44] et la Dispense de permis de travail de courte durée (120 jours ou moins) pour les chercheurs [Politique d’intérêt public R186]. Dans ces cas, je sais que les personnes éligibles sont considérées comme des travailleurs; par contre, serait-il possible que le demandeur soit quand même encore étudiant, dans notre université ou dans une université étrangère?
2. Est-ce que le fait d’être encore étudiant ou non influence l’éligibilité au permis de travail C44 ou à bénéficier de la dispense de permis de travail de courte durée 120 jours ou moins pour les chercheurs (R186)?
3.Existe-t-il un document qui fournit plus de détails sur ce qui est considéré comme du travail versus ce qui est considéré comme des études? Par exemple, on me parle de période de résidence en entreprise, d’intervention en entreprise, est-ce que l’étudiant doit alors posséder un permis de travail, s’il se rend en entreprise plus de 20 heures par semaine? Est-ce que faire des appels téléphoniques à partir du domicile ou conduire des entrevues en entreprise est considéré comme du travail ou bien comme des études?
4. Quelle est la part de travail qui peut être effectuée durant la période de rédaction du mémoire ou de la thèse?
Réponses :
1. Oui c’est possible que le demandeur soit quand même étudiant (au Canada ou à l’étranger). Par contre, vous devez garder en tête que la dispense de permis de travail de 120 jours pour les chercheurs s’appliquent pour les demandeurs qui se trouvent à l’extérieur du Canada, il est donc peu probable que ces demandeurs soient étudiants au Canada mais pourraient l’être à l’étranger. Tout dépend si le demandeur rencontre les critères d’éligibilité de permis de travail ou de la dispense. Le fait d’être encore étudiant ne vient pas empêcher que le demandeur fasse ces demandes, mais il doit être en mesure de démontrer qu'il est raisonnable qu’il travaille et étudie en même temps, l’agent prendra en considération le nombre d’heures de travail par semaine versus le nombre de cours auxquels l’étudiant est inscrit par exemple.
3. Non nous n’avons pas ce genre de document, mais nous nous penchons sur la question puisqu’il y a effectivement plusieurs situations où il y a un flou à savoir si un permis d’études est suffisant et si un permis de travail est requis. Par contre, de façon générale, les stages constituent un travail, car on considère habituellement que les stagiaires entrent sur le marché du travail du Canada et qu’ils prennent la place de citoyens canadiens ou de résidents permanents. Cette notion s’applique aux stages qui s’inscrivent dans un programme d’études, qui ne donnent pas lieu au paiement d’un salaire ou qui donnent lieu au paiement d’une commission.
4.Les étudiants sont autorisés à travailler hors campus pour un maximum de 20 heures/semaine avec leur permis d’études.

threads.subject: Entrée Expresse-Ajout/retrait de personnes à charge -- REP-2020-2465
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Merci d'avoir communiqué avec la boîte aux lettres des représentants de l'immigration.
Question :
J'aurai une question concernant le programme Entrée Expresse
Si quelqu'un se marie ou divorce APRÈs avoir reçu une invitation et avoir déjà téléchargé les documents demandés pour
l'évaluation de sa demande de résidence permanente, comment doit-on procéder?
Il me semble que lors d'une conférence offerte par IRCC à laquelle j'avais assistée, l'agente avait dit qu'on devait déclarer le nouveau conjoint pour le contrôle sanitaire et de sécurité, mais qu'il ne pourrait pas être personne à charge qui accompagne. Il n'y aura pas le choix que de le parrainer par la suite.
Pour le divorce, en revanche, l'ex-conjoint sortirait du dossier, mais le dossier ne serait pas rouvert pour un nouveau calcul des points.
AI-JE BIEN COMPRIS LA PROCÉDURE QUI SERA APPLIQUÉE DANS L'UNE ET L'AUTRE DES DEUX SITUATIONS? SinOn, SVP, me corriger.
Réponse :
Pour évaluer une demande au regard de l’article L11.2, un bureau de traitement doit examiner l'information contenue dans le profil d’un demandeur au moment de sa sélection et celle qu'il a fournie dans sa DERP. Une fois qu'une DERP a été présentée, elle ne peut être refusée au titre de l’article L11.2 en raison d’un changement de situation, sauf dans l’un des cas suivants :
- l’agent établit que le changement est survenu avant que le demandeur ait présenté sa DERP et que ce changement aurait donné lieu au refus de la demande au titre de l’article L11.2;
- depuis que sa situation a changé, le demandeur ne satisfait plus aux exigences minimales du programme pour lequel il fait demande. Par conséquent, même si la demande respecte les exigences de l’article L11.2, elle peut être refusée en raison des exigences du programme.
Par exemple, si un demandeur se marie avant de présenter sa DERP, mais n’en informe IRCC qu’après avoir présenté sa DERP, le mariage peut alors être pris en considération dans le cadre de l’évaluation au regard de l’article L11.2.
Si toutefois un demandeur se marie après avoir présenté sa DERP, puis en informe IRCC, le mariage ne peut pas être pris en considération dans le cadre de l’évaluation prévue dans l’article L11.2. Le changement de situation du demandeur peut toutefois déterminer s’il satisfait aux exigences du programme. Voir les instructions ci--dessous pour plus de détails.
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Nous espérons que cette information vous sera utile.
Cordialement,

threads.subject: validity of passport in times of COVID -- REP-2020-2486
threads.question:
Good afternoon,
R72(1)(e)(ii) Requires all clients to be in possession of a passport or an acceptable identity document at the time of landing. Officers are empowered at landing to waive the requirement to provide a valid passport usually if no identity concerns exist. However it is at the discretion of the reviewing officer to waive the requirement to present a passport, in order to prevent delay in landing all clients should make every effort to hold a valid passport at the time of landing. R179(c) requires all clients to hold a valid passport or document that may be used to enter the country that issued it or another country. The requirements of both R72 and R179 can be waived through the application of humanitarian and compassionate consideration, this practice is common in the application of R72, but uncommon in R179. The application of humanitarian and compassionate considerations is highly discretionary, and there is no general policy on application in these cases. Applicants who are required to hold a passport as a part of their application should make every effort to hold a valid passport. If a IRCC client is unable to obtain a passport due to Covid-19 disruptions, this should be flagged in their application for a new or extended work permit; or their permanent resident application.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Thank you for your inquiry.
Under normal circumstances, a study permit cannot be issued to those intending to complete a program of study via distance learning, since physical presence in Canada is not required.

threads.subject: STUDY PERMIT| STAGE [1] APPROVAL : POLICY CLARIFICATION REQUEST :--REP-2020-1612
threads.question:
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry.
The 2-stage assessment process for study permit applications only applies to study permit applications made outside of Canada and does not apply to in-Canada study permit applications. Students may begin a program via distance learning from outside Canada without a study permit, as a study permit is not required for this type of program. The two stage assessment was a facilitative measure that was introduced in response to travel restrictions as a result of COVID-19 and allows this time spent studying before an approval is received to count towards a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP).
A study permit is still required for programs inside Canada which are normally offered in-person but have moved to an online format due to COVID-19, unless they are shorter than 6 months in duration and therefore exempt from requiring a study permit under R188.
The foreign nationals in question would therefore not be able to begin studying without a study permit, unless they had applied prior to the expiry of a previous study permit and therefore benefit from maintaining their status, or if the program falls under R188 and no study permit is required.
I trust this information is of assistance to you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Distance learning / Online Studies in Canada without a permit -- REP-2020-2275
threads.question:
Hello,
Foreign nationals without a study permit will not be granted an extension of their authorized stay as a visitor simply for the purpose of completing a short-term course or program of less than 6 months that would last beyond their original authorized period of stay. Paragraph R188(1)(c) was not put in place to allow foreign nationals to take short-term courses, one after the other, simply by extending their temporary resident status—in effect, making it possible for them to complete a whole certificate, diploma or degree without ever having a study permit. (IRCC) recognizes that long-term visitors and foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting 6 months or less at any time during their stay in Canada. It is therefore recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards or work on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student. Section R215 provides an exemption to allow certain foreign nationals to apply for a study permit after entry to Canada.
Thank you kindly,

threads.subject: PGWP Length -- REP-2020-2387
threads.question:
Good day,
This is in response to your enquiry regarding validity length of PGWP.
The length of the PGWP is based on the length of the program as indicated by the DLl on the letter of graduation/letter of program completion. If the letter of graduation notes that the applicant completed a 1 year program (for example 2 semesters and a scheduled break), the officer will issue a PGWP of 1 year. Regularly scheduled breaks (for example, scheduled winter and summer breaks) should be included in the time accumulated toward the length of the post-graduation work permit.
If the letter of graduation notes that the applicant completed a 8 month program, the PGWP will be issued for the length of 8 months.
For more information on the length of PGwP please visit our website: Work in Canada after you graduate: about the process

RESPONSE REP-2020-2622: The holder of a Temporary Resident Permit (TRP) is considered to be a temporary resident, however to a request for a new temporary resident permit is made under section 24 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. In order to benefit from an extension of status during the application processing period as per subsection 183(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (ie: formerly known as implied status), an application under section 181 of the IRPR is required. Therefore, no person requesting a new TRP is provided an extension of status by law.
QUESTION REP-2020-2643: Is there any immigration measure that protects the minor in this scenario (Minor held SP and parents held WPs but parents were refused WP extension -all are now out of status) and permits her to attend elementary school? She is not authorized to study until restoration is granted, but this could take many months.
RESPONSE REP-2020-2643: As per subsection 30(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act: Every minor child in Canada, other than a child of a temporary resident not authorized to work or study, is authorized to study at the pre-school, primary or secondary level. In your scenario, the parents have no status in Canada, therefore since the child is a minor, is in Canada and the child's parents are not temporary residents without authorization to work or study, the child is authorized by the Regulation to study up to and including the Secondary level of school. There is no requirement for the minor child to hold temporary resident status.

Question: If an undergraduate student completes their academic program May 1 2015, and plans to begin a graduate program Sept. 1
2015, what should they do in the following situations:
Situation #1: If their study permit is valid until 2016, for example, do they need to take any action in Aug 2015 after the 90 day period has passed? (e.g. apply for a visitor record during that time, while they wait for their next program to begin? Or perhaps apply for
a new study permit?)
Response: The foreign national must apply to extend their study permit before their current study permit becomes invalid (i.e. 90 days after they complete their program of study). If they apply for the extension before their study permit has become invalid,
they can remain in Canada legally under implied status.
Situation #2: If their study permit expires in July 2015, for example, can they apply to extend their study permit from within Canada before
July 2015 and remain in Canada legally while they wait for the new study permit?
Response:
Yes. Please see the above response.
Situation #3: Can they work between May 1 and Sept 1 as a scheduled academic break, as per IRPR 186 (v)(iii)?
Response: When a student completes a program of study and is waiting to start a new program of study, the break between the two programs is not considered a regularly scheduled break. Students in this situation do not meet the requirements of R186(v)
and are therefore not authorized to work between two programs of study.

threads.subject: Arranged employment points under MI 29(2)(a)(iii)-- REP-2020-2482
threads.question:
Good day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: In regard to the interpretation of “over a continuous period of work in Canada”, must the continuous 1 year period of work in Canada be accumulated immediately before submission of the PR application? Scenario 1: The foreign national holds a work permit valid for the next 2 years (issued under paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations), has a full-time indeterminate job offer from the employer who is specified on the work permit, has already accumulated one year of full-time work in Canada for the employer named on the work permit over a continuous period of one year, and is currently outside Canada for a period of 6 months (during the validity of the work permit) working remotely for the Canadian employer named on the work permit. Can a foreign national in this situation claim points for arranged employment while outside Canada under MI 29(2)(a)(iii)? Scenario 2: The foreign national holds a work permit valid for the next 2 years (issued under paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations), has a full-time indeterminate job offer from the employer who is specified on the work permit, has already accumulated one year of full-time work in Canada for the employer named on the work permit over a continuous period of one year, and has just resumed employment in Canada after a period of 6 months (during the validity of the work permit) working remotely from outside of Canada for the Canadian employer named on the work permit. Can a foreign national in this situation claim points for arranged employment under MI 29(2)(a)(iii) immediately after their return to Canada, or must they wait to accumulate another year of continuous work experience in Canada for the employer before being eligible to claim points for arranged employment?
Answer: Yes, 29(2)(a)(iii) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system specifies that the foreign national must be working for the same employer to qualify for points for arranged employment. The one year of full-time continuous work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work must be accumulated for the same employer in Canada.
For both scenarios, the applicant would qualify for arranged employment points as per 29(2)(a)(iii) as the foreign national works for an employer specified on the permit and has accumulated a total of at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work in Canada for the employers who made the offer. The applicant must prove that they continue to work for the same employer.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

I am an RCIC and I have a question regarding study permits. I know that if a student starts a study program and then leaves the program and remains without studies for more than 150 days, he/she becomes non compliant with the study permit conditions. My question is -
1*1and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada

If the study permit is still valid even after 150 days, does that person technically becomes "out of status" by remaining without studies for more than 150 days and not applying to change her status to visitor/worker before the end of the 150 days period OR does he/she still has some kind of status as the study permit is still valid?

The student must still comply with their study permit conditions which means they must be actively pursuing their education. If the student's in-class courses are temporarily moved to an online-only format or suspended completely because of COVID-19, to stay compliant the student must:

Answer: The onus is on the applicant to inform us of any changes to their personal information, including marriage. Family members can be added to the application at any time during the process prior to obtaining permanent resident status. The applicant must add their spouse by uploading a Letter of Explanation to their application. The officer reviewing the file will then contact the applicant with the documentation needed to add the spouse to the application, regardless of if the spouse is accompanying the applicant to Canada.
Officers will review the application as per section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to ensure that the applicant continues to meet the eligibility criteria of the program. The applicant should re-calculate their score as married before applying online for permanent residence. If the re-calculated score is less than the lowest score in the round of invitations, the applicant should decline the invitation to apply, as this will lead to refusal. If the applicant declines an invitation, they will be entered back into the Express Entry pool of candidates, and considered in future rounds of invitations, if still eligible. The client would not appear to qualify for an ICT WP (Intra-Company Transferee-Work Permit). The client is on the payroll of a company in Canada. The client does not appear, therefore, to have been employed continuously outside Canada by the company that plans to transfer them to a similar full-time position. The client appears to have been employed continuously outside Canada by the Canadian company and is seeking to relocate to Canada to work. This does not meet the threshold for an ICT WP.

Hello,
This e-mail is in reply to your inquiry to IRCC's Immigration Representatives e-mail inbox.
Question: If an undergraduate student completes their academic program May 1 2015, and plans to begin a graduate program Sept. 1 2015, what should they do in the following situations:
Situation #1: If their study permit is valid until 2016, for example, do they need to take any action in Aug 2015 after the 90 day period has passed? (e.g. apply for a visitor record during that time, while they wait for their next program to begin? Or perhaps apply for a new study permit?)
Response: The foreign national must apply to extend their study permit before their current study permit becomes invalid (i.e. 90 days after they complete their program of study). If they apply for the extension before their study permit has become invalid, they can remain in Canada legally under implied status.
Situation #2: If their study permit expires in July 2015, for example, can they apply to extend their study permit from within Canada before July 2015 and remain in Canada legally while they wait for the new study permit?
Response: Yes. Please see the above response.
Situation #3: Can they work between May 1 and Sept 1 as a scheduled academic break, as per IRPR 186 (v)(iii)?
Response: When a student completes a program of study and is waiting to start a new program of study, the break between the two programs is not considered a regularly scheduled break. Students in this situation do not meet the requirements of R186(v) and are therefore not authorized to work between two programs of study.
We understand that there are concerns with the above responses and are currently exploring options to address these concerns.

The Use of a Representative form (IMM 5476) form has two purposes: (1) it designates a representative, and (2) it gives authority to disclose an applicant's personal information to that representative. However, the IMM 5476 needs to be linked to a specific application, as it gives authority to represent and disclose personal information concerning a specific application only. If the applicant wants to disclose their personal information to an individual (whether they have a representative or not), they have the option to complete the Authority to Release Personal Information to a Designated Individual form (IMM 5475) allowing the designated person the ability to obtain information such as application status and change their address if they move. Question:
Can PGWP holders who work as self-employed individuals in Canada be eligible to apply for Permanent Residency under the Canadian Experience Class or Federal Skilled Worker and claim points for work experience in Canada as a self-employed?
Answer:
Self-employment cannot be counted towards work experience in Canada for the Canadian Experience Class. However, there is no bar to self-employment for the Federal Skilled Workers program. If the applicant is self-employed (you must declare this in the work history section of the application) in Canada, they are not entitled to CRS points for Canadian work experience pursuant to Section 15(7)(b) of the Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry. If it was foreign self-employed work experience however, then they may claim points for foreign work experience. Declare the experience as self-employment in the application and the appropriate points may be awarded by the system.
If the applicant is self-employed, you should include articles of incorporation or other evidence of business ownership, evidence of self-employment income and documentation from third-party individuals indicating the service provided along with payment details (self-declared main duties or affidavits are not acceptable proof of self-employed work experience). This is covered in the completeness check for Express Entry.

Question 1: For non LMIA based work permits where: The foreign worker receives a promotion, which includes a change in job title, change in salary, where the job duties remain very similar to the previous position, and where the new position falls under the same NOC code as the previous position-is a new online offer of employment and work permit application required before the foreign worker can assume the new role?
Answer: While the job title is printed on the work permit, it is the National Occupational Code (NOC) that we assess against when issuing the work permit and conducting compliance inspections. There are usually many different titles associated to a single NOC code. As per
209.2(1)(a)(ii), employer must provide the foreign worker with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as, but not less favourable than, those in the same offer. So as long as the duties, education requirements, salary, etc. of the occupation continue to match the NOC code then there should be no requirement for changing the work permit, and therefore, no requirement to submit a new offer of employment through the Employer Portal. As per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act Regulations (IRPR), a foreign worker is only required to obtain a new work permit when the employer, work location or occupation changes. The employer is required [R209.2(1)(b)] to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection. For more information, see the section “Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions” in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website. We hope this information is of assistance

threads.subject: OPEN TO CLOSE WORK PERMIT -- REP-2020-2488
threads.question:
Hello,
General scenario: Work under implied status when we do open work permit to closed work permit.
If someone is working on PGWP (open work permit) with Employer A and has applied to a new closed work permit with employer B (based on LMIA under process-decision not received). Can he/she continue to work with employer A or Employer B on implied status or he/she has to stop working and can resume work after approval of a new closed work permit.
As per section 186(U) ofIRPR which states "until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date".
Based on this it seems that he/she can continue working with Employer A but I am not sure if I am interpreting this section accurately,
Please let me know if my interpretation is right or wrong and if wrong then what exactly 186 (u) states.
中 and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTioN: Please let me know if my interpretation is right or wrong and if wrong then what exactly 186 (u) states.
RESPoNSE: For your information, IRCC is moving away from using the term 'implied status' as it is not reflective of the status extended by law under R183(5) and the authority to work without a permit under R186(u). Soon, you will see the term
'maintained status' and 'authority to work' used on our public pages.
You are correct in your interpretation. The conditions imposed on the current work permit are carried over into the period of work authorized by R186(u). If a person holds an open work permit they may work for any employer, or occupation and location unless those are limited by conditions on the document. The holder can move to a new employer during the 'work without a permit' period and their employer would only be limited on issuance of the new employer-specific work permit.
If a person holds and employer-specific work permit and applies for an open work permit, they are limited to continueing to work for the original employer and occupation as those are the 'conditions' on the current work permit. They can move to a new employer after receiving the open work permit.

Dear
Please find below, the answers to your questions:
To ensure an officer that is assessing a file is “alert, alive and sensitive" to the best interests of the children included in the application, must the applicant request considerations under Section 25 in the cover letter or are officers directed to consider children as a standard file assessment protocol?
Humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) considerations, submitted in the context of a permanent resident status application must be assessed if requested by foreign national in Canada and can be assessed when requested by a foreign national overseas in line with wording of subsection 25(1) of the IRPA. Applicants have the burden of justifying the basis of their H&C submissions. The H&C decision must include an assessment of the best interests of any child directly affected by the decision.
The Minister can also exercise his own initiative (section 25.1(1) of the IRPA) but officers are not directed to consider children as a standard file assessment protocol. There is no obligation to include an assessment of the H&C (including the best interests of a child) but the Minister has discretion to approve deserving cases not covered by the legislation.
- Are children's best interests taken into consideration by default or only by default on H&C applications? Best interests of the child will be taken into consideration on H&C applications if the considerations related to the best interest of a child are sufficiently clear from the material submitted. For other applications, the onus is on the applicants to submit evidence and relevant information regarding the child's situation if they really want the decision maker to take it into account. As mentioned in the previous answer, the Minister can also exercise his discretion and own initiative (section 25.1(1) of the IRPA) but this is not an obligation. But on any other file (work permit, SINP, etc.), one must request H&C considerations? If applicants specifically request to have their H&C considerations considered, an assessment of these has to be provided in the decision. If there is no request for H&C considerations, the Minister can exercise his own initiative (section 25.1(1) of the IRPA) but it is not a standard file assessment protocol.

If there is a specific request for H&C considerations, the officer has an obligation to assess accordingly. The decision must include an assessment of the H&C considerations.
