### R215 (1) (f)(ïi) -- REP-2020-2528
Good day,
This is in response to your inquiry regarding the foreign national's eligibility to apply for a study permit from within Canada.
Foreign national, who is a visitor on implied status, may apply for a study permit from within Canada provided they have completed a course or program of study that was identified as a prerequisite for their admission program of study, and if they submit with their application both:
- a letter of acceptance received from a DLl before or after the completion of the prerequisite course that confirms the course is a prerequisite for admission to the main program
- proof of successful completion of the prerequisite course, such as a letter from the destination DLl explicitly confirming that the student has completed the prerequisite course or program of study or a notification of completion from the institution at which the prerequisite course was taken.
Foreign nationals are not eligible to apply for a study permit from within Canada if they are either of the following:
- unable to provide a letter of acceptance issued by a DLl either before or after the prerequisite course that proves the course is a prerequisite for entry to the main program admitted to a program with a language requirement, but a specific language training course or program is not specified in the letter of acceptance as a prerequisite for entry to the main program (for example, wording such as “must provide proof of English proficiency” does not indicate the need for a prerequisite)
Foreign nationals cannot start studying until they receive their study permit.
For more information on how to apply for a study permit if you are already in Canada as a visitor, visit the IRCC website-Study permit: How to apply

threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION: If a TRP/OWP holder submits an IMM5710 before expiry of the current TRP/OWP and checks off TRP and OWP as the reasons for the application, I understand from your below responses that there is no implied temporary TRP status (as that is conferred by s. 24 to which implied status doesn't apply) but does s.183 apply to the FN's work status-that is, can the foreign national continue to work under s.183 once the IMM5710is submitted and until a decision is reached?
RESPONSE: Paragraph 186(u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) governs the authority to work without a permit until a decision on an application submitted under section 201. The application for work permit renewal would trigger this authority and allow the person to continue to work under the conditions imposed on their current work permit. Therefore, in this situation since the request for renewal of the work permit is made before the expiry of the current permit, paragraph 186(u) of the IRPR would apply.
Please note that it is not section 183 of the IRPR that authorized the work without a permit during processing but paragraph 186(u).
Thank you,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/permits/subsequent-permits.html
RESPONSE: All Temporary Resident Permits (TRPs) are issued under section 24 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Therefore, there is no trigger of subsection 183(5) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) so the period of authorized stay is not extended during the processing time.
The difference between 'new' and 'subsequent' TRPs is that for the 'subsequent' TRP, there is no break in status as the application for the TRP was submitted prior expiry of the existing TRP. In this situation, if the decision on the TRP is made after the expiry of the existing TRP, IRCC will indicate that there was no break in continuity. As indicated in the Program Delivery Instruction: the client shouldn't suffer a break in status due to processing times. However, there is no regulatory coverage of that period as with a temporary resident extending their status under section 181 of the IRPR which triggers the extension of the period of authorized stay until a decision is made under subsection 183(5) of the IRPR.

Bonjour
Merci de nous avoir contacté avec votre demande. Veuillez trouver notre réponse ici-bas.
Question
l’employé est disposé a travailler à temps partiel, est-ce que l’employeur peut l’engager a temps partiel sur la base de l’offre
d'emploi confirmée à temps plein?
Ou faut-il que l’employeur fasse une nouvelle offre d’emploi à temps partiel sur le portail employeur et le TET fasse une nouvelle demande de permis de travail à temps partiel?
Réponse
L'employeur s’est engagé à respecter les conditions de travail propre à l’offre d'emploi actuel. Il a cependant l’option d'offrir
des alternatives qui sont essentiellement les mêmes mais non moins favorables.
Cela inclut les heures de travail ainsi que les heures supplémentaires.
Dans le cas où l'employeur décide de réduire le nombre d'heures au point ou l'employé passe d'un poste à temps plein à un poste à temps partiel, une nouvelle offre d'emploi devra être soumise par l'employeur. Par la suite le travailleur devra soumettre une demande de prorogation ou modification des conditions du permis de travail afin de le lier avec les conditions de la nouvelle offre. Cet option semble approprié au cas mentionné dans votre requête.
Il est important de noter que, dans l’optique ou un nouveau permis de travail est demandé, l'employeur est responsable de continuer à offrir un emploi selon les termes de l'offre lié au permis de travail actuel et ce jusqu'à la délivrance du nouveau permis.
Nous espérons que ceci répond à vos questions.
Cordialement,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

Full-time post-secondary students may work without a work permit on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student [R186(f)]. This authorization is valid for the period for which they hold a study permit at the institution and during which they are enrolled in full-time studies.
"On-campus" is defined as employment facilities within the boundaries of the campus. The students are only allowed to work on the campus of the educational institution at which they are registered in full-time studies. If an institution has more than one campus, the student can work at different locations on those campuses provided they are within the same municipality. If an institution has campuses in different cities, the student is restricted to working on the institution's campus where they are registered as a full-time student.
Students may work on campus as teaching or research assistants and may be located at a library, hospital, or research facility affiliated with the institution, but located outside the physical boundaries of the institution's campus. This is allowed provided that the work is strictly related to the student's research grant.

threads.question:
beyond April 30, 2020? -- REP-2020-2438
Good day,
Students who started short programs (8 to 12 months in length) in the spring, summer or fall 2020 semester may complete their entire program of study outside of Canada and still maintain post-graduation work permit eligibility, provided that they meet all the other applicable program requirements. These students are exempt from the requirement to complete at least 50% of their program of study in Canada and in class.

threads.subject: Inquiry about refugee application withdrawals -- REP-2020-2761
threads.question:
Hello
If a client has been issued an Acknowledgement of Claim (AOC), they are considered to have made a claim. However, at any point prior to the referral of a claim to the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), or the determination that the claim is not eligible for referral, the client may withdraw their claim to IRCC or CBSA. Such a withdrawal is not considered a withdrawal for the purposes of paragraph A101(1)(c) of IRPA. This means that if the person concerned makes a refugee claim at a later date, it cannot be determined ineligible under A101(1)(c).

threads.answer:
outside of Canada? -- REP-2020-2841
Hello,
QUESTION: Or can the WP extension be uploaded on a day that the TFW is outside of Canada on a short, temporary trip?
RESPoNSE: In order to complete the Application to Change Conditions or Extend my Stay or Remain in Canada as a Worker (IMM 5710) the applicant must be physically in Canada. Section 199 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations states: A foreign national may apply for a work permit after entering Canada... If the foreign national is presently outside of Canada, they have not entered Canada before this particular application and there is no guarantee that they will be authorized to enter Canada on their return.
The IMM 5710 is an application to 'extend my stay or remain' in Canada, since the foreign national is not presently in Canada they have no period of authorized stay to extend since it ended on their departure from Canada as per R183(4)(a).
In addition, the IMM 5710 asks for the applicants 'current country or territory of residence' and indicates that the Country or Territory should be 'Canada'. If the applicant is not actually present in Canada for immigration purposes it is not their 'current country' and therfore, they would be misrepresenting a material fact.

threads.subject: for approval-Study and Work Permit at the same -- REP-2020-2850
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Can a study hold a work permit and study permit at the same time? If yes, can he work full-time on his work permit and claim that work experience for his PR application? If yes, must he study part-time on his study permit or he can study full-time and still be able to claim points for education and work experience while working on a work permit?
Answer:
Yes, a student can hold a study permit and a work permit at the same time. However, pursuant to paragraph 87.1(3)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) states, any period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) nor shall the student's work be awarded CRS points for Canadian work experience, unless the study program is part time (less than 15 hours and the school can substantiate that fact).
Please note the onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements of the program.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

mailbox
1. one of the changes is that authorized representatives cannot perform translations of documents. What about an incidence where the documents were translated by a certified translator overseas and a notary certificate was attached but the notary certificate had stamps that are not in English and not translated or sometimes I have had cases where the entire statement from the notary was written in a foreign language. Usually it's just fixing a deficiency that was done overseas and cannot be easily rectified once the documents are in Canada with the principal applicant. "If the translation is being done in Canada, applicants should use the services of a certified translator who is in good standing with their provincial or territorial organization and certified to translate documents". Also stated in the PDI, the definition of a 'certified translator' is: "... a member in good standing whose certification can be confirmed by a seal or stamp that shows the translator's membership number of a professional translation association in Canada or abroad" The notary certificates is considered the same as an affidavit? As stated in the instructions, the affidavit must also be translated "In all situations, supporting documents that are in a language other than English or French must be accompanied by an official translation of the original document, or of a certified copy of the original document in English or French. 2. For international certified translations, those originating from many countries, don't have a regulated translators (no membership number). As such, the stamps are from the employment location or agency not from the translator. In Canada, most translators are self-employed. I am not certain how the quoted policy applies in this case from reading the website. Does Canada accept foreign translations done in accordance with the policies of other countries? For
example, the notary does not write "I certify this is a true copy" on the copy but rather on the notary certificate, for example. It is done that with documents originating from Ukraine and Russia usually.
For international translations, the PDI states the following "If the translation is being done outside of Canada, applicants should use the services of a translator who is accredited (officially recognized or authorized) in the country where the translation is being completed.
Also, "in situations where the translation cannot be provided by a certified translator, it must be accompanied by an affidavit swearing to the accuracy of the translation and the language proficiency of the translator."
The translation of either the original or certified true copy should be part of the translation. The stamp/seal in question (which is not in English) is the stamp confirming that the document is a certified true copy? If this is the case, then the stamp/seal would also have to be translated to English/French. As stated in the PDI – "All stamps and seals that are not in English or French must also be translated. " allowing the office to compare the notified true copy with the notary certificate.
3. I noticed also that many translation agencies operating overseas do not stamp every single page of the copy nor of the translation. This has never been an issue with applications submitted in the past but wondering if it will be in the future? "When a certified copy of the original document is submitted, the accompanying translation must be of the certified copy and the translator must stamp both the certified copy and the translation". Please note, it does not speak to every page having to be stamped.
Please refer to the Program Delivery Instructions on Translation of supporting documents for applications-Canada.ca for more information.

threads.subject: COOP WP -- REP-2020-2729
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I know that IRCC is working on addressing the issue of COOP WP applications made outside of Canada. What would be a proper way for a students to apply for COOP WP if they are outside of Canada?
The liaison officer suggested to make an application from within Canada and add an explanation letter. However those applications are being refused. Work permit application made outside of Canada are being processed slowly or not at all and some students (returning students who are currently in their home country) may not have biometrics and in some places biometric collection is reserved for study permit applications or family reunification PR applications only
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Apply for a co-op work permit from outside Canada
If students already applied for a study permit, but haven't yet travelled to Canada, they need to apply for a co-op work permit. A co-op work permit will let them complete the work placement they need to graduate.
If they apply for their co-op work permit from outside Canada and arrive in Canada before IRCC can process it, they will need to ask us to send their work permit once it's approved.
Apply with your study permit
If students haven't already applied for a study permit, they can apply for a co-op work permit at the same time.
The acceptance letter from a designated learning institution must confirm that a co-op or internship placement is part of the program's curriculum. They can then apply for a study permit and we'll process their co-op work permit with study permit application at the same time.
For more information, please visit our website.
Thank you and have a great day,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Dear
Please accept our apologies for not responding sooner. Please find below our responses to your questions.
Question 1: If a work permit holder comes in advance of her family to Canada, has established in Canada and now wants her husband and children to join her in Canada, then can the spouse and children travel to Canada from Europe showing evidence of their relationship to the foreign worker and proof of her establishment in Canada? Or, do they need to apply for a travel authorization letter? Or, do they need to apply for a spousal work permit and children's study permit at the visa office and then travel with that? Currently they don't have pre-approval letters because they are visa-exempt nationals.
Response: The Order exempts immediate family members of Canadians, permanent residents, and persons registered as an Indian under the Indian Act from the travel restrictions, but it does not explicitly exempt spouses or common-law partners and dependent children of foreign workers from the travel restrictions. Therefore, in order to enter Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic, family members of foreign workers (spouses, common-law partners and dependent children) must meet both of the following criteria:
1. be specifically exempt from the travel restrictions under the Order in their own right (for example, hold a work permit as per paragraph 3(1)(l) of the Order or work permit approval letter as per paragraph 3(1)(m) of the Order). If they are not otherwise exempt, they need to obtain a written authorization—an FRL—to enter Canada under the following exemption of the Order: o 3(1)(b) a person who is authorized, in writing, by an officer designated under subsection 6(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to enter Canada for the purpose of reuniting immediate family members;
2. be entering for a non-discretionary reason. There are separate program delivery instructions that explain what constitutes non-discretionary travel for holders of work permits and work permit approval letters. For those seeking to qualify under the family reunification exemption, the non-discretionary reason will be examined by an IRCC officer when they assess if an FRL can be issued, by Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers at boarding, if available, and by border services officers upon entry at the port of entry (POE).
If the family members did not apply as a group (for example, one of the parents has a valid work permit and is in Canada, but their dependants are overseas), the dependants will have to self-identify to obtain an FRL from IRCC. Dependants of a foreign national can request an FRL from IRCC to be exempt from travel restrictions. Foreign nationals who present themselves at check-in for a flight to Canada without the appropriate authorization letter will not be boarded.
If a dependant of a foreign worker is already exempt under a separate provision of the Order, there is no need for the officer to assess the need for an FRL. For example, a foreign worker who received a letter of introduction (LOl) and has
Cioyenneté Canada an active job offer and is seeking to reunite with their immediate family member does not require an FRL from IRCC. They are already exempt under the Order as an LOl holder and already meet the non-discretionary travel test as they have an active job offer from an employer that is currently operating.
If a spouse or common-law partner of a foreign worker is seeking entry to Canada for the purpose of reuniting with them, they must also qualify for an exemption under the Order. What is important is whether they really are a spouse of the temporary resident in Canada. In addition, the officer should consider whether their purpose of travel is non-discretionary (meaning they are establishing themselves for the duration of their spouse's permit in Canada) so that the foreign national will not be refused entry to Canada for failing the non-discretionary test at the POE.
If a family member's purpose of travel to Canada is to work, only then does their work permit situation become relevant. If they received an LOl for an open work permit, are accompanying or joining the principal applicant, and plan to establish themselves in Canada, they do not need proof that a job offer is lined up for them after the 14-day quarantine period. The LOl allows them to meet an exemption under subsection 3(1) of the Order, and establishing themselves with their spouse enables them to pass the non-discretionary test.
Study permit applicants whose letter of acceptance is from a designated learning institution (DLl) on the list of institutions with an approved COVID-19 readiness plan do not require written authorization.
Study permit applicants whose letter of acceptance is from a DLl that is not on the list of institutions with an approved COVID-19 readiness plan require written authorization to travel
Please refer to the following useful links:
How to unite with immediate family members who are in Canada temporarily
How to request a written authorization
Question 2: What is the email address for the travel authorization letter? I’m familiar with the email address for such letters where the person in Canada is a citizen/permanent resident. However, do we use the same email address when the principal family member in Canada is on a work permit?
Response: Please refer to the following IRCC web pages for information on:
- How to unite with immediate family members who are in Canada temporarily How to request a written authorization
Question 3: If a French citizen who possesses a valid LMiA now applies online for a work permit and receives a work permit approval letter to travel to Canada, then can his French citizen spouse and children accompany him to Canada on his trip to activate his work permit (and settle in Canada)? Or, do they have to join him at a later date after he's established in Canada? If they are able to travel with him, then do they need to apply for their own separate letters of introduction from the visa office (ie. file an application for an open spousal work permit and study permit) even if they are French visa-exempt nationals and don't really need these items?
Response: Family members can either accompany the principal applicant or join him/her at a later date provided that they are eligible for one of the exemptions under the OIC Minimizing the Risk of Exposure to COVID-19 in Canada Order (Prohibition of Entry into Canada from any Country other than the United States/Attachment). Please refer to Q1 for more details.
Best regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Passport related matters for visa application -- REP-2020-2315
threads.question:
Good day,
Yes, it is possible to request a replacement TRV counterfoil be affixed to a client's new passport so long as it is still valid. A replacement counterfoil would be issued to the original validity of the document. If the foreign national would prefer a TRV with a different validity, they would need to submit a new application and pay the associated fees.
In order to request a replacement counterfoil, clients can submit a web form request indicating the type of enquiry
(Replacement Documents, Amendments to documents and Verification of status documents) and simply provide the
supporting rationale and both the residential address and mailing address in the 'Your enquiry' field. Once the appropriate office receives the request, they will send the client instructions on how to pay the $30 and where to submit their original passport and self-addressed stamped (traceable means only) envelope.
If the information about the client's place of birth was not communicated in their original TRV application, they would not be eligible for a replacement TRV; they will need to submit a new application given information was not part of the original assessment of the client's application.
We do recommend the client get a new passport with the correct place of birth as it would help avoid any complications when applying as well as when travelling.
Otherwise, we recommend that the client, upon applying for a new TRV, note their correct place of birth on their application, present an explanation of their situation, proof that they are in the process of applying for a new passport with the correct information (if applicable), and that they submit a certified copy of their birth certificate as a supporting document.
Please note that failure to present this information would constitute misrepresentation and may lead to a 5 year exclusion order.
If they do travel with the passport with the incorrect place of birth, we also recommend that they carry a certified copy of their birth certificate with them when they travel as supporting evidence to avoid the possibility of being found inadmissible for misrepresentation.
I hope this provides some clarity.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

When a TRV applicant receives their COPR from IRCC, in order to enter into Canada with a temporary status, they must apply for either a temporary visa or an ETA (according to their country of origin).

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
1. Are foreign translators allowed to provide these translations? The website says translators in Canada and abroad but the definition of certified translators only list those who are in Canada. If the translations are being done in Canada, applicants should use the services of a certified translator who is in good standing with their provincial or territorial organization and certified to translate documents. If the translation is being done outside of Canada, applicants should use the services of a translator who is accredited (officially recognized or authorized) in the country where the translation is being completed. Should the accuracy of the translation appear suspect, IRCC reserves the right to request a retranslation by a different translator.
2. If foreign translators are allowed, what is the definition of a certified translator abroad? Do they have to be certified by the Canadian embassy, belong to a translation group, etc.? A certified translator is someone who is accredited (officially recognized or authorized) in the country where the translation is being completed. The certified translator is a member in good standing of a professional translation association in Canada or abroad. Their certification number must be confirmed by a seal or stamp that shows the translator's membership number. A translator who is in the process of receiving their certification or accreditation is not considered a certified translator for IRCC's purposes.
3. Chinese documents are usually translated by the Notary office in China. Will these be acceptable translations? Immigration Officers are familiar with translations provided by the Notary office in China and these are deemed acceptable. We trust that this information will assist you. Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
In order to provide immigration advice or representation for consideration, an individual must be authorized under section 91(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or under section 21.1 of the Citizenship Act. This includes:
- A lawyer who is a member in good standing of a law society of a province, or a notary who is a member in good standing of the Chambre des notaires du Quebec
- Any other member in good standing of a law society of a province or the Chambre des notaires du Quebec, including a paralegal
- A member, in good standing, of the Immigration Consultants of Canada Regulatory Council (ICCRC). Paid employees of Non-Governmental Organizations (NGO) and Service Provider Organizations (SPO) are compensated for their work, including when they are providing immigration advice, and so must be authorized under section 91(2) of IRPA or section 21.1 of the Citizenship Act. Therefore, in order to provide immigration or citizenship advice or representation, paid NGO/SPO employees must also be members, in their own right, of a Canadian provincial/territorial law society, the Chambre des notaires du Quebec or the ICCRC. This applies regardless of whether or not the organization paying the employee receives funding from IRCC, and regardless of whether or not the organization or employee receives a direct fee from the client. The ultimate goal of IRPA s91 is to protect clients by ensuring that those providing advice and representation have the level of professional expertise necessary to assist in often complex immigration and citizenship matters. Note that while paid employees cannot provide immigration or citizenship advice or representation, they can provide immigration or citizenship information, including administrative help. Anyone (including paid NGO/SPO employees) is allowed to provide immigration information, such as directing someone to the IRCC website; helping someone to use a computer to view/upload or download an application form; and providing administrative support in completing IRCC application forms such as transcribing responses provided by an applicant into IRCC applications forms and translating a document or providing a verbal translation for someone. Attached you will find a document which provides additional information regarding the provision of immigration and citizenship information by paid NGO/SPO employees. It includes examples of immigration advice versus immigration information, as well as example scenarios. We trust that this responds to your query.
Regards,

threads.subject: Adding non-accompanying spouse after e-APR in Express Entry -- REP-2020-2774
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Can a principal applicant make his non-accompanying spouse (currently staying with PA in Canada on a temporary status) as now accompanying after e-APR under Express Entry? Will this cause recalculation of CRS points? Is this practice valid to gain more CRS points?
Answer: Yes, family members can be added to the application at any time during the process, but must be added prior to obtaining permanent resident status. All family members must be examined as part of the electronic application for permanent residence, whether they are accompanying the principal applicant or not. The differing points grid in Express Entry was developed to reflect the increased economic success in Canada seen where the principal applicant has a spouse possessing certain competencies. IRCC does not support the use of these provisions in any kind of “strategic" way. We recommend that spouses who intend to live together in Canada, state that in their applications. Changing the partner's status from “non-accompanying" to “accompanying" during the processing of an application, up to the time of landing, may not constitute misrepresentation; however, this choice was never intended to be used as a strategy. Rather, it allows families to accurately describe their situation and intentions and to comply with section 16 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act on the obligation to answer truthfully. Therefore, the principal applicant's Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score will be recalculated to account for the change in situation, at all points in the process.
We trust that this information will assist you.

The authorization to work under R186(w) only applies to students who applied for their work permit prior to their study permit expiry date. Graduates who applied for a PGWP while under implied status are not eligible to work while waiting for a decision on their PGWP.

There are some key points for consideration:
Length of the program (For example 8 months = 8 months validity for PGWP) Program of study hours completed (For example 900 hours = 8 months validity for PGWP)
For example:
1. An eligible 900 hour program of study would correspond to an eight month OWP;
2. An eligible 1,350 hour program of study would correspond to a 12 month OWP; and
3. An eligible 1,800 hour program of study would correspond to a 3 year OWP (as per the PGWP policy that completion of a two+ year program of study results in eligibility for a three year OwP).

with an additional one (1) month of OWP access. For example, a 1,000 hour program would result in the issuance of a 9 month OWP (i.e., 1,000/112 = 8.9 months). Officers will round up to the next full month.

threads.subject: CRS Points-Express Entry -- REP-2021-0012
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
I am a Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant registered under
I would like to have your clarification for the following:
The Express Entry system calculates the points for work experience based on months. For example, if a person started working on Jan 31 2020, when it's December 1, 2020, the system will calculate the points based on one year of work experience as the system will calculate points based on the period January to December (12 months). We know that the client would not have a year of work experience yet at that point yet.
When considering the Canadian Experience Class, if the client receives an invitation to apply in that condition, but completes that full 12 months by the time of the submission, would their application be accepted? Or should we wait for the full completion of one year to accept an invitation to apply?
Thank you for your clarification.
Warm regards,
mmigration, Refugees Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
The Express Entry system calculates the points for work experience based on months. For example, if a person started working on Jan 31 2020, when it's December 1, 2020, the system will calculate the points based on one year of work experience as the system will calculate points based on the period January to December (12 months). We know that the client would not have a year of work experience yet at that point yet.
When considering the Canadian Experience Class, if the client receives an invitation to apply in that condition, but completes that full 12 months by the time of the submission, would their application be accepted? Or should we wait for the full completion of one year to accept an invitation to apply?
Answer:
The IRCC system calculates work experience by calculating months and not actual days worked in the month. IRCC is aware some applicants are receiving an ITA a month or two early and we advise the candidate not to delay their eAPR or turn down the invitation if the work experience is continuing. If the work genuinely ended before accumulating one year of work however, they should decline the invitation.
IRCC examining officers are aware of this, and when looking at the application they will take into consideration factors such as the continuous work status, the Offer of Employment Letter from the same employer, and whether the applicant reached the experience required by the time the application is processed.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Hello,
1) If a student who is currently on scheduled break (May-Aug 2020), however, their Fall semester (Sept. to Dec.2020) have
been suspended due to covid-19. Would students in this case be allowed to work off-campus for 20 hrs/week during the suspended fall 2020 semester? Also, would students in this situation have to change their status within 150 days if they continue to remain in Canada (considering their last classes was in April 17, 2020 and will restart their semester in Jan 2021)? If so, when would the 150 days begin: from April 2020 (last classes) or Aug 2020 (end of scheduled break)? You can continue to work even if COVID-19 has forced you to become a part-time student or take a break in studies if you were:
- a full-time student, and
- authorized to work on or off campus while you studied
If you're working off campus, you can work up to 20 hours per week during an academic session. You can work full time during scheduled breaks in the academic year. You don't need to tell us if you're taking an authorized leave, but you do need to provide proof that your leave is authorized and that it's no longer than 150 days, if we ask for it. More information can be found at this link: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/prepare-arrival/study-permit-conditions.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/prepare-arrival/study-permit-conditions.html)
2) For students who are going to be studying online from their home countries for Fall 2020 term, would these students require at minimum a study permit approval in principle to count their time towards PGWP eligibility? Foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than 6 months in duration at a Canadian designated learning institution (DLl). Therefore, they require an approved study permit prior to the end of their studies for this time to be counted towards their PGWP.
3) Would visitors in situation below (i.e. eligible to apply for their study permits to be processed within Canada), who are begin their studies while their study permit application is being processed, be able count the time studied while awaiting for a decision on their study permit application towards their PGWP.
a.Foreign nationals who are in Canada as visitors and are authorized to apply for a study permit from within Canada under section R215(1)(f) may begin their studies once they have submitted their study permit application, provided the application has been submitted before the expiry of their visitor status. They are required to cease studying if their study permit application is refused. threads.subject: Fédération des cégeps-Étudiants mineurs accompagnateurs d'un étudiant international (parent) -- REP-2020-
threads.question:
Bonjour,
La présente est en réponse à votre message du 27 janvier 2021.
Tel qu'indiqué sur le site web d'IRCC, les enfants mineurs qui souhaitent étudier au Canada doivent présenter une demande de permis d’études avant leur entrée au Canada. Ceci comprend les enfants mineurs qui sont accompagnés de leurs parents qui possèdent déjà un permis d’études ou de travail valide.
Si les enfants viennent au Canada en compagnie de leurs parents qui sont titulaires d’un permis d’études ou d’un permis de travail valide, ils n'ont pas besoin de fournir une lettre d’acceptation d'un établissement lorsqu'ils présentent une demande de permis d'études.
Un enfant mineur d’un parent qui n’est pas autorisé à travailler ou à étudier au Canada (par exemple, un parent qui est au Canada à titre de visiteur) n’est pas admissible à étudier au Canada sans permis d’études. Ces enfants mineurs doivent demander un permis d’études à partir de leur pays de dernière résidence permanente.
Les permis d’études pour les élèves du primaire sont délivrés pour une période d’un an et peuvent être renouvelés, alors que les permis d’études délivrés aux élèves inscrits à une école secondaire (de la 9º à la 12º année dans toutes les provinces et tous les territoires à l’exception du Québec, et de la 9º à la 11º année au Québec) peuvent se voir délivrer un permis pour la durée totale prévue de leurs études dans une école secondaire du Canada (maximum de quatre ans).
Les enfants mineurs qui fréquentent la maternelle et les classes préscolaires ne sont pas tenus d’avoir un permis d’études valide.
Important : De manière générale, les personnes qui demandent un permis d’études, y compris celles qui étudient aux niveaux primaire et secondaire, doivent fournir une lettre d’acceptation de l’établissement d’enseignement en question au Canada. Les demandeurs peuvent fournir soit la lettre d’acceptation originale soit une lettre sur support électronique.
Il existe une exception à cette exigence : Les enfants mineurs qui accompagnent un membre de la famille qui a demandé un permis de travail ou un permis d’études avant d’entrer au Canada et se l’est vu accorder ne sont pas tenus de fournir une lettre d’acceptation d’un établissement d’enseignement.
Nous espérons que ces renseignements vous seront utiles.
Merci,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

I am an RCICand I need your assistance on the below: Can a student apply for PGWP while awaiting his or her study permit extension?
A student can apply if they have a valid study permit. If the student is on implied status, meaning waiting for their study permit to be processed/extended and applies for a PGWP, they would not be able to work until they receive the PGWP.
For e.g. a student has applied for his study permit extension prior to the expiration of his previous study permit and has now successfully completed his pending course while the study permit extension is still in process. Please see
the below timeline for easy reference:
- Previous study permit was valid until March 31, 2020
- Applied for study permit extension before March 20, 2020 Pending course completed on August 17, 2020 Official transcript and graduation letter are dated September 20, 2020
- The study permit extension is still under process giving the student an implied status
Considering the above scenario and the study permit is still in process, would the student have to apply for PGWP within 90 days from the date of official transcripts/graduation letter; i.e., from September 20, 2020 to December 20, 2020, in order to work full-time after PGWP application? OR the student can wait for the new study permit and apply for PGWP and still can work full-time after PGWP application, as the new study permit will have a new validity period and the 90 days rule will not be applicable in this case?
The student does not have to wait until they physically receive their diploma or attend their graduation ceremony to apply for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP).
All you need to apply for a PGWP is
an official letter from your school that confirms you've completed your study program, and
- an official transcript, or a copy of your transcript from your school's website.
Students have 18o days after their school issues their final marks to apply for a post-graduation work permit. To be eligible for a PGWP, their study permit must have been valid at some point during these 180 days. The study permit will expire on the date marked on the permit or 90 days after the day you complete your studies, whichever comes first. Students can work full-time while waiting for a decision on their post-graduation work permit application if, at the time you submitted their
application, they had a valid study permit and completed their program of study.

threads.subject: 12 month bar H&C applications, applicability to dependent children -- REP-2020-2766
threads.question:
Good day,
I have a client (principal applicant-PA), for whom I am in the process of putting together an H&C application. PA has two daughters, years old, who can be included in her application as dependent children who are presently in Canada.
PA just informed me that her ex-husband recently entered Canada and intends to file a refugee claim, with the assistance of another lawyer. PA's husband wants to include the two daughters in his refugee claim, given that they too were affected by the persecution he suffered (but not the PA, she was already separated from the ex-husband at the time of the events).
Can the daughters still be included in PA's H&C application, or must they choose between their mother's H&C and their father's refugee claim? I am obviously aware of the prohibition on submitting an H&C application while a refugee claim is in process and the 12 month bar following a negative refugee decision; but in this case, it is the dependent children, and not the PA, who would have a pending refugee claim. There is no guidance in the H&C operational bulletin. ([https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-) manuals/permanent-residence/humanitarian-compassionate-consideration/intake-who-may-apply.htiml#refugee-claim)
Please advise. Thanks!
Page 1720
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Good day
In your query, you wish to know whether a person – specifically, your client's two daughters – may be included as a dependent in both a refugee claim and an H&C application at the same time. You note that, while it is clear from the Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs) that a principal applicant cannot submit an H&C application while a refugee claim is in process and for 12 months following, this is not as clear in the case of the dependent children.
Respons e
The bar on applying for H&C while a refugee claim is in process and for 12 months following applies equally to dependents as it does to the principal applicant. The daughters cannot be included in both the H&C application and the refugee claim at the same time and will have to choose between their mother's H&C application and their father's refugee claim.
Note that, if the daughters choose to not file a refugee claim at this time and their father receives a positive decision on his claim and goes on to file an application for permanent residence as a protected person, he may include the daughters in his application for permanent residence at that time provided that they still meet the definition of“family member" in R1(3).
Similarly, if the daughters choose not to be included in their mother's H&C application at this time, their mother may ask to have them added to the H&C application at any point before it is finalized provided the bar on H&C does not continue to apply to the
daughters and that they continue to meet the definition offamily member" in R1(3).
Background
A review of the exceptions to applying for H&C contained in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) under A25(1.2) (known as the H&C bar) reveals that this section does not distinguish between the principal claimant and/or applicant and their dependents. Instead, this section lays out the exceptions to applying H&C in reference to the foreign national, a status
that applies to both the principal applicant and their dependents. For example, the section states,
A25(1.2) The Minister may not examine the request if
(b) the foreign national has made a claim for refugee protection that is pending before the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division
Thus, it is becomes clear that this section of the Act applies to both the principal applicant and any dependents who wish to request H&C consideration.
Furthermore, when filing a refugee claim as a family, it is important to note that, while the claims may be joined, each person is
distinguished as an individual in the IRB decision as all have technically made a claim for protection. In other words, a dependent is considered a claimant in their own right rather than just an extra element of the principal claimant's claim. Thus, if the children's father includes his two daughters in his refugee claim, besides the father, the two daughters will also be considered to have a pending refugee claim.
Bringing these two elements together, it becomes clear that, if the daughters were to be included in their father's refugee claim, they would fall under the description of foreign nationals who have made a claim for refugee protection that is pending before the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division. Thus A25(1.2) would apply and the daughters would be barred from applying for H&C.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Changes to compensation due to fluctuations in exchange rate -- REP-2020-2857
threads.question:
Good day
Thank you for reaching out to us about salaries and benefits paid in foreign currencies. You will find below the answers to your questions.
I understand that an employer is responsible for providing a foreign worker with wages that are substantially the
same but not less favourable than those in the offer of employment.
That is correct.
In the case where an employer is providing wages or allowances to an foreign worker, and the amount of the wages or allowances are converted from a foreign currency to Canadian currency, would the employer continue to be compliant if the Canadian value of the allowances decreased as a result of fluctuations in the exchange rate between
the foreign currency and the Canadian currency?
When submitting a job offer, the employer will indicate the Canadian wage that will be paid to the foreign national. If this salary is paid in a foreign currency, it must be identified under the "alternative compensation scheme" section of the offer and the conversion of the foreign currency into Canadian currency will be added under the wage section of the offer. The conversion must be made only at the time of the offer and must not be modified even if the exchange rate of the two currencies changes.
For example, if the applicant was eligible for an international assignment allowance of USD$500 per month, and at the time of application the allowance was noted in the Offer of Employment as CAD$700 based on the exchange rate at the time, if 6 months into the assignment, the allowance decreases to CAD$650 due to fluctuations in the exchange rate, how would IRCC view this change? In this case, as long as it was determined under the "alternate compensation scheme" that the allowance was set at US$500 and at the time of reporting the conversion equaled to C$700, the employer will have to continue to pay the amount of US$500 without adjusting the exchange rate.
Would the employer still be considered compliant since the exchange rates are outside of their control? The employer will continue to pay the same amount in foreign currency as indicated in the offer.
The same question can be asked about fluctuations that occur due to changes in the EPF Statutory Rate that impact the amount of allowance a foreign worker receives. Would pre-emptively indicating in the Offer of Employment that the foreign worker's wages and allowances are subject to fluctuations in the exchange rate address any compliance issues that could arise from decreases or increases in the value of the wages or allowances caused by these fluctuations. The same would be true in this scenario, and the foreign currency indicated in the job offer should be the same and no less favorable even if the exchange rates between the two currencies change.
Please note that in all cases that the employer must comply with provincial labour legislations.
We trust you will find this information useful.
and Cizenship Caneda
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: question sur un permis d études -- REP-2020-1491
threads.question:
Cioyenneté Canada
Bonjour à vous,
Un étudiant étranger m’a contacté pour me poser des questions et je ne suis pas certaine de mes réponses.
Description de la situation: Un Cégep du Québec a signé une entente avec une école privé étrangère afin de pouvoir donner des cours aux étudiants des pays étranger. L’établissement donnera deux sessions de cours (automne et hiver) respectant les critères d’enseignement du Cégep. Les étudiants pourront se voir décerner une attestation d’études collégiales du Cegep du Québec à condition de compléter un stage chez un employeur au Québec. Ainsi, les étudiants étudieront dans l’établissement étranger deux sessions et à la 3 e session, ils viendront au Canada pour compléter leur stage obligatoire.Une fois le stage terminé, ils pourront recevoir une attestation collégiale du Cégep. Ils demanderont donc un permis d’études et un permis Coop lors de la venue pour leur stage.
Mes questions sont :
1) Est ce que le temps passé hors Canada sera admissible au permis de travail post diplome ou bien seulement le temps passé en stage sera admissible (étant dionné que le diplome est décerné par le Cégep )?
2) Si seulement le temps passé au Canada est admissible ,faudrait il que le stage ait une durée minimum de 8 mois afin de décrocher un permis post diplome (sachant que la durée minimume d’un post diplome est de 8 mois ) ?
3) Si le stage dure 8 mois en mode continuel (donc aucun congé ), est ce que les agents vont considérer les période supposées de congé ? Par exemple, si le stage dure de juillet à février, est ce que la période de juillet et aout va etre calculée ou bien les agents vont considérer ces deux mois comme des congés habituels scolaires donc considérer une période de 6 mois au lieu de 8 mois ?
Merci beaucoup pour votre réponses
Cordialement
mmigration, Refugees
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Merci d’avoir contacter IRCC. Vous trouverez les réponses à vos questions ci-dessous :
1) Est ce que le temps passé hors Canada sera admissible au permis de travail post diplôme ou bien seulement le temps passé en stage sera admissible (étant donné que le diplôme est décerné par le Cégep )? Le temps passé hors du Canada ne sera pas admissible au permis de travail postdiplôme même si les études sont faites à une institution canadienne. Sauf dans des circonstances particulière (COVID-19), le temps passé hors du Canada ne compte généralement pas en vers l’admissibilité au programme de permis de travail postdiplôme.
2) Si seulement le temps passé au Canada est admissible, faudrait-il que le stage ait une durée minimum de 8 mois afin de décrocher un permis postdiplôme (sachant que la durée minimum d’un post diplôme est de 8 mois)? Si le temps passé au Canada est uniquement pour compléter un stage, ce temps ne compte pas vers la période admissible au permis de travail postdiplôme. Si l’étudiant complète une partie de ces cours au Canada, un minimum de huit mois est requis afin d’être admissible à un permis de travail postdiplôme.
3) Si le stage dure 8 mois en mode continuel (donc aucun congé), est ce que les agents vont considérer les période supposées de congé ? Par exemple, si le stage dure de juillet à février, est ce que la période de juillet et aout va etre calculée ou bien les agents vont considérer ces deux mois comme des congés habituels scolaires donc considérer une période de 6 mois au lieu de 8 mois ? Dans le cas où un étudiant étudie au Canada pendant une tel période, les congés scolaires prévus au calendrier (comme ceux prévus l’hiver et l’été) ne seront pas soustraits de la durée du permis de travail postdiplôme. Si vous avez d’autres questions, n’hésitez pas à consulter notre site web ou de nous contacter encore. Cordialement,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

Foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of 6 months' duration or less [R188(1)(c)]. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months). However, (IRCC) recognizes that long-term visitors and foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting 6 months or less at any time during their stay in Canada.
It is recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards. threads.subject: ACQUIRED WORK EXPERIENCE IN QUEBEC-Home Child Care Provider Pilot and Home Support
threads.question:
Worker Pilot -- REP-2020-2718
Greetings,
Please accept our apologies for the delay in responding to your enquiry. You will find below the answers to your questions.
1. Can a Home Child Care Provider ( CNP 4411 OR 4412) who acquired her work experience- 24 months in the province of Quebec apply for PR under the Pilot and Home Support Worker Pilot ? Given that she genuinely has the intention to move outside Quebec. Actually her intention is that once she obtains her open work permit is to find a job in same category outside Quebec and fully move outside Quebec.
Based on the information provided, the question appears to be for a caregiver who acquired 24 months work experience in the province of Quebec, who intends to move outside of Quebec once she obtains her permanent residence. Only applicants who indicate on their Schedule 19a-Home Child Care Provider (HCCP) or Home Support Worker (HSW)- Education and Language Assessment [IMM 5982] that they have not yet completed at least 24 months experience are issued an occupation-restricted open work permit under the HCCP/HSW Pilots (TR-to-PR process). Those who indicate that they have already met the work experience requirement are not be issued this occupation-restricted work permit, though they could be eligible for a bridging open work permit (straight-to-PR process).
The work experience gained in the province of Quebec can count as qualifying experience for caregivers applying under the straight-to-PR process, provided it otherwise meets all other criteria. Please refer to the Program Delivery Instructions specific to the Qualifying Canadian work experience for more details on what constitutes eligible experience. Caregivers applying under the TR-to-PR process will receive an occupation-restricted open work permit that will have the following condition: "may not engage in employment in the province of Quebec".
To note, all officers assessing applications submitted under Federal economic immigration programs are required to assess the intent of the applicant to reside outside Quebec as a permanent resident, under terms of jurisdiction governing selection of economic immigrants outlined in the Canada-Quebec Accord. For this reason, immigrants applying under the federal Economic Class programs must intend to establish in Canada outside Quebec, and must satisfy an officer regarding that intent. Assessing the genuineness of intent to reside can be supported by a range of documents/information, including but not limited to the applicant's own declaration or affidavit of intent, job offers, rental agreements, home purchases or utility bills from outside of Quebec. It is up to the applicant to provide sufficient proof to satisfy the officer that they intend to reside outside of Quebec as a permanent resident.
2. when is the program re opening ? and what is the quota for 2021?
The HCCP and HSW Pilots' caps are counted per calendar year. Therefore, caps were reset to zero (and the HCCP Pilot reopened) on January 1st, 2021.
As indicated in IRCC's Help Centre answer to the question Is there a limit on the number of caregiver applications you accept under the pilots?, we process up to 5,500 applications each year under the caregiver pilots: •2,750 applications for the Home Child Care Provider Pilot •2,750 applications for the Home Support Worker Pilot
We trust this answers your questions.
Thank you kindly,

Spouses and common-law partners of post-graduation work permit holders, including the new public policy 18 month open work permit, may be eligible to apply for an open work permit under the C41 exemption for (spouses and common-law partners of skilled workers). A dependent spouse or common-law partner is eligible to apply for an open work permit under Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemption code C41 if the principal foreign worker
- holds a work permit that is valid for a period of at least 6 months, or, if working under the authority of section R186 without a work permit, presents evidence that they will be working for a minimum of 6 months;
- is employed in an occupation that falls within National Occupational Classification (NOC) skill type 0 (management occupations) or skill level A or B (which generally includes professional occupations and technical or skilled trades [see the NOC website]);
- physically resides or plans to physically reside in Canada while working.
More information can be found at this link: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes/public-policy-competitiveness-economy.html#skilled-workers](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/foreign-workers/exemption-codes/public-policy-competitiveness-economy.html#skilled-workers)

5. You have a valid passport.
a. The work permit will be issued for up to 18 months from the date of approval or until your passport expires, whichever comes first. For example, if your passport is valid for 6 months, then you will be issued an open work permit for 6 months.

threads.answer:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: To meet the MEC under the Express Entry FSW category, one must have accumulated, over a continuous period, at least 1 year of paid, full-time work experience (or the equivalent in part time work) in their primary occupation that is skill type 0, A or B within the last 10 years.
It is well known that primary teachers work for 9-10 months of the year and then are off work for scheduled summer breaks. I believe that these scheduled summer breaks can make it difficult for teachers to prove the minimum 1 year continuous paid requirement to qualify for FSW.
Where an American teacher does not have a formal contract clearly stating the term of employment, would providing a letter from the school stating that he/she was employed on a year-round basis with scheduled breaks for the summer (or that his/her term of employment was considered 1 entire year) plus evidence of pay stubs issued continuously all year (including throughout the scheduled summer break) be sufficient to prove the 1 year continuous paid requirement to qualify for FSW?
Presumably the law was not written with the intent to automatically disqualify teachers from ever qualifying under FSW because of the fact that they have scheduled summer breaks.
Answer: To meet the minimum work experience criteria for the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program, the applicant must have accumulated at least one year of continuous full-time (or the equivalent in part-time) paid work experience in a skilled occupation listed in Skill Type O, or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification (NOC), as per R75(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. To answer your question, if a teacher is able to demonstrate that they are a permanent full-time teacher, where summer and winter breaks were considered paid vacation with full pay or income averaging, work experience should be entered continuously for the number of years worked. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.
We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.subject: Clarification on instructions given in "implied status letters" -- REP-2021-0134
threads.question:
Hello,
I am writing to seek clarification on the instructions given to applicants who are applying for work or study permits in Canada. I have attached the letter for your reference. It refers to R186(u) IRPR, which at the time of this writing this email, provides:
186 A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit
(u) until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date;
But two statements in the letter contradict R186(u):
1) “..you are authorized to continue working with the same conditions until June 01, 2021 or until a decision is made on your application, whichever is first."
2) “this extended period of work is authorized as per subsection 186(u) of the IRPR."
R186(u) does not specify a validity date for implied status. I would argue that no such legislative provision exists to restrict the period of implied status (until June 1 or any other date). Likewise, an extension should not be applicable for the same reason.
I would very much appreciate your clarification on the above, if my understanding of the existing legislation is incorrect.
Thank you for your attention.
threads.answer:
Hello,
QuESTioN: R186(u) does not specify a validity date for implied status. I would argue that no such legislative provision exists to restrict the period of implied status (until June 1 or any other date). Likewise, an extension should not be applicable for the same reason.
I would very much appreciate your clarification on the above, if my understanding of the existing legislation is incorrect.
RESPoNSE: Please note that the 'interim proof of authority to work' letter is only provided to applicants who are renewing
work permits. There is no similar letter for applicants applying to renew their study permit.
The status in not implied’ but maintained if the work permit renewal application is submitted prior to the expiry of their existing work permit. Yes, you are correct in that the Regulations state that the period of authorized stay is extended until a decision is made and that a person who is applying to renew their work permit will have authority to work under R186(u) until a decision is made as long as they continue under existing work permit conditions or unless they leave Canada.
The letter is provided to applicants as proof that they have continued authority to work and the date is added to give employers and other stakeholders a more concrete period of time of authorized work. IRCC has found in the past that employers and stakeholders are reluctant to accept an unknown period such as until a decision is made'. Should the application not be processed within the date on the letter clients may contact IRCC to request continued proof if needed. In addition, there is no requirement that the applicant must present this letter to anyone it is only provided as a service to the client.
The letter has a 120 day validity that corresponds with IRCC Service Standard for in-Canada applications. Historically, IRCC meets our service standard more than 90% of the time. During the initial COVID-19 pandemic period the processing tine has gone beyond our service standard. However, IRCC has reduced our current processing time back to the service standard.
The letter also indicates that : This extended period of work is authorized as per subsection 186(u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. This statement would provide the evidence that they can continue working until a decision is made.
For clarity: the applicant may continue working until a decision is made if they meet all the requirements of R1 86(u) regardless of the date in the letter. The letter is simply a document to provide surety to employers and other stakeholders that the applicant may continue working.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:

Hello,
QuEsTion:When applying for work permit inside Canada for a visitor (as per public policy
announced on August 24, 2020)who has already applied for visitor record and is now on
implied status, dões the applicant needs to apply for restoration as well while submitting
work permit application online? What happens if the initial application of visitor record if
refused and then work permit file is picked up for processing.
RESPONSE: A foreign national who applies under section 181 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations for an extension of their stay prior to the expiration of their initial period of authorized stay has their period of stay extended by law under subsection 183(5) of the IRPR -you call this 'implied' however the status is not implied it is real status that is maintained.
Since the foreign national's period of authorize stay is extended until a decision is made on their application, they are considered to have valid status during the processing period. As such, they would meet one of the eligibilities for the visitor in Canad to apply for a work permit. The foreign national would not need to restore their status and they would not have lost it.
If the work permit application, which is also a request to extend status in Canada, is submitted prior to the decision on the first application, the period of authorized stay under R183(5) is extended until a decision is made on the second application. In the link you have provided below it references 'the permit was expired' there is no 'permit' for a visitor there is only the period of authorized stay, therefore the second application would continue the period of authorized stay until decision.

threads.answer:

Due to the impacts of coronavirus disease (COVID-19), we
- have temporarily changed how we process applications
- can't provide accurate processing times
This is to make sure that we can prioritize applications from people who meet the requirements to enter Canada.
Apply online
If you're applying for a study permit, you should apply online, whether you're outside of Canada or already in Canada.
When you apply, you should
- submit as many of the documents needed for a complete application as possible
- include a letter of explanation for any documents that are missing due to COVID-19
If you can't apply online because of a disability or because there's a problem with the online application, you can apply on paper.

We'll process your application in our regular study permit process if you
- submit a complete application, and will attend a DLI with an approved COVID-19 readiness plan
We'll process your application in 2 stages if
- you submitted your application on or before December 15, 2020
- your application is incomplete due to COVID-19 (for example, you’re missing your biometrics or medical), and
- your program begins in the winter 2021 semester
If we process your application in 2 stages, this is what will happen: Stage 1: We check your eligibility
In this stage, an officer reviews your application for
- a letter of acceptance from a DLI
- a Quebec Acceptance Certificate (if you'll be studying in Quebec)
- proof that you have enough money for
o tuition fees o living expenses for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada, and
o return transportation for yourself and any family members who come with you to Canada
- any family ties you may have to Canada
- evidence that you'll leave Canada when you no longer have legal status
If your application passes this first stage, we'll let you know by email or in your online account. This doesn't
guarantee that we'll approve your application and issue you a study permit.
Stage 2: We check your application for admissibility and any changes to your eligibility
In this stage, an officer reviews your application for
- a medical exam, if needed
- police certificates, if needed • your biometrics
- any information that changed after we reviewed your application for eligibility
If your application passes this second stage, we'll approve it. If you applied for a co-op work permit, we'll now assess your co-op work permit application.
At this point, if you meet the requirements, you may be able to travel to Canada and
- begin your studies, or
- continue your studies, if you've already started studying online

threads.subject: EXPRESS ENTRY: CRS points for arranged employment - "currently working in Canada" question -- REP- 2020-2412
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: We would like to seek clarification on how CEC candidates should go about indicating their offer of employment in the IRCC portal when they submit their Express Entry profile in situations where they normally work in Canada, they are temporarily overseas but not comfortable travelling back to Canada immediately due to COVID. They continue to work remotely for a Canadian employer for whom they have worked for over a year in Canada and will return to as soon as travel is more practicable. In reviewing the Ministerial Instructions with respect to the Express Entry System and the corresponding Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), we noticed that such a scenario does not fall outside of the “arranged employment” definition but there is a gap in the EE portal because this situation of a foreign national who has a valid job offer while being temporarily overseas does not seem to be contemplated. A foreign national does not appear to be required to be physically in Canada at the time of claiming the “arranged employment" points as long as they meet all other requirements (they worked in Canada for a year already, have a valid employer-specific work permit, currently working for that employer (there is a mention that they must be working for that same employer but there is no specific exclusion of remote work nor is there a qualifier such as "in Canada"), and they have an offer for at least one continuous year after it is expected their PR visa is issued. As such, our interpretation is that a candidate who has a valid LMlA-exempt work permit, has worked in Canada for at least one year in the last 10 years and has an ongoing job offer for continuous work in Canada once they arrive back in Canada, would have to answer “yes" to the question about current work in Canada in order to get prompted to answer the questions that are relevant to the 29(2)(a) definition of arranged employment. Although this does not factually represent the current situation of a work permit holder working outside of Canada due to COVID, we submit that this should be an appropriate temporary measure, provided that the candidate has proof of their previous one year of work experience in Canada based on that work permit, the work permit is still valid and the employer continues to offer them employment in Canada. Please let us know whether IRCC would consider revising the EE application portal to better reflect the fact that the temporary remote work outside of Canada does not preclude a candidate from claiming arranged employment points if all other criteria under section 29(2) of the Mls are met. Otherwise, we will proceed to answer the question “incorrectly” in the portal and properly explain the unique situation in detail in the representative's cover letter.
Answer: Express Entry's arranged employment points are modelled on the arranged employment provisions in section 82(1) and section 82(2)(a) of the regulations for Federal Skilled Workers in IRPA, which references both employment in Canada, and the applicant being physically in Canada to receive CRS points for arranged employment. IRCC's treatment of arranged employment must be consistent across the regulations and the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions. If the applicant's job offer is recognized for a worker currently established outside Canada, the Immigration Officer must be satisfied that the applicant intends to become a permanent resident (establishing in Canada and meeting the residency obligations). The intent of this type of job offer is to make permanent residence more accessible to skilled workers who have demonstrated the ability to integrate into the Canadian labour market. The purpose of the Canadian work experience requirement is to select workers who can economically integrate in Canada, which is demonstrated in part by the accumulation of 1,560 hours of continuous, skilled Canadian work experience on their employer-specific work permit. Remote work does not constitute Canadian work experience and would therefore not count for the job offer.
We would recommend that the applicant request a Permanent Residence LMIA from ESDC to support the job offer, which is free of charge. If the applicant chooses to proceed with the course of action outlined in your email (“to answer the question “incorrectly" in the portal and properly explain the unique situation in detail in the representative's cover letter”), the onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives
mailbox.
Question:
If an Express Entry candidate is issued an ITA under CEC before they actually have the 1-year of valid Canadian work experience, can they still submit an application for permanent residence as long as the application is submitted after having completed their 1-year of valid Canadian work experience?

Answer:
The IRCC system calculates work experience by calculating months and not actual days worked in the month. IRCC is aware some applicants are receiving an ITA a month or two early and we advise the candidate not to delay their eAPR or turn down the invitation if the work experience is continuing. If the work genuinely ended before accumulating one year of work however, they should decline the invitation.
IRCC examining officers are aware of this, and when looking at the application they will take into consideration factors such as the continuous work status, the Offer of Employment Letter from the same employer, and whether the applicant reached the experience required by the time the application is processed.
