threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your question. Please find the response below
Q: Can you please advise whether the bars to in-Canada H&C applications under A25(1.2) apply only to the principal applicant (PA) or also to their accompanying family members in Canada? For example, if a spouse has her own pending refugee claim or less than 12 months passed from her own refugee claim refusal/withdrawal-is she eligible to be included as the accompanying family member into her husband's H&C application? For greater clarity: the PA himself in this scenario would not be in any circumstances triggering A25(1.2) bars.
A: The bars to in-Canada H&C applications under A25(1.2) apply to the principal applicant (PA) and their accompanying family members in Canada.
The Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs) for Humanitarian & Compassionate: Intake and who may apply, explain that people who have filed a refugee claim in Canada may be subject to a twelve month bar on submitting an H&C application for permanent residence. This process is commonly referred to as "the H&C bar".
The PDls indicate that people who have made refugee claims are barred from submitting an H&C application for twelve months if they have: a refugee claim that is pending before the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) made a claim for refugee protection that was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the RPD, and they have a pending pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) application
Similarly, if a person has filed a refugee claim with the RPD that was rejected, determined to be abandoned or determined to be withdrawn after substantive evidence has been heard, they are barred from H&C consideration if less than 12 months has passed since the date of the
- RPD decision in cases where there has been no appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) or application for leave and judicial review submitted to the Federal Court
- latest decision in any process in cases where there has been an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) or application for leave and judicial review submitted to the Federal Court
Failed refugee claimants are subject to the 12 month bar unless they qualify for an exception on the basis of either of the following:
- inadequate medical or health care in the country of origin leading to a risk to life upon removal best interests of a child (BIOC).
In this particular scenario, the spouse would be barred from H&C and is not eligible to be included unless she qualified for one of the exceptions. Cordially,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Examination of Residency Obligation-- REP-2020-0373
threads.question:
Greetings,
Amid the introduction of the Exit/Entry Program in cooperation with the CBSA, we have the following questions regarding residency obligation that need your kind clarification.
A28(2)(b) prescribes the level of sufficiency required of a PR when demonstrating compliance with his/her residency obligation during an examination. In our observation, there are no provisions specifying the level of sufficiency required of a PR when demonstrating compliance outside of an examination. Therefore, we are wondering if there are any circumstances where PRs can be required to demonstrate compliance with his/her residency obligation, when not being subject to an examination that 's described under A15(1)? If such circumstances exist, what is the level of sufficiency required in those cases?
Also in our observation, officers have the authority to prepare an inadmissibility report under A44(1) against a PR for non- compliance with the residency obligation, but the preparation of such a report does not necessarily need to result from a prior examination. Therefore, can an officer lawfully prepare an inadmissibility report under A44(1) against a PR in Canada who is not
subject to an examination, for non-compliance with residency obligation, based on the information obtained from CBSA under the Exit/Entry Program?
Your clarification is greatly appreciated.
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your patience with our responses to this inquiry.
As IRPA 18(3) explains, "Even though a person seeking to enter Canada is not, in accordance with regulations made under subsection 26(2), required to appear for an examination, an officer may require the person to do so." There may be occurrences when an officer may require a person to demonstrate compliance with his/her residency obligation and the provisions would remain the same as when the person is subject to an examination.
IRPA A44(1) allows an officer to prepare an inadmissibility report in relation to a permanent resident or a foreign national "who is in Canada". The procedural requirements and legal obligations related to gathering information from the person for the purpose of writing an A44(1) report will depend on whether the person is still subject to examination Pursuant to A15(1), individuals who make applications under the IRPA are subject to an examination for various reasons, including to determine whether that person has a right to enter Canada or may become authorized to enter or remain in Canada pursuant to A18(1).
Thank you,

Question: Would work by a foreign national, pursuant to a regular open work permit that confers temporary resident status (i.e. NOT a work permit issued through DFAIT), as a locally engaged employee at a consulate in Canada qualify as Canadian work experience under s.15 of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system?

and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear
Q. In your request you ask whether the restrictions from submitting an H&C application under 25(1.01) and (1.2) apply to potential PRRA applicants from countries on either the ADR (administrative deferral of removal) or TSR (temporary suspension of removal) list.
Response
Subsection 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) allows for an individual to make an application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations (H&C application) to the Minister. Nevertheless, as you noted in your enquiry, there are restrictions and exceptions to this.
These restrictions and exceptions are not affected by whether an individual comes from a country under an ADR or a TSR. Instead, these restrictions and exceptions apply only to individuals who fit the conditions described by the clauses in the legislation, regardless of whether they come from a country under an ADR/TSR or not. To determine whether these restrictions and exceptions apply in the case you have brought forth, one must review the relevant sections ofIRPA and see whether they apply.
In reviewing your enquiry, it appears that the most relevant section ofIRPA to consider is 25(1.2)(b.1) which notes:
The minister may not examine the request if (b.1) the foreign national made a claim for refugee protection that was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division and they made an application for protection to the Minister that is pending;
To fit under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) ofIRPA, the individuals would need to have been found ineligible to have their claim referred to the Refugee Protection Division and, they would need to have filed a PRRA application that is still before the Minister. However, if the CBSA has not contacted the individuals to notify them of their opportunity to submit a PRRA application and, more specifically, if the individuals have not yet submitted their PRRA application, they would not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) and would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
From the description provided in your enquiry, it would appear that the individuals were found ineligible to have their claims referred to the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board. However, as you state that CBSA has not contacted the individuals yet to start their PRRA process, it would appear that they have not yet filed a PRRA application. If this is the case, then, based on this limited information, these individuals would still be eligible to file an H&C application.
Q. You also ask what other processes they would qualify for in order to obtain permanent status based on their ongoing
mmigration, Refugees nmigration, Réfugiés establishment in Canada while waiting for the opportunity to explain their fear of return.
Various different pathways towards permanent residence exist, each with their own requirements. Which pathway is the best fit depends on a person’s individual circumstances.
While IRCC cannot advise on individual cases, ongoing establishment in Canada is one of various factors taken into consideration when assessing an application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
However, if the individuals have temporary resident status in Canada and meet the other minimum requirements (including employment, language, or educational requirements), the individuals may be eligible to apply under various economic classes such as the Provincial Nominee class or the Canadian Experience Class.
Background
A more full review of the most relevant restrictions and exceptions to section 25(1) ofIRPA follows.
According to subsection 25(1.01) ofIRPA, a designated foreign national may not make a request under subsection 25(1) until five years after the day:
- a final determination is made on their claim in the case of someone who filed a refugee claim but has not filed an application for protection (PRRA application);
- a final determination is made on their application for protection in the case of someone who has made an application for protection (PRRA application); or
- on which they become a designated foreign national in any other case.
It is important to emphasize that the restrictions set out in subsection 25(1.01) above do not apply to all foreign nationals. They only apply to persons who fit the definition of a designated foreign national as set out in subsection 20.1(2) ofIRPA. Thus, for persons found to be a designated foreign national, there is a five year restriction from applying for H&C consideration. However, if the individual does not fit the definition of a designated foreign national as set out in 20.1(2) of IRPA, then the restrictions in subsection 25(1.01) do not apply to them.
In looking at the specifics of the case you have put forth, there is insufficient information to determine whether the foreign nationals in question are designated foreign nationals as defined under subsection 20.1(2) of IRPA and whether the restriction under 25(1.01) applies in this case. However, as Section 20.1 is not often invoked, it is not likely that this restriction applies in this case.
Similarly, subsection 25(1.2) sets out the exceptions to subsection 25(1). These are cases where the Minister may not examine an H&C application made under 25(1). Most relevant to this enquiry appear to be paragraphs 25(1.2)(b) through (c). Paragraphs 25(1.2)(b) and (b.1) note that the Minister may not examine a request for H&C consideration made under subsection 25(1) if
the person is a foreign national who still has a claim for refugee protection before either the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division; the person is a foreign national who made a refugee claim that was determined to be ineligible to be referred to the Refugee Protection Division and then that same person made a PRRA application that is still before the Minister.
Paragraph 25(1.2)(c) refers to a 12 month bar on applications for H&C consideration; however, this bar only applies to foreign
nmigration, Réfugiés
nationals who's refugee claim was rejected or determined withdrawn after substantive evidence was heard.
Again, in looking at the specifics of your case, you refer to, “individuals... [who] enter Canada and are referred for a PRRA because they are not eligible to claim refugee protection... [but] the CBSA will not contact them to start their PRRA process as they are not considered "removal ready"...". As these individual were deemed ineligible to have their claims referred to the Immigration and Refugee Board, it cannot be said that they still have a claim pending before either the Refugee Protection Division or the Refugee Appeal Division. Similarly, it cannot be said that substantive evidence on their claim was heard. Thus, the exceptions under 25(1.2)(b) and (c) do not apply.
To fit under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) ofIRPA, the individuals would need to have been found ineligible to have their claim referred to the Refugee Protection Division and, they would need to have filed a PRRA application that is still before the Minister. However, if the CBSA has not contacted the individuals to notify them of their opportunity to submit a PRRA application or if the individuals have not yet submitted their PRRA application, they would not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1) and would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
Again, as you note that the CBSA has not contacted these individuals to start their PRRA process, then it would appear that these individuals do not fall under the exception described in 25(1.2)(b.1). Instead, the individuals would still be able to make a request for H&C consideration under 25(1).
Hoping the above information addresses your concerns.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good Day,

Question: There are certain trades such as Electricians, Automotive service technicians that require mandatory licensing before working in that field with those designations. However, in order to be eligible for the licensing one needs to first complete an apprenticeship and then after completing apprenticeship hours become eligible to write the licensing exam. Under Canadian Experience Class, we understand that the employment requirements are not necessarily are required to be met. Can an applicant applying under CEC, claim points for a trade NOC such as an automotive service technician Apprentice or Electrician apprentice without being registered with the trade school? Some trade school and some trades require few hours of training as well before being able to register for the apprenticeship program as well. Kindly advise, if a CEC candidate is able to claim experience successfully under a trade NOC as an apprentice without the necessary licensing or registering with the trade school as an apprentice.
Answer: Yes, an Express Entry candidate would be able to claim apprenticeship work experience under the Canadian Experience Class, as long the work experience also meets all other criteria of the program. This includes having at least 12 months of full time (or the equivalent of part-time) Canadian skilled work experience in one of more NOC O, A, or B occupations within the 36 months before the date of application receipt, as per 87.1(2)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. The work experience must have been gained by working in Canada under temporary resident status with authorization to work and be remunerated by the payment of wages or a commission. Any period of employment gained when the applicant was in full-time studies does not count towards work experience for this program. Additionally, during that period of employment, the applicant must have:
- performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation(s) as set out in the occupational description of the NOC [R87.1(2)(b)]; and
- performed a substantial number of the main duties, including all the essential duties, of the occupation(s) as set out in the occupational description of the NOC [R87.1(2)(c)].

# Hello,
Foreign nationals may study in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study as long as it is 6 months or less in duration. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months).
A professional training program is a type of additional education or training usually offered to professionals already in the field. Professional development is generally “accredited"; that is, it is recognized by an industry, association, or profession. Professional training is offered through community colleges, universities, CEGEPs, career colleges, professional associations, or unions.
In general, professional training programs require participants to complete both a study and work component in order to successfully complete the program, and obtain the given credential. However, unlike co-op/internship programs in post- secondary institutions (e.g., universities, community colleges) such programs often consist of a full-time work component and a part-time study component. The work component often comprises more than 50% of the study component.
Applicants wishing to participate in professional training programs must apply for a study permit to cover the study portion, if the study component is more than six months at a designated learning institution; and apply for the appropriate work permit if there is a work portion. More information can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/other-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/other-) considerations.html

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
An applicant completes a three-year college program in Canada. Subsequently, they complete a bachelor’s degree outside of Canada. They receive an educational credential assessment for that degree which states it is from a recognized institution and is equivalent to a Canadian degree. Credits from the college degree are applied towards the bachelor's degree, allowing the applicant to complete the degree in less than the standard amount of time (say two years instead of three).
How many points would be awarded for education? Would it be based on a bachelor's degree, (120 points if single) or on ‘Two or more certificates, diplomas, or degrees. One must be for a program of three or more years' (128 points if single).
Answer:
A candidate will only be awarded education points under the Comprehensive Ranking System and the Federal Skilled Worker selection grid for having 'two or more post-secondary program credentials' if the educational credentials represent separate certificates, diplomas or degrees. To get points for having two or more post-secondary credentials, at least one of the credentials must be for three or more years of study.
Based on the information provided, the applicant should declare only a single post-secondary program credential of three years or more. This is because they did not complete a three year program then another program. The first program became the Bachelor's. Therefore, the applicant should input only their Bachelor's Degree and the appropriate points will be awarded.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Expiry of translated documents
A translation cannot change over time and should be valid indefinitely unless the original document has changed or has expired. If the signature of a certified translator or notary has expired, it does not invalidate the translation. As long as the translator's certification was valid at the time of signature, the translation remains valid.
The only time the translation would expire and a new translation would be required is if the original document has expired or has changed and the applicant submits a new document.

threads.answer:

Thanks you for your question.
Question:
Could you kindly advise if your Public policy on exemptions to work permit conditions when changing employment: COVID-19 program delivery includes work permit extension applicants who are still waiting for a decision on a new LMIA required for their new position and have applied for their new work permit pending LMIA approval?
Answer:
If no LMIA is provided and the position that the applicant is applying for is an LMIA required position, then the application is incomplete. This would disqualify them from being eligible for the 'interim authority to work' since the officer can't be satisfied that the application is for an employer-specific work permit, but then give 60 days concurrent processing to the applicant to provide the LMIA. The concurrent processing option will basically give the applicant a 60 day extension to provide the LMIA before a determination is made on their application.
For in-Canada processing, the concurrent processing option will be allowed only for foreign nationals whose work permits will be expiring within two weeks and whose employers have previously submitted an application for an LMIA. The foreign national must provide CIC with proof of a valid job offer as well as proof that the employer has submitted a request to Service Canada for a new LMIA. The application will be initialized and the processing fee will be applied. Applications will be held by CIC for 60 days, after which a determination regarding the work permit will be made.

threads.subject: Remote Work -- LMIA-Exempt work permits -- REP-2021-0039
threads.question:
Hello,
Question: Is a physical work location in Canada mandatory? If a company meets all other requirements and is able to justify that it is indeed operating (revenue, employee salaries and benefits etc, provides a good or service requirements are all evidenced), is a fully-remote employee/foreign national applying for a work permit going to have an issue?
Response: To sum up, based on your scenario, the company does not have a physical location in Canada but is operating outside of Canada and the question is, can the employer provide a job offer for a foreign national who will not/does not intend to travel to Canada in order to work.
A physical work location is mandatory. As per R196 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, a "foreign national must not work in Canada unless authorized to do so by a work permit or these Regulations". A work permit authorizes a foreign national to work in Canada.
In addition, an employer must identify a physical job location when they submit an offer of employment through the Employer Portal. This information, along with the other elements in the offer of employment, will be assessed should the employer be selected for inspection under the Employer Compliance regime as per subparagraphs 209.2(1)(a)(i) and (iii) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations:
209.2 (1) An employer who has made an offer of employment to a foreign national referred to in subparagraph 200(1)(c)(ii.1) must comply with the following conditions:
o (a) during the period of employment for which the work permit is issued to the foreign national,
▪ (i) the employer must be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made, unless the offer was made for employment as a live-in caregiver,
- (ii) the employer must comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works,
(iii) subject to subparagraph (viï), the employer must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer,
▪ (iv) the employer must make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse;
▪ (v) the employer, in the case of an employer who employs a foreign national who is subject to an order or regulation made under the Emergencies Act or the Quarantine Act, must not do anything that prevents the foreign national from complying with the requirements of the order or regulation, including requiring the foreign national to do anything that is contrary to those requirements,
L'nmndion (vi) the employer, in the case of an employer who employs a foreign national who is subject to a provincial law that governs public health in response to COVID-19, must not do anything that prevents the foreign national from complying with the requirements of the law, including requiring the foreign national to do anything that is contrary to the law, and
▪ (vii) the employer, in the case of an employer who employs a foreign national who, in accordance with an order made under section 58 of the Quarantine Act, is required to isolate or quarantine themselves for a period on entry into Canada, must provide the foreign national with wages during that period that are substantially the same as those set out in the offer of employment; and
o (b) during a period of six years beginning on the first day of the period of employment for which the work permit is issued to the foreign national, the employer must
▪ (i) be able to demonstrate that any information they provided under subparagraph 200(1)(c)(ii. 1) or section 209.11 was accurate, and
▪ (ii) retain any document that relates to compliance with the conditions set out in paragraph (a).

threads.subject: Politique d'intérêt public : Voie d'accès à la résidence permanente des travailleurs de la santé -- REP-2021-0068
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Ma question concerne le programme cité en objet. Je comprends que la demande doit être envoyée par la poste. La liste de contrôle des documents ne semble laisser qu’une seule option concernant les formulaires : les originaux sont exigés. Ma question : Est-ce qu’une demande sera jugée incomplète et retournée au demandeur si des copies des formulaires sont envoyées? Je pense notamment aux membres de la famille ou personnes à charge d’un demandeur qui se trouvent hors du Canada. Il est possible que ces personnes se trouvent dans des pays où les conditions sont extrêmement difficiles et qu’il soit périlleux, voire impossible, d’effectuer l’envoi vers le Canada des formulaires originaux. La même question s’applique aux photos format passeport de ces personnes hors du Canada.
Tel que vous le mentionnez, la Liste de contrôle des documents (IMM 1015) indique que les formulaires originaux doivent être fournis.
Toutefois, notez que des instructions ont été publiées pour la période de pandémie de COVID-19. Ainsi, si une nouvelle demande ne contient pas tous les documents à l’appui (les frais connexes sont exigés), le demandeur doit joindre à sa demande une explication démontrant qu'il est touché par l’interruption des services découlant du nouveau coronavirus.
À noter que les demandes jugées incomplètes qui ne sont pas accompagnées d’une explication, ou pour des raisons sans lien avecl’interruption des services découlant des incidences du nouveau coronavirus, peuvent être rejetées aux termes de l’article R10, et les frais associés à la demande seront remboursés au demandeur. Le motif du rejet ne doit pas être lié à l’interruption des services.
Ainsi, pendant cette période, si une demande est soumise avec des photocopies des formulaires signés ou sans les photos format passeport requises, les demandes ne seront pas retournées. Les orignaux de même que les photos doivent être soumis à une date ultérieure, lorsque cela est raisonnablement possible.
Si les documents sont manquants pour des raisons exceptionnelles et non liées aux incidences du coronavirus, veuillez également fournir des explications et, si possible, des preuves à l’appui. L'évaluation se fera au cas par cas.
Pour plus de détails, consultez les pages suivantes : Résidence permanente : Exécution des programmes sur la COVID-19; Comment présenter une demande?; Guide 1016-Guide de demande pour la voie d’accès à la résidence permanente des travailleurs de la santé (pandémie de COVID-19).
N'hésitez pas à nous contacter pour toute question.
Cordialement,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Représentants immigration

Question: Individual holds a closed work permit limiting work location to Ontario (employer's office is located in Individual would like to work remotely from Toronto, Ontario. threads.answer:
Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
Question: Individual holds a closed work permit limiting work location to Ontario (employer's office is located in Individual would like to work remotely from Toronto, Ontario. Employer is not moving and job is not changing. Is a new work permit required or is remote work in a different city in Canada not subject to the location restriction?
Answer: There are two sets of conditions to consider in employment location – those imposed on the employee under section 185 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) and those imposed on the employer under 209.3 of the IRPR. If the location is imposed on the work permit, the foreign worker must change their conditions to move locations.
For foreign workers working remotely on a temporary basis due to the Covid situation, it is recommended that employers submit a voluntary disclosure to notify IRCC of the changes.
For scenarios where an employer wishes to make teleworking permanent and valid post-Covid, we recommend that the employer submit a new offer of employment and have the worker submit an application to change conditions as a worker.
We would also recommend that employers include teleworking arrangement information in any new offer of employment.
We hope this information is of assistance.

Bonjour,
La présente est en réponse à votre message du 23 novembre, 2020.
Les demandeurs doivent présenter une demande de permis de travail postdiplôme (PTPD) dans les 180 jours qui suivent l’obtention d'une confirmation écrite -par exemple, une lettre ou un relevé de notes officiels -de la part de l’établissement d’enseignement désigné (EED) indiquant qu'il a répondu aux exigences liées à la réussite de son programme d’études.
Le calcul des 180 jours commence le jour où les notes finales de l’étudiant sont communiquées ou à la réception d’un avis officiel écrit confirmant que l’étudiant a terminé avec succès son programme d’études, selon la première éventualité. Il incombe au demandeur de produire une preuve de la date à laquelle il a reçu son relevé de notes. Les agents peuvent aussi confirmer cette date auprès de l’EED.
Nous espérons que ces renseignements vous seront utiles.

threads.answer:

Question:

1. Can the applicant obtain points for a valid job offer without applying for a new LMlA since the applicant is working for the same employer that is making the job offer pursuant to an LMlA based work permit?

An officer may exercise their discretion and request further documentation such as, but not limited to, lease/rental/purchase agreements outside Quebec, letters of support, etc., in order to satisfy them of the applicant's intent to reside in a province other than the Province of Quebec. I have been approached by a client who received his PR in the Year 2002. However, he had to leave Canada due to family issues and has not been able to fulfill his residency obligations. He is out of Canada for more than 10 years.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Before processing an application for voluntary renunciation, an officer determines whether the applicant is a permanent resident. An applicant who has already lost permanent resident status, for example, through a negative residency determination, is a foreign national.
The client must apply for a permanent resident travel document (PRTD) so a determination can be made on their status.
Since your client has not fulfilled his residency obligation, it is likely a negative residency determination will be made unless there is consideration for humanitarian and compassionate factors connected to the application.
According to IRPA 20.O(1), a foreign national must wait five years from the date they became a foreign national in order to apply to become a permanent resident.

Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Can you please confirm if work experience gained in Canada (on an employer specific work permit, and while
studying as a PhD) counts as Canadian work experience under Express Entry?
Answer: Pursuant to paragraph 87.1(3)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), any period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) nor shall the applicant be awarded CRS points for Canadian work experience. However, depending on the applicant's circumstance, they may still meet the program requirements for Canadian work experience. Applicants can meet the 1 year of skilled work experience in Canada in the last 3 years before applying in a number of different ways, including an equal amount in part-time work (for example, 15 hours a week for 24 months is equal to 1 year of full time work). The applicant should provide additional documentation to prove that they were not engaged in in full-time studies (example: a letter from the school) to help satisfy the officer that they have met the requirement. Please see our website for additional information. Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements.

As a general rule, it is best not to submit additional documents that have not been specifically requested by IRCC unless they are to inform the department of a significant change in the applicant or sponsor's circumstances (change in relationship status, withdrawal of sponsorship, birth of a child etc.). IRCC staff are required to review any such documents and match them to the relevant file which may impact our productivity in general as well the specific file in particular. Maximum numbers for different categories of supporting documents included in the checklist are intended to streamline our operations as much as possible and any significant additions to these numbers do slow down the process.
Furthermore, additional proof of relationship, such as you describe, is only requested in a very small proportion of cases where the evaluating officer is not satisfied with the documentation already on file.

Dear Sir/Madam:
I would like to request for some insights on a situation where a person is on PGWP. As per regulation a foreign national can be on implied status as a temporary resident if an application is completed/submitted before the expiry of his/her current status.
In the case of a PGWP holder who found a job offer under the home child care provider pilot and completed/submitted a PR application and at the same time specific work permit as a home child care provider before his pgwp expires, will he also merit the implied status as a worker and can continue working while waiting for the said work permit ?
Pls. clarify with regulations.
Thank you.
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Dear
Our sincere apologies for the delay in our response.
Question: In the case of a PGwP holder who found a job offer under the home child care provider pilot and completed/submitted a PR application and at the same time specific work permit as a home child care provider before his pgwp expires, will he also merit the implied status as a worker and can continue working while waiting for the said work permit ?
Response: Please note that the Immigration Representatives Mailbox will only reply to general immigration program or policy related enquiries and cannot comment on specific cases. We are replying based on the general scenario that you have described.
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have maintained their status (sometimes referred to as implied status) as a temporary resident during that period. If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
Therefore, a caregiver would have maintained status as long as the HCCP/HSW permanent residence application (including an HCCP/HSW occupation-restricted open work permit application) is submitted before the expiry of the current work permit.
However, individuals who are on temporary status in Canada may consider submitting a separate work permit application or an extension of their existing work permit under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) or the International Mobility Program (IMP), even if they have already applied under the HCCP/HSW pilots. Permanent residence (PR) applications take longer to process and the COVID-19 pandemic has caused more delays. This affects when IRCC can issue the work permit related to the PR application. Even though they will have maintained status, it may be harder to get some government services or benefits. Also, if their PR application is refused, rejected for being incomplete, or returned for being over that year's cap, we'll return the related work permit application as well. If this happens: they'll lose their maintained status if they are not eligible to restore their status, they'd have to leave Canada

- Any post-secondary certificate issued by a Canadian institution, whether it is online or in-person study, will qualify for education points under Express Entry (90 points for 1 year post-secondary credential)
- Work experience attained in Canada while the person is registered in a full-time study program may not be considered as Canadian work experience under Express Entry Canadian Experience Class
Answer:

(b) “credentials obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program" are excluded from earning Canadian education bonus points. As always, the onus is on the applicant to provide the appropriate documentation. At time of assessment, the IRCC reviewing officer will use their discretion when evaluating information and supporting documents in the application.
- Work experience attained in Canada while the person is registered in a full-time program may not be considered as Canadian work experience under Express Entry Canadian Experience Class.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

Hello,
Foreign nationals may study in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study as long as it is 6 months or less in duration. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months).
A professional training program is a type of additional education or training usually offered to professionals already in the field. Professional development is generally “accredited"; that is, it is recognized by an industry, association, or profession. Professional training is offered through community colleges, universities, CEGEPs, career colleges, professional associations, or unions.
In general, professional training programs require participants to complete both a study and work component in order to successfully complete the program, and obtain the given credential. However, unlike co-op/internship programs in post-
secondary institutions (e.g., universities, community colleges) such programs often consist of a full-time work component
and a part-time study component. The work component often comprises more than 50% of the study component.
Applicants wishing to participate in professional training programs must apply for a study permit to cover the study portion, if the study component is more than six months at a designated learning institution; and apply for the appropriate work permit if there is a work portion. More information can be found here: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-) citizenship/corporate/publications-manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/temporary-residents/study-permits/other- considerations.html

threads.subject: Concurrent restoration applications -- REP-2020-2793 --
threads.question:
Dear IRCC,
Can a foreign national apply to restore their status to worker, if they have a restoration to visitor application already in process? Many foreign nationals in Canada submitted restoration to visitor applications in late December 2020, to comply with the December 31st deadline extension that was created by IRCC's public policy. However IRCC then renewed this public policy, on December 31st, allowing such foreign nationals to have until August 31, 2021 to apply to restore their status. If a foreign national becomes eligible to apply to restore their status to worker (for example, by receiving a positive LMIA) whilst awaiting the outcome of the restoration to visitor application, can they submit a restoration to worker application and have it processed? This would be done to allow the work permit to be issued to the applicant in Canada, and also allow them to apply for interim authorization to return to work.
I look forward to your reply, and thank you for your guidance.
Kind regards,
threads.answer:
Dear
Please note that a foreign nationals can only restore their status to what they had before it expired. If they are eligible after restoration, they may also be able to apply for a different permit. For example, if a foreign national had a work permit, then applied for a visitor record, then lost their status, they can apply to restore their visitor status and if they meet eligibility for a work permit, they can apply for a work permit after their status as a visitor has been restored.
Due to COVID-19, IRCC has implemented various public policies that may benefit foreign nationals who would like to apply for a work permit.
For information on restoration and public policies, please visit our website: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-)
refugees-citizenship/services/coronavirus-covid19/restoration-extension-trv.html

threads.answer:
Bonjour
Merci pour votre patience.
Question: Cependant, quelles sont les paramètres pour une personne ayant un permis de travail fermé et qui désire effectuer de la diffusion sur des chaînes en ligne?
Si cette personne le fait sur une chaîne non-canadienne avec rémunération? Si cette personne le fait pour le plaisir sans rémunération?
Réponse : Si la personne fait de la diffusion sur une chaîne en ligne non canadienne, que ce soit avec rémunération (si la source de rémunération est étrangère) ou non, un permis de travail ne serait pas requis puisque la personne n’entrerait pas sur le marché du travail.
Si la personne fait de la diffusion en ligne sur une chaîne canadienne, rémunérée ou non, un permis de travail serait requis puisque le travail entrerait en concurrence directe avecles activités des citoyens canadiens ou des résidents permanents sur le marché du travail au Canada.
Nous vous remercions d’avoir communiqué avecla Division de la prestation des programmes des résidents temporaires d’IRCC. Nous ne pouvons répondre aux demandes de renseignements portant sur des cas précis, mais nous vous encourageons à communiquer avec la ressource compétente indiquée ci--dessous pour obtenir de l’aide.
1) Pour obtenir de plus amples renseignements au sujet des programmes d'IRCC, veuillez consulter le Centre d'aide.
2) Pour savoir où en est rendu le traitement de votre demande, vous pouvez vérifier l'état de votre demande en ligne
3) Pour toute autre question, veuillez communiquer avec le Ministère selon le moyen approprié indiqué sur la page Contactez--nous.
4) Si vous avez déjà communiqué avec le Centre de soutien à la clientèle ou le bureau migration au sujet du traitement de votre demande et/ou des motifs de la décision, et avez besoin de renseignements supplémentaires, vous pouvez communiquer avec l’Unité des cas et conseils au Règlement des cas par courriel.
Cioyenneté Canada
5) Si vous éprouvez des problèmes techniques avecle Portail de l'employeur, veuillez envoyer votre question à la boîte aux lettres du Portail de l'employeur. Les employeurs devraient s'assurer de réviser le Guide d'inscription ainsi que le Guide d'utilisation du Portail des employeurs.
6) Les employeurs qui souhaitent embaucher un travailleur qui se trouve à l’extérieur du Canada et qui vient d’un pays dispensé de l’obligation de visa et qui est possiblement dispensé d’une étude d’impact sur le marché du travail (ElMT) ou d’un permis de travail, peuvent envoyer un courriel à l’Unité pour la mobilité internationale des travailleurs afin d’obtenir un avis. Il n’y a pas de frais associés pour les demandes d’avis. Les avis fournis par l’Unité pour la mobilité internationale des travailleurs peuvent être pris en compte par l’agent des services frontaliers mais ne garantissent pas que le travailleur sera dispensé d’une ElMT ou d’un permis de travail ou qu’il sera admis au Canada.

threads.subject: Applying for Permanent Residence outside Canada-Relocating to Canada on WP prior to decision on PR --
threads.question:
REP-2021-0050
Hello,
Question:
1. A foreign national created their profile in the Express Entry pool as a Federal Skilled Worker, received their Invitation to Apply and submitted an Application for Permanent Residency while residing outside of Canada. As this foreign national is also in receipt of a positive LMiA and pre-approved Work Permit, can s/he enter Canada and await the processing of their PR application while on lawful status as a worker in Canada?
2. If yes to the above, who would need to be notified of this change? And via webform?
Response:
Under the current rules governing travel restrictions, foreign nationals who hold a valid work permit or were issued a port of entry decision letter on their work permit application may be eligible to enter Canada. Officers will assess the work permit application against the job offer –the job offer must be valid and a position exists. If a job offer is provided in order for the foreign national to travel to Canada, i.e., to overcome travel restrictions, and the officer determines/finds that there is no actual job waiting, the work permit application may be refused.
Before boarding travellers, airlines must be satisfied that a foreign national is exempt from the travel prohibition. An approved PR must present a valid COPR dated pre-March 18, along with other relevant travel documentation. They can't board by virtue of having a COPR issued after March 18th, but if they have a work permit and can enter, then they stay in Canada and wait for their PR to be processed.
A PR applicant who received an ITA for PR through Express Entry and has a port of entry letter on their work permit application and a permanent job offer with an LMIA can enter Canada as a TR (not as a PR). The foreign national must meet the travel exemptions related to foreign workers in the OiC and have a genuine job offer.
If the foreign national managed to enter into Canada by virtue of their work permit, they should notify IRCC of their new address via the IRCC Webform.
Thank you kindly,

Question: Recently, we have a client approaching us and would like to apply to the CEC program under Express Entry. However, his situation is a little bit tricky. What is the proper procedure to follow when an individual has received an ITA under Express Entry and they cannot produce their non-accompanying dependents for a medical examination because they do not have custody of the minor child and the
child's other parent is not co-operating?
Will IRCC accept the file as complete with a Statutory Declaration outlining the attempts that the parent has made to have the

threads.answer:

Question: What is the proper procedure to follow when an individual has received an ITA under Express Entry and they cannot produce their non-accompanying dependents for a medical examination because they do not have custody of the minor child and the child's other parent is not co-operating? Will IRCC accept the file as complete with a Statutory Declaration outlining the attempts that the parent has made to have the child medically examined before the deadline to submit the e-APR?

accompanying dependent. All non-accompanying dependents (NAD) must be examined, regardless of custody
arrangements pursuant to A16(2)(b) & R30. Only the A25(1) Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) provision could
be used to exempt the principal applicant from having to meet this requirement if ever the circumstances are such that
there are humanitarian and compassionate reasons why the non-accompanying dependent could not be examined. The
applicant would need to make the case for an A25 H&C exemption and the officer will determine if the case is sufficient to warrant an exemption from the requirement that the dependent be examined. Please note that each application is considered on its own merits with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision.
We trust that this information will assist you.

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
Hi there,
The current Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system set out the criteria for which a Canadian credential wil count for Additional Points in the EE CRS. In particular, under subsection 30(3), the points are only assigned if:
a) studied in Canada at a Canadian educational institution
b) enrolled in full time study for at least 8 months; AND
c) was physically present in Canada for at least 8 months Additionally, points will not be assigned if more than half of the program was "distance learning". Given the current COVID situation which has necessitated that many students are studying online from overseas, and given IRCC's temporary measures respecting PGWP eligibility that takes into account online, overseas studies, will IRCC also lift the eligibility criteria listed above so that credentials completed during COVID can continue to count as eligible Canadian credentials and be awarded the additional EE points? This is a major issue, especially for graduate students, who are well-aligned for Canadian permanent residence under Federal Skilled Worker (or later under CEC), but who require the additional CRS points in order to be competitive in the EE pool. These students have supported Canadian institutions and the Canadian economy throughout the pandemic, making the difficult decision to study despite the challenges of online/overseas program delivery (with no reduction in tuition fees), who through no fault of their own are unable to travel to Canada, and thereby may be rendered ineligible for these important Additional Points. I work with a large number of business graduate students (MBA, specialized Master's students completing degrees in Al, Supply Chain, Marketing, Business Analytics, Finance, etc), who are highly skilled and educated and whose skills and Canadian education may be important to Canada's economic recovery; however, without the additional points for their completed Canadian degree, they may struggle to meet EE cut off scores. I would respectfully encourage IRCC to look at this issue and amend the Ministerial Instructions in light of the COVID impacts on Canadian educational credentials. Answer: The Department is continuing to monitor programs affected by COVID.
The current Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system set out the criteria for which a Canadian credential wil count for Additional Points in the EE CRS. In particular, under subsection 30(3), the points are only assigned if:
a) studied in Canada at a Canadian educational institution
b) enrolled in full time study for at least 8 months; AND
c) was physically present in Canada for at least 8 months Additionally, points will not be assigned if more than half of the program was "distance learning". We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:

1. A student got a completion letter on May 4, 2020. He had applied for a study permit extension in March which he received on August 15, 2020 valid until Aug 30, 2020. If he has files for PGWP on Aug 28 2020. Does the 90 day Study Permit expiry limit apply on study permit extension as well? mmigration, Réfugiés

regular PGWP application in this case?
2. Applicant came to Canada on Caregiver WP of 2 years expiring in March 2021. She went to her home country for 6 weeks for her marriage. How can she complete her 2 years experience in Canada, does she need a new LMIA to extend her work permit to complete her missing 6 weeks. If no LMIA needed, what are her other options to extend work permit or complete missing 6 weeks. If she applies under the new HCCP program now, (PR plus work permit), would she maintain an implied status after her original work permit ends in March 2021, as applications under this pilot program are taking longer times.
3. General question-How to get Study Permit online application for a person on a visitor visa present in Canada and get it processed from New York Visa Office from a) RCIC APR Portal b) MyCIC account?
I want to thank you in advance for your time and effort for providing your answers to the above queries.
Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions or concerns.
Thanks and regards,
threads.answer:
Good Day,
Please note that the Immigration Representatives Mailbox will only reply to general immigration program or policy related enquiries and cannot comment on specific cases. We are replying based on the general scenarios that you have described.
1. A student got a completion letter on May 4, 2020. He had applied for a study permit extension in March which he received on August 15, 2020 valid until Aug 30, 2020. If he has files for PGWP on Aug 28 2020. Does the 90 day Study Permit expiry limit apply on study permit extension as well? Does he need to submit a restoration application along with a regular PGWP application or just regular PGWP application in this case? If the student applied for the PGWP before the expiry of their study permit, no restoration is required. If the student submits the PGWP after their study permit expires, restoration on the study permit would be required. For more information on restoration when applying for a PGWP, please see: Work in Canada after you graduate: how to apply
2.Applicant came to Canada on Caregiver WP of 2 years expiring in March 2021. She went to her home country for 6 weeks for her marriage. How can she complete her 2 years experience in Canada, does she need a new LMlA to extend her work permit to complete her missing 6 weeks. If no LMiA needed, what are her other options to extend work permit or complete missing 6 weeks. If she applies under the new HCCP program now, (PR plus work permit), would she maintain an implied status after her original work permit ends in March 2021, as applications under this pilot program are taking longer times.
Under the Home Child Care Provider (HCCP) and Home Support Worker (HSW) pilots, the period of 24 months of required employment does not include
- any extended absence from Canada (including any time worked for an employer outside Canada) •periods of unemployment •prolonged sickness parental leave
A reasonable period of vacation time will be counted towards meeting the work experience requirement. For example, a 2-week period of paid vacation leave within a given 52-week period in which the applicant was engaged in qualifying work would qualify, whether that period of vacation was taken in Canada or outside Canada.
Should a candidate require additional experience to meet the requirements, they may: extend their current work permit, supported by a new LMlA, to continue to accumulate the work experience, or apply for a new work permit (including under the new HCCP/HSW pilots, that currently incorporate an open work permit application).
A temporary resident must apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have maintained their status (sometimes referred to as implied status) as a temporary resident during that period. If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph 186(u) and section 189 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations
(IRPR) (the right to continue working or studying under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal) apply only as long as the person remains in Canada.
Therefore, a caregiver would have maintained status as long as the HCCP/HSW permanent residence application (including an HCCP/HSW occupation-restricted open work permit application) is submitted before the expiry of the current work permit.
However, individuals who are on temporary status in Canada may consider submitting a separate work permit application or an extension of their existing work permit under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) or the International Mobility Program (IMP), even if they have already applied under the HCCP/HSW pilots. Permanent residence (PR) applications take longer to process and the COVID-19 pandemic has caused more delays. This affects when IRCC can issue the work permit related to the PR application. Even though they will have maintained status, it may be harder to get some government services or benefits. Also, if their PR application is refused, rejected for being incomplete, or returned for being over that year's cap, we'll return the related work permit application as well. If this happens: they'll lose their maintained status •if they are not eligible to restore their status, they'd have to leave Canada
For more information on this topic, please refer to the following website pages, Help Centre questions and answers, and Program Delivery Instructions (PDIs): Caregivers webpage
Information for Caregivers: Keeping your temporary resident status

threads.subject: Temporary Resident Status Questions -- REP-2020-2792
threads.question:
Good morning,
Please see responses to your questions below,
1. Is a foreign worker able to have multiple Work Permit applications in cue for processing at the same time for the same employer? Response: There is no limit on the number of work permit applications a client may submit. An application will only be placed into the processing queue once it is deemed completed under IRPR section 10; if a client submits multiple applications, each one will be assessed on its own merits including submission of necessary documents and proof of payment for required fees
2. Is a foreign worker able to have multiple Work Permit applications in cue for processing at the same time under different categories (for example: an Open Work Permit as the Spouse of Skilled Worker and an LMIA-based Work Permit?)? Response: See above. The client must provide the necessary documents and fees required for the specific work permit category of an application forit to be assessed as complete and placed into processing.
3. In an in-Canada extension application (for example, an application to change conditions/extend stay as a Worker or Visitor) an applicant is required to state the duration of their stay. If the end date indicated on the application form passes before a decision is reached on the application:
a. Will IRCC still proceed with adjudicating the application and issue a decision OR will the application be cancelled? Response: An officer will not refuse an application solely because the end date indicated by the client has passed. The officer will assess whether the applicant continues to meet the requirements of section 200 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, and whether they still meet the eligibility of their work permit category (including still having a genuine job offer in the case of an employer-specific work permit application).
b. If the application will be cancelled, does the individual then have the ability to apply for restoration? Response: If the applicant's initial work permit expired while their work permit extension application was pending and this application is refused/withdrawn/cancelled, their temporary resident status is no longer maintained under R183(5). They will then have 90 days from the final decision/cancellation/refusal date to apply for restoration if they would like to remain in Canada as a temporary resident.
c. If a decision will be issued, what date will IRCC use as the expiry date since the date requested in the application will have passed? Response: For employer-specific work permit applications, the work permit expiration is based on the duration of the job offer. For open work permits, the expiration date will vary depending on the specific program the applicant has applied under.
and Cizenship Caneda
d. Does the individual continue to have implied status until a decision is reached on the application? Response: As per R183(5), if the client submitted an application to extend their status before the expiry of their current work permit, their status is not "implied" but maintained until a decision is rendered on this application. They may also continue working should they meet the requirements of R186(u).
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Questions-Études sans permis de travail -- REP-2021-0037
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Le ressortissant étranger qui détient un permis de travail valide n’est pas autorisé à étudier au Canada pendant plus de six mois, à moins d'obtenir un permis d'études. Toutefois, les activités suivantes ne sont pas considérées comme des études aux fins de la Loi sur l'immigration et la protection des réfugiés (LIPR) et ne nécessitent pas de permis d’études : cours préscolaires (pré-maternelle) d’intérêt général ou d’auto-amélioration, apprentissage à distance et cours vérifiés.
Un étranger peut étudier sans permis d’études dans les cas suivants :
- Enfants mineurs qui se trouvent au Canada [L30(2)] Membres de la famille ou membres du personnel privé d'un représentant étranger accrédité [R188(1)a)] Membres des forces armées d'un État désigné au sens de la Loi sur les forces étrangères présentes au Canada [R188(1)b)] Cours de courte durée [R188(1)c)]
Par conséquent, le titulaire du permis de travail peut poursuivre des études de moins de six mois au Canada sans obtenir de permis d'études.
Merci,
Représentants immigration (IRCC)

threads.question:
Hello,
Please see our response below in red:
Example 1: subsequent and consecutive course
TW residing in Canada with a PGWP that expires December 31, 2023. The TW enrols for a short-term course of 4 months in duration that does not lead to a degree, diploma or certificate without obtaining a study permit. Upon completion of their 4- month course on August 31, 2022, the TFW decides to immediately enrol for a subsequent short-term course of 4 months in duration that begins on September 1, 2022 that will be completed by December 31, 2022 (e.g., within their period of authorized stay in Canada) that also does not lead to a degree, diploma or certificate. Does the TW need a study permit to enrol for the second 4-month course? No, as long as each course is less than 6 months, a study permit is not required.
Example 2: subsequent and non-consecutive course
A spouse of a work permit holder residing in Canada with a VR that expires August 31, 2024. The VR-holder enrols for a short-term course of 4 months in duration in Fall 2021 that does not lead to a degree, diploma or certificate without obtaining a study permit. The following Summer 2022, the VR-holder decides to enrol for another short-term course of 4 months in duration that will be completed by December 31, 2022 (e.g., within their period of authorized stay in Canada) and that also does not lead to a degree, diploma or certificate. Does the VR-holder need a study permit to enrol for the second 4-month course? Also No, as long as each course is less than 6 months no study permit is required.
More information on study permits and public policy can be found here.
Thank you kindly,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your follow up inquiry.
Foreign nationals in Canada without a study permit wishing to enrol in a subsequent course or program of study must apply outside Canada and obtain a study permit in the normal manner (e.g., at a Canadian visa office abroad).
Foreign nationals without a study permit will not be granted an extension of their authorized stay as a visitor simply for the purpose of completing a short-term course or program of less than 6 months that would last beyond their original authorized period of stay
For more information, please visit our website.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
Foreign nationals who are in Canada as a visitor or temporary worker do not need a study permit for a course or study program that lasts 6 months or less [R188(1)(c)]. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to 6 months). The duration of the course or program of study is often a more important consideration than the number of months the foreign national intends to study. With the exception of exchange programs, even if foreign nationals plan to study for 6 months or less, if the course or program is longer than 6 months, they need a study permit.
For more information on study permit applications, please visit our website.
I hope that this information is helpful to you.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Accelerated studies If a student completes their studies in less time than the normal length of the program (that is, they have accelerated their studies), the post-graduation work permit should be assessed on the length of the program of study.
For example, if the student is enrolled in a program of study that is normally 1 year in duration, but the student completes the requirements for the program of study within 8 months, they may be eligible for a post-graduation work permit that is valid for 1 year.

threads.answer:
Hello,
QUESTION: For a work permit as an Independent Professional under CETA, the website states the following is required:
a university degree or a qualification demonstrating knowledge of an equivalent level
My question is does the degree or qualification need to be in the field or related to the occupation in Canada for which the work permit is sought? Or can it be in an unrelated field so long as it is a degree or qualification as set out.

With respect to parents and grandparents sponsorship I understand that the co-signer should only be the spouse or the common law partner of the sponsor.
In the case of a separated spouse with no legal separation papers or document nor divorce, and is still married. They declared that they are separated for three consecutive years due to relationship breakdown. However, the co-signer is willing to sign the
sponsorship undertaking considering that they have two children together with the sponsor.
The question is can they proceed with the application to sponsor the parents ? the sponsor was fortunate to get into the draw, though she did it herself without having a counsel. Can you please enlighten this situation. Your advice is greatly appreciated. Thank you very much.

and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
Even if the sponsor is separated from their spouse (regardless of legal papers or the duration of the separation), unless they are divorced, they are still considered spouses of one another and therefore, a separated spouse can co-sign the sponsorship application.
It should be noted that a co-signer is equally responsible as the sponsor to provide basic requirements: food, clothing, shelter, fuel, utilities, household supplies, personal requirements and other goods and services, including dental care, eye care and other health needs not provided by public health care to the sponsored person. In addition, the co-signer is bound by the undertaking, and remains responsible for their relative(s) for the duration specified for the applicable family class category, which is 20 years for the parents and grandparents program.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox (IRCC)

threads.subject: Question for EE-CEC Stream -- REP-2020-2675
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to ’s Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Question:
My question is: "Will work experience (under PGWP) gained while the applicant was engaged in full-time distance learning in Canada (the entire program is delivered online, no study permit is required) qualified for Express Entry-CEC stream?"
According to IRCC website,
When a study permit is required
Foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or training that is more than 6 months in duration at a designated learning institution (DLI) in Canada.
The following activities are not considered studies for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and do not re quire a study permit:
- pre-school (pre-kindergarten)
- courses of general interest or self-improvement
- distance learning
- audited courses (typically by sitting in on an academic course, but without obtaining credit for it, or having the ability to obtain credit for it retroactively)
Distance learning
Distance learning can be through e-learning, correspondence, or internet courses. Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place.
Since by definition distance learning does not require one to be in Canada, a study permit cannot be issued for this type of course. For example, if a foreign national authorized to work in Canada is prohibited from engaging in studies as per a condition of their work permit, they are allowed to engage in distance learning courses.
Eligibility to apply for the Canadian Experience Class (Express Entry)
Citoyenneté Canada
Any period of employment when the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). [R87.1(3)(a)]. Officers should verify the work permit information in GCMS.
My question:
Because distance learning is NOT considered study for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and does not require a study permit. I think the work experience (under a valid PGWP) gained while applicant was studying full-time through distance learning (the entire program is delivered online, no study permit is required) in Canada is qualified for CEC work experience. Am I right? Please kindly confirm.
Answer:
No, for the purposes of this section, a period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study is not to be included in calculating a period of work experience. This includes full-time distance learning.
Distance learning is a process by which technology is used in ways where the student does not have to physically be in the place where the teaching is taking place.
As always, the onus is on the applicant to provide the appropriate documentation. At time of assessment, the IRCC reviewing officer will use their discretion when evaluating information and supporting documents in the application.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,

From Dear officer:
This email is to seek clarification in respect to a remark often seen on work permits of accompanying spouses of students (C42):
Note: Open work permit only valid while spouse is a full-time enrolled student at a designated learning
institution.
Our understanding of this remark is that its purpose is to ensure a good administration of the Act by making sure that an accompanying spouse will not be able to have a valid work permit while the student would abandon their studies or otherwise not respect the conditions imposed on foreign students by the IRPA and IRPR. For example, if a student enters Canada with a three-year study permit for a bachelor's degree, but decides to abandon their studies after one semester, we want to avoid giving a freeby 3-year open work permit to the spouse.
However, this remark may cause an issue when the student does complete their studies in the full respect of the Act and its regulations. By applying the remark strictly, the accompanying spouse (C42 holder) should cease employment as soon as the
and Cizenship Canada
student gets their final transcript or completion letter. They therefore lose the benefit of the traditional 90-day window that students have after graduation to extend their stay as a worker with the PGWP and thus, having reasonable time to find a level 0, A or B job that would allow their spouses to maintain their employment, should the couple wish to extend their stay after graduation. There exists the alternative, for the student, to have a 20-hour-a-week skilled job which would allow the spouse to extend their open work permit right after graduation, but a good proportion of dedicated students will have difficulties having such a part-time job while studying, and often while having other obligations such as caring for children.
Also, the strict application of the remark may mean that when extending their open work permit, the accompanying spouse may actually have lost their status (and therefore have to restore their status instead of extending it).
Based on the above, our question is:
When a C42 work permit bears the above-mentioned remark, would IRCC consider that this permit remains valid, and loses validity, at the moment when the student completes their studies? If IRCC considers such a permit to be valid, would it become invalid upon the first to occur on either the day that is 90 days after the day on which the study permit holder completes their studies, or the day on which the C42 work permit expires?
Thank you very much, kind regards,
