Question: My client received points for 2 years work experience even though he had completed 23 months. Based on the points for 24 months (while he had acquired Canadian work experience for 23 months only), he received ITA for PR application. At the time of ITA, he was short of experience by 2 days. Please advise if we should: decline the ITA or apply for PR under the same ITA but after 2 days as applicant will complete 24 months after 2 days or, accept ITA and apply for PR without any delay?
Answer: Sometimes applicants will receive an ITA before they accumulated 12 months of work experience. We are aware that the system calculates work experience by months and not actual days worked and that some applicants may receive an ITA a month or so early. There is no need to decline the ITA or delay submission of your application as long as the applicant meets the Express Entry minimum entry criteria and possess the qualifications for which they received their CRS score at the time their invitation to apply (ITA) is issued, or their e-APR was received by IRCC, as per section A11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. IRCC examining officers are aware of this, and when looking at the application they will take into consideration factors such as the continuous work status, the Offer of Employment Letter from the same employer, and whether the applicant reached the experience required by the time the application is processed.
Question: The applicant has Canadian education. He has an original degree certificate as proof of education. But, he has
unofficial transcript instead of official one for the same program.

An unofficial transcript would be acceptable in addition to the degree or certificate. If necessary, an Officer may ask for a copy of the official transcript at a later date.

threads.subject: Dividend is ok for ICT business owner? -- (REP-2021-0836) -- REP-2021-1341

Dear IRCC,
Thank you for your reply.
Is a Retained Earning considered to be acceptable as a form of salary as well?
Best regards,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Question: Is a Retained Earning considered to be acceptable as a form of salary as well?
Answer: For the purposes of the LMlA-exemption code for intra-company transferees (C12), the foreign national must have an 'employer-employee' relationship with the Canadian entity. Retained earnings are not acceptable as salary as they are corporate income and not paid out to employees.
Previously, we indicated that Dividends are an acceptable form of salary as it can be legally paid to owners in Canada. This answer was not complete. Even though legal in Canada, paying dividends instead of salary does not create the employer-employee relationship and would not meet the requirements for the issuance of a work permit for an intra-company transferee. In addition, salaries are required to be reasonable and stable, whereas dividends can fluctuate based on the corporate active business income.
The employer compliance regulations sections require that the employer pay the wages that are not less favorable than those provided in the offer of employment. As dividends can drop in price, or be suspended or eliminated at the discretion of the corporate authority, they are not guaranteed salary.

threads.subject: Express Entry-Points for Canadian educational credential -- REP-2021-1131
threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question:
In many cases, programs of study that are typically held in person were forced to pivot to online delivery during the pandemic. My questions revolve around the impacts of online learning on international students’ ability to claim CRS points for Canadian education credential.
The Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system states the following:
30 (5) For the purpose of this section, the following are not eligible credentials:
- (b) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program; or My questions below relate to this exception and assume that the international student is physically present in Canada:
1. If a school defines the course as on campus but due to covid they had to pivot to online delivery, is it considered distance learning or not since it’s defined by the institution as on campus?
2. How does IRCC calculate course duration? Is it based on duration of study (i.e. weeks), number of courses completed or number of credits obtained?
3. If an international student starts a course online then finishes the course on campus, is it considered completed by distance learning or in person?
Answer:
1. Any course that is completed online is considered distance learning.
2. The course duration is defined by the school. They decide if it is a 1 year course or 8 month course and how many credits are required to complete the course. The province reviews and as long as they agree the school becomes “designated” (DLI). The information for course duration can be found on their websites.
3. If the international student completed more than half the program by distance learning then it would be considered to have been completed by distance learning. If more than half the course was completed in person then it would be considered as having been completed on campus.
1*and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada Informat dlodr tet Iomtin ct For Express Entry, there have been no changes to how CRS points are awarded for education. A Canadian educational credential cannot be awarded if the credentials were obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted
to more than half of the program length.

threads.subject: Clarification on Temporary Resident Visa -- REP-2021-1346
threads.question:
Hello,
Question: Our client, a citizen of Argentina, has extend his work permit as well as his wife’s (also citizen of Argentina) open spousal work permit. Their W-1 temporary resident visas have expired. However, our client holds a B-1 temporary resident visa valid until 2023 and his spouse holds a valid V-1 temporary resident visa valid until March 2022. Can they use their existing B-1 and V-1 temporary resident visas to travel internationally and re-enter Canada? Or, should they apply for a new temporary resident visas matching their current status as foreign workers, W-1?
Answer
The ability to re-enter Canada with a given visa will depend on whether the foreign national has been issued a single-entry or multiple-entry visa and the type of visa issued. For example, a B-1 visa is issued to someone who is entering Canada as a business visitor. To enter again on a B-1 visa, the individual must provide evidence they meet the requirements of a B-1 visitor, for example, a letter of invitation from the invitor when they appear at a port of entry. If the foreign national's visa has expired, they should apply to extend the visa to allow them re-entry to Canada. For more information, please visit this webpage.
Additionally, as different visas have different conditions attached to them, it may be in the best interest of the foreign national to have a visa that aligns with their current status. Ultimately, the onus is on the foreign national to satisfy the officer that they meet the necessary requirements for their category and desired status.
We trust you will find this information useful and thank you for your patience.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: EXPRESS ENTRY CANDIDATES-Clarification of section 3(1)(t) of current OIC -- REP-2021-1242
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
We are writing to seek clarification of how PR approvals of overseas candidates will be treated under the latest version of the Order in Council ([https://orders-in-council.canada.ca/attachment.php?](https://orders-in-council.canada.ca/attachment.php?) attach=41036&lang=en)
Section 3(1)(t) of the Minimizing the Risk of Exposure to COVID-19 in Canada Order (Prohibition of Entry into Canada from any Country Other than the United States) Order in Council states:
“..section 2 does not apply to ...(t) a person whose application for permanent residence was
approved under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, and who received written notice
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
of the approval, but who has not yet become a permanent resident under that Act;"(e.a).
Is it possible to please clarify how exactly “written approval” will be defined in this scenario? Does an overseas Express Entry candidate who received a “virtual landing” letter or COPR portal invite by email while they were physically outside of Canada be considered to have received “written notice” of the approval of their PR application, and be permitted to board a flight to Canada without a PR card or PRTD?
The reason we ask is because we are still finding that many applicants are receiving very confusing communication from IRCC with regard to getting “landed” virtually, even though the applicants have been trying to notify IRCC for several months that they are not currently inside Canada. Per section 71.1 of IRPR they would therefore not be considered eligible for “virtual landing” but they are being left in a strange grey zone where they are also not being issued PR visas and COPRs in order to get on a flight and complete their PR landing at a Canadian port of entry as they would have been permitted to do prior to the pandemic.
Many thanks,
Page 4523
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Please be advised that "written notice of the approval" in the context of permanent residence as mentioned in section 3(1)(t) of the Minimizing the Risk of Exposure to COVID-19 in Canada Order (Prohibition of Entry into Canada from any Country Other than the United States) Order in Council, is defined by IRCC as receiving a Confirmation of Permanent Residence (CoPR). An individual who is outside of Canada and whose application for permanent residence has been approved, will receive a CoPR (and permanent resident visa if applicable) which they will use to travel to Canada to be landed at the port of entry. If the applicant has been approved and is in Canada, they will receive a virtual landing letter or an invitation to the permanent residence portal to complete their landing. Through the portal they will have access to their eCoPR.
If a client has been landed virtually while they are outside of Canada, they should contact the processing office to advise that they are outside of Canada. In turn, they will be informed of the next steps on how to move forward with their application.
Sincerely, Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good morning,
Question: Avant son entrée au Canada, le TET avait signé un contrat de travail avec l’employeur A. Il était supposé travailler dans la ville
A. Toutefois, avant son entrée au Canada toujours, il a changé d’emploi pour l’employeur B qui avait des places disponibles sur un EIMT positif. L’EIMT positif de l’employeur B indique des lieux de travail dans la ville B. Ce changement d’employeur est autorisé par le contrat de travail et le PTAS. À l’arrivée au Canada, au point d’entrée, le TET se voit délivrer un permis de travail qui indique : Employeur : Employeur B No EIMT : EIMT positif de l’employeur B Emplacement de l'emploi: Ville A Nous trouvons cela très étrange que l’agent des services frontaliers ait émis un permis de travail avec le bon nom d’employeur, le bon numéro d’ElMT, mais qu’il ait choisi d’indiquer la ville A comme emplacement de l’emploi. La ville B est clairement indiquée comme lieu d’emploi à l’EIMT positif de l’employeur B. Est-ce une erreur qui doit être corrigée en demande une modification d’un document d’immigration valide : [https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/services/demande/formulaires-demande-guides/demande-modification-fiche-relative-droit-etablissement-confirmation-residence-permanente-documents-resident-temporaire-](https://www.canada.ca/fr/immigration-refugies-citoyennete/services/demande/formulaires-demande-guides/demande-modification-fiche-relative-droit-etablissement-confirmation-residence-permanente-documents-resident-temporaire-) valides.html?

Tous les permis de travail du PTAS doivent être imprimés avec la condition suivante : Employeur MEX/CCSAWP approuvé uniquement. Valable pour travailler dans TOUTES LES PROVINCES. Minor children who are already in Canada accompanying a parent who is permitted to study or work may study in Canada without a study permit at the pre-school, primary and secondary levels in the following scenarios:
- they are either accompanying parents claiming refugee status or are claimants themselves;
- one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident;
- one of their parents (biological or adoptive) is authorized to work or study in Canada; this includes temporary residents who are o work permit holders, o study permit holders, o visitor status holders (e.g., visitor record holders) who are either authorized to work without a permit, as per section 186 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), or authorized to study without a permit, as per section R188; or

Minor children of a temporary resident (visitor) who is not authorized to work or study require a study permit to study in Canada.

threads.answer:
Hello,
In general, all temporary residents (including students) are required to leave Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay (i.e. when their permit expires). However, as per section R181, a temporary resident may apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, this period is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)].
Such a person is considered to have legal status as a temporary resident during the processing period and can continue to work under maintained status (while respecting the conditions of their study permit work authorization), so long as their new application remains in progress and has not yet been finalized.

threads.subject: Permanent Residence for Temporary resident permit holders -- REP-2021-1340
threads.question:
Dear ImmReps,
I have questions concerning PR for TRP holders, namely:
1. According to the Operational Instructions and Guidelines published by IRCC regarding “Temporary resident
permits: applying for permanent residence", the following is noted regarding “Break in continuity":
A break in continuity occurs when TRP holders, without authorization for re-entry, leave
Canada, or when they do not apply for a subsequent permit before the expiration of their existing permit. In both situations, a new TRP could still be issued but the permit holder's electronic file would be marked with a break in continuity, affecting eligibility for permanent resident status.
Even with authorization to re-enter, prolonged periods of absence from Canada may lead to a
finding that there has been a break in continuity of residence in Canada.
In light of the above, would a short absence from Canada during the summer for no more than 2 weeks at a time, with authorization (i.e. the permit authorized re-entry), be considered a break in continuity?
2. Since each TRP holder must apply for PR separately from other eligible family members, and there is nothing in the Act and regulations that sets out a minimum age by which an eligible TRP holder can apply for PR, we therefore understand that minors can apply on their own for PR as TRP holders. Could you kindly confirm if our
understanding is correct? If our understanding is incorrect, please provide us with the legislation/policy that states otherwise. I am looking forward to hearing from you. Kind regards,
Lim.Elina
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please see the response to your two inquiries below:
1. A short absence from Canada during the summer for no more than 2 weeks, with authorization (i.e. authorized re-entry) would not be considered a break in continuity. A break in continuity occurs when TRP holders, without authorization for re-entry, leave Canada, or when they do not apply for a subsequent permit before the expiration of their existing permit. Even with authorization to re-enter, prolonged periods of absence from Canada may lead to a finding that there has been a break in continuity of residence in Canada. An officer must be satisfied that the
requirement of continuous residence has been met. If necessary, an officer may request
documentation to demonstrate the reason for absences from Canada.
2. Your understanding is correct. There is no provision to allow members of the permit holder class to include accompanying family members in their applications for permanent residence. At the time of the applicant's original entry to Canada, any accompanying family members would have required their own TRP. In order to be considered for permanent residence, such individuals would need to submit their own applications under the permit holder class as a principal applicant.
Please see [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/publications-) manuals/operational-bulletins-manuals/permanent-residence/non-economic-classes/permits.html for further information.
We hope you find this information useful.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Please confirm that for programs that are being fully delivered online while applicants are outside Canada.
Answer:
There is no specific length for the second post-secondary credential. However, it must meet the below requirements.
Pursuant to R73.1, a Canadian educational credential means any diploma, certificate or credential, issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions.
In addition, the credential must meet the requirements stated in the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions – MI 11(3) and MI 30 (1)-(5).
For Express Entry, there have been no changes to how CRS points are awarded for education. A Canadian educational credential cannot be awarded if the credentials were obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program length.

threads.subject: How does transferring schools or using transfer credits impact eligibility for a Post-Graduation Work Permit? --
threads.question:
Good Morning,
I am writing to confirm and clarify a couple questions related to post-graduate work permit (PGWP) eligibility.
IRCC states that to be eligible for a PGWP, a student must have completed a qualifying study program at a DLi that is at least eight months long that led to a degree, diploma or certificate. It is also a requirement that the student maintain full-time status as a student in Canada during each semester of the study program. IRCC also seems to recognize that students may transfer between DLIs for PGWP eligibility, as it states that the combined length of study must be at least 8 months and only studies completed at the DLI will be counted. However, IRCC does not seem to elaborate on how it may handle cases where a student may transfer from a DLI with a non-
PGWP eligible program to a DLI that is a PGWP eligible program.
My questions are as follows:
1. If a student transfers from a DLI but non-PGWP program to a DLI PGWP eligible program, is the student's eligibility for a PGWP affected? In other words, if a student completes three semesters at a DLI/non-PGWP eligible program that is considered equivalent to first year studies and then transfers to the DLl school and program that is eligible for PGWP and completes three more years of study before getting a bachelor's degree, will the student be eligible for a PGWP?
i. In other words, say a student studies at both School A for three semesters of university transfer credit, which will be accepted by School B as one full-time year of first year undergraduate degree studies, and also School B for three years of study to get a Bachelor's degree after completing the year at School A. School A is a DLI but the program is not eligible for a PGWP. School B is a DLI and eligible for PGWP. Does the initial first year study at School A, whether or not it is part-time or full-time, have any effect on the student's eligibily for a PGWP after completing the degree program on a full-time basis at School B?
2. If a student completes three or four semesters at a DLI but non-PGWP program but studies part-time in one of the semesters before transferring to the DLl and PGWP eligible program and completing three more years of study before gettting a bachelor's degree, is the student still eligible for a PGWP?
3. Are transfer credits considered part of “each semester” that a student must maintain full-time status or only the semesters completed at the degree-issuing institution?
4. When IRCC refers to “study program", do you mean the credential (degree, diploma or certificate) or just the program/time completed at the DLl issuing the degree/diploma/certificate?
Any advice or clarification you can provide on these questions would be greatly appreciated. Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to your reply.
Regards,
threads.answer:
## REP-2021-1472
Good morning,
Thank you for your email, below are responses to your inquiries.
1. Based on the students PGWP eligibility, the semesters taken in the school that is eligible for PGWP will be counted. For example if the client completed one year at non DLl or a school that is not eligible for PGWP, and one year at a PGWP eligible school, then only one year would be counted towards PGWP eligibility. The transfer credits from non PGWP programs are not eligible.
2.The client will have to study full time for the full duration of the program to be eligible for PGWP. If the client attended a school as a part time student and then transferred to another DLl for another program that is PGWP eligible, then the client is not eligible for PGWP.
a. For example: the client study's at ICM and takes one semester Part time and then transfers these credits to get advanced standings at the U of Min the 2ⁿd or 3rd year, then their PGWP application will be refused because they did not study full time for the full duration of the program.
3. Transfer credits are assessed at the beginning of each program. The school decides if the transfer credits provide advanced standing in the program or not. If the transfer credits are from a PGWP eligible school then the client is eligible for PGWP according to the duration of their program. If the transfer credits are from overseas, then those credits are not counted towards the PGWP.
4. The term study program within IRCC refers to certificate/degree/diploma issued from Non DLI PGWP and DLI PGWP eligible schools.
I hope this information is helpful.
Thank you
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: W: Proof of citizenship-Canadian parent's citizenship certificate not available -- REP-2021-
threads.question:
Hello
Thank you for your email.
In the case you described (Canadian citizen parent granted citizenship prior to the birth of a child abroad) acceptable proof of citizenship for the Canadian parent includes a copy of the Canadian parent's citizenship certificate or citizenship card.
A valid Canadian passport, though acceptable as a piece of identification, is not acceptable as proof of citizenship for the purposes of an application for a citizenship certificate. However, an applicant may still wish to include it in their application as supporting documentation to their claim.
You may refer to this page for more information on which documents may be used to prove Canadian citizenship: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/documents.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/proof-citizenship/documents.html)
If, for some reason, an applicant cannot provide the requested proof of citizenship they must include a letter explaining why the document is missing from the application package (i.e.; why they can't obtain it). If the Canadian parent's citizenship certificate has been lost or stolen, would recommend that the Canadian parent apply for a replacement certificate concurrently with the proof of citizenship application for their child, ensuring that both individuals will have their proof of citizenship as needed, should both applications be approved. An explanation of this scenario within the package containing both applications would provide clarity and context for our processing network should your clients wish to proceed in this manner.
Hope that helps.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Hello,
Please see our response to your question.
Question: We are seeking confirmation as to when the conditions of a newly extended work permit becomes
effective on a hiring employer. While the issued work permit typically includes an "In Force
From," the work permit holder and employer would usually only become aware this date upon receipt of the issue permit. This is usually several days or week after the work permit was issued and the "In Force From" date.
Given the timing of the notification of the "In Force From" date, in a case where the newly approved wage exceeds the previous wage, would the employer be expected to make retroactive payment to the affected worker to cover the period between the "In Force From" date and the date they received the new work permit?
Answers to Question 1 & 2:
Question 1: We are seeking confirmation as to when the conditions of a newly extended work permit becomes effective on a hiring employer. While the issued work permit typically includes an "In Force From," the work permit holder and employer would usually only become aware this date upon receipt of the issue permit. This is usually several days or week after the work permit was issued and the "In Force From" date.
Answer to question 1: As per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) paragraph 209.1(1)(a), an employer “ must comply with the following conditions during the period of employment for which the work permit is issued to the foreign national” (emphasis added). A foreign national may begin work on the day the work permit is issued to them (i.e. Printed). When foreign nationals receive their work permit at a port of entry, they are authorized to work from the moment the document is in their hand. For foreign nationals who apply after entry to Canada, their work permit is printed and mailed to them, however, they are notified electronically on the date that their work permit is issued to expect it.
Question 2: Given the timing of the notification of the "In Force From" date, in a case where the newly approved wage exceeds the previous wage, would the employer be expected to make retroactive payment to the affected worker to cover the period between the "In Force From" date and the date they received the new work permit?
Answer to question 2: As per the IRPR during the period of the work permit' issued on the basis of an offer of employment the employer is required to pay the wages set out in the offer. If there is a period of time that the wages were not paid or were less favourable than the offer, the employer must be able to provide justification for this discrepancy. If an employer is not meeting, or may not have met, their regulatory responsibilities as an employer, they can voluntarily disclose this information to us.

threads.question:
Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience.
Question: Can an individual have two eAPR pending at the same time under different streams (FSW and CEC)? We understand that you cannot have two express entry profiles at the same time. However, the issue regarding whether an individual can have two eAPR pending does not seem to be addressed anywhere online.
In other words, if a Foreign National was issued an ITA to apply under FSW and submitted the eAPR and sometime has passed and they now qualify for CEC and have set up a subsequent EE profile and were issued a new ITA under CEC -is there any requirement to withdraw the first pending eAPR that was filed under the FSw? Answer: An applicant may have more than one application in progress, but only one can be finalizes with permanent resident status granted. At the point where one of the applications in progress has been approved, any other pending application should be administratively withdrawn and the applicant notified. The applicant can only obtain permanent residence under one program.

threads.answer:
Hello Mr.
Thank you for your email.
Paragraph 10(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations requires that a positive decision from Service Canada be included with a work permit application for it to be considered complete. IRCC acknowledges that there are times where a work permit will be expiring and an application for an LMIA was submitted with sufficient time for a decision to be rendered but that decision has not yet been made. The Department, therefore, allows a grace period of 60 days for the LMIA application to be finalized. This is an exceptional measure and allows foreign nationals to benefit from maintained status as per subsection 183(5). It also allows the foreign national the authority to work without a work permit as per the conditions on the existing permit while the work permit application is being processed.
During normal processing times, IRCC has found that 60 days is sufficient for employers who submitted their LMIA application 30 to 60 days in advance of the work permit application. However, the current longer processing times for LMlAs is a result of prioritization during the COVID-19 pandemic and should be resolved soon. IRCC is satisfied with the concurrent processing facilitation measure balanced against the legal requirement in the regulations.
Thank you,

RESPONSE: Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and its regulations, status and authorization are two separate things. Therefore, the answer is separate for clarity. In addition, a PR application has no effect on any temporary resident status.
Status: A person who is in Canada with valid temporary resident status and applies under section 181 of the IRPR for an extension of that status, may be extended by operation of law under R183(5) if a decision has not been made on that application prior to the expiration of their present status. If this person leaves Canada, their status as a temporary resident ends. On their return to Canada, the border services officer will make a new decision under A22 to allow the person entry to Canada.
Work: The pargraph you have quoted R186(u) only applies if an application to renew a work permit has been submitted under R201 and on the expiration of the existing work permit the person may be authorized to work without a permit as long as they remain in Canada and continue meeting the conditions of the work permit that existed at time of application.
Therefore, if a person holds a valid work permit and applies to renew that work permit (for PGWP under a different work permit category), on the expiration of the work permit, if no decision has been rendered and the person remains in Canada, their temporary resident status is maintained by R183(5) and they would be authorized to work without a permit as per R186(u).
If during the period that the work permit renewal application is processing, the person leaves Canada, their temporary resident status ends but their authorization to work under the work permit remains valid until the work permit expiry or a removal order is issued.
On the return to Canada of the person : Existing work permit is still valid -the border services officer will determine if the person still meets requirements of A22 for temporary resident status and if satisfied may admit the person as a temporary resident and the existing work permit would provide authority to work until its expiry. The person would only have valid temporary resident status until the expiry of the work permit. If after entry, the work permit expires and still no decision on the work permit renewal application is made then both R183(5) and R186(u) would provide maintained status and authority to work without a permit.
Existing work permit has expired and no decision is made on the work permit renewal application: The border service officer will determine if the person meets the requirements of A22 for temporary resident status. If the person is allowed entry as a temporary resident they will not have the authority to work without a permit under R186(u) as they have left Canada. In addition, the validity of their status will be 6 months unless the border services officer indicates differently in writing.
Further information on maintained status and the authority to work without a permit may be found in the publically available instructions for officers here: Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status) and R186(u)— Pending decision on work permit renewal

How are employment requirements defined?
Employment requirements represent prerequisites generally requested by employers and/or professional associations to enter a given occupation. Several types of requirements are listed:
- type and level of education including specific subject matter if relevant, starting with the lowest possible requirement for entry into the occupation;
- specific training required, including apprenticeship, on-the-job, or internal training;
- experience in a related occupation, especially for supervisory or managerial occupations;
- licences, certificates or affiliations; and/or
- other requirements not dependent on formal education, such as athletic abilities, artistic talent, or presentation of a portfolio.
While some occupations have very specific employment requirements, others have a wide range of acceptable
requirements. The following terminology is used to indicate the level of the requirement:
- "Is required" indicates a definite requirement.
- "Is usually required" means that the qualification is generally expressed as required by a majority of employers, but is not always mandatory.
- "May be required" describes requirements that some employers may impose, but are not universal.
Qualities related to personal suitability that may have an impact on employability are not described in the classification. These factors are subjective and determined by employers and are assessed during the hiring process. Thank you,

threads.subject: duration of visitor records -- REP-2021-1533
threads.question:
Good day,
Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and its regulations, status and authorization are two separate things. A visitor record provides status as a temporary resident and conditions may also be imposed on the issuance of a visitor record. Therefore, once the temporary resident leaves Canada, the status ends, which means that the visitor record becomes invalid.
A work permit provides authorization to work, and depending on the circumstances, may also provide proof of status (R194). Foreign nationals may hold an authorization to work and not have an status in Canada -refugee claimants being an obvious example (R202). Thus, if a person leaves Canada while holding a work permit, their status as a temporary resident ends, but the authorization to work exist until the work permit expires or the person is issued a removal order (R209).
On the persons return to Canada, the border services officer will determine if the person still meets the requirements of A22 for admittance as a temporary resident. If they are satisfied and allow the person to enter Canada, the authority to work still exists as the work permit is still valid (R196). However, unless the border service officer indicates otherwise, the validity of the existing work permit is the 'period of authorized stay' as this is a condition imposed by an officer under R185.
Regards,

threads.question:
Good morning,
Question: If a client is in Canada on a Post-Graduate Work Permit (PGWP), and applies jointly for a Temporary Resident Permit and an Open Work Permit (TRP/O WP) before the expiry of the PGWP, would said client benefit from implied/maintained status to remain and work in Canada until a decision is made on the TRP/O WP applications?
Answer: Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and its regulations (IRPR), status and authorization are two separate things. Temporary resident status is maintained when a foreign national applies for an extension of that status as per section 181 of the IRPR. If a decision is not made by the time their existing status expires, the temporary resident status is maintained by law as per subsection 183(5) of the IRPR. A temporary resident permit is issued under section 24 of the IRPA. An application for a TRP is not an application for extension of status as per section 181 of the IRPR, therefore on the expiry of the existing status there is no continuation of that status by operation of law as per subsection 183(5). For clarity, no, temporary resident status is not maintained when a TRP is applied for.
Authorization to work is obtained on the issuance of a work permit or when authorized by section 186 of the IRPR. A foreign national who holds a work permit and applies for a subsequent work permit under section 201 of the IRPR, is authorized to work without a permit under paragraph 186(u) of the IRPR until a decision is made on the work permit application, unless they leave Canada. threads.answer:
Good morning,
Question: If we use CETA, do we have to submit any application, paperwork etc. in Canada? Is the work permit issued at the airport/the port of entry?
Response: There are a number of LMIA exempt work permit categories that a foreign national may apply for under CETA; each category has its own set of eligibility requirements which the foreign national must meet in order to be issued a work permit under CETA. Foreign nationals should be able to provide all supporting documents that will demonstrate to a processing officer that they meet the work permit category's eligibility criteria. For more information on the requirements of each category, see: Canada-European Union (EU) Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)
A foreign national may apply at the port of entry (POE) if they are eligible to do so under R198(1), however due to the complexity of the work permit category for Investors under CETA (T46), foreign nationals should apply for their work permits through Canadian missions abroad as border service officers may not have operational capacity to process these types of applications at the POE. When foreign nationals apply for a work permit outside of Canada and their application is approved, they will be issued a letter of introduction (LOl) which the foreign national can present upon arrival in Canada to have their work permit issued at the POE. Having the application processed before entering Canada expedites the admission process at the POE.

I am looking for clarification on the following question:
Can a caregiver who is working in Quebec on an employer-specific work permit as a TFW in an eligible occupation use that work experience to apply through the Home Child-Care Provider or Home Support Worker Pilot?
For example, if the caregiver has 16 months of work experience and then moves to Ontario and is then issued an occupation-specific work permit, will they be able to apply using the 16 months accumulated in Quebec and then the 8 months completed in Ontario?

中 Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Greetings,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox.
The work experience gained in the province of Quebec can count as qualifying experience under the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker Pilots, provided it otherwise meets all other criteria. Caregivers applying with less than 24 month experience will receive an occupation-restricted open work permit that will have the following condition: "may not engage in employment in the province of Quebec".
As indicated on the website:
When you have 24 months of qualifying work experience, send us proof. You must send us proof of your qualifying work experience no later than 36 months after you get your work permit. - all 24 months of total work experience is gained in the 36 month period before you send us proof this includes past and future work experience •it was full-time work of at least 30 hours of paid work each week you weren't a full-time student while you were working
Make sure to keep any documents to show that you have 24 months of work experience such as: •job offers
- contracts pay stubs tax information issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)
Please refer to the Program Delivery Instructions specific to the Qualifying Canadian work experience for more details on what constitutes eligible experience.
All officers assessing Federal economic immigration program applications are required to assess the intent of the applicant to reside outside Quebec as a permanent resident, under terms of jurisdiction governing selection of economic immigrants outlined in the Canada-Quebec Accord. For this reason, immigrants applying under the federal Economic Class programs must intend to establish in Canada outside Quebec, and must satisfy an officer regarding that intent. Assessing the genuineness of intent to reside can be supported by a range of documents/information, including but not limited to the applicant's own declaration or affidavit of intent, job offers, rental agreements, home purchases or utility bills from outside of Quebec. It is up to the applicant to provide sufficient proof to satisfy the officer that they intend to reside outside of Quebec as a permanent resident.

threads.subject: Hiring psw -- REP-2021-1660
threads.question:
Hi there,
Can a private retirement home company hire Personal Support Workers from abroad with LMIA?
Or what is the way, I know domestic employer can hire through HS WP pilot, but what about retirement homes?
Thanks in advance
Regards
Cioyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representative Mailbox.
Question 1:
Can a private retirement home company hire Personal Support Workers from abroad with LMIA?
Response:
Please refer to the Refusal to process Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)-required work permit applications for caregivers received on or after June 18, 2019 for information on whether the personal support worker can apply for an LMIA work permit outside Canada.
Question 2:
What is the way, I know domestic employer can hire through HSWP pilot, but what about retirement homes?
Response:
The intent of the Home Child Care Provider and Home Support Worker Pilots is to meet the needs of private individuals
and families requiring full-time care in their own home.
Group home settings, including retirement/senior homes, as well as daycares, do not qualify under these pilots; the place of work must be a private residence. This applies even if the caregiver resides with multiple clients requiring care.
The pilots align with the description of work performed in the National Occupational Classification (NOC) codes 4411 and 4412. Work performed in nursing home or senior healthcare facilities would more closely align with other NOCs
and as such do not qualify under this pilot.
In 2020, the occupational group for Nurse Aides, Orderlies and Patient Service Associates, National Occupational
Classification (NOC) 3413, was added as an eligible occupation under the “NOC C Initiative” of the Provincial Nominee Program, allowing provinces and territories to use additional allocation spaces to address a permanent labour shortage in the occupation, based on their own labour market priorities.
The Government recognizes that some employers are facing difficulties finding workers, including personal support workers and other essential services. In August 2020, IRCC introduced a temporary public policy allowing certain temporary residents in Canada with valid visitor status to apply for an employer-specific work permit from within Canada, if they have a job offer. This public policy benefits employers who face challenges hiring the workers they
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
need, as well as temporary residents who would like to contribute their labour and skills to Canada's recovery from the pandemic. This temporary measure will be in place until February 28, 2022.
We trust that this information will be of assistance.
Regards,
The Immigration Representative Mailbox

Good afternoon,
In regards to your inquires on students changing their DLl study program, if students changed their study program within the same DLl after receiving their visa but before traveling to Canada, then this change would not affect their previously approved study permit application. As long as they attend the same DLl, they do not need to reapply for a study permit. When traveling to Canada, they must bring the original and updated LOA from the same DLl along with the original POE letter issued by IRCC, and other required documents to present to CBSA officers. If a student changes their program of study to a different DLl after their visa is issued, they will have to submit a new study permit application to IRCC.
Students should immediately submit their new LOA to IRCC using the online web form if they made any changes to their program of study within the same DLl or to a different DLl while their study permit application is still in process.

With regards to your question on family size, it may vary depending on which member of an extended household decides to submit a sponsorship application. However, the definition of dependent child goes on to state that the dependent does not have a spouse or common law partner of their own.
Furthermore, even if he were not married and would therefore count as his father's dependent, the 20-year-old son could co-sign the application and add his income to his father's should that be how the family decided to proceed.

Good day,
Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and its regulations, status and authorization are two separate things. A visitor record provides status as a temporary resident and conditions may also be imposed on the issuance of a visitor record. Therefore, once the temporary resident leaves Canada, the status ends, which means that the visitor record becomes invalid.
A work permit provides authorization to work, and depending on the circumstances, may also provide proof of status (R194). Foreign nationals may hold an authorization to work and not have an status in Canada -refugee claimants being an obvious example (R202). Thus, if a person leaves Canada while holding a work permit, their status as a temporary resident ends, but the authorization to work exist until the work permit expires or the person is issued a removal order (R209).
On the persons return to Canada, the border services officer will determine if the person still meets the requirements of A22 for admittance as a temporary resident. If they are satisfied and allow the person to enter Canada, the authority to work still
exists as the work permit is still valid (R196). However, unless the border service officer indicates otherwise, the validity of the existing work permit is the 'period of authorized stay' as this is a condition imposed by an officer under R185.
Regards,

obtained either in Canada or abroad (in the latter case accompanied by a ECA). In this case the credential is Canadian and it is from a private college. It meets the relevant definition as per R73(1) so points for Education should be granted.
Relevant definition:
"73 (1) The following definitions apply in this Division.
Canadian educational credential means any secondary school diploma or any post-
secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian
program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and

"Points for Canadian educational credential
Eligible credentials

Canadian educational credential means any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary

Hello,
Students can work full-time while waiting for a decision on their post-graduation work permit application if, at the time they submitted their application, they:
had a valid study permit,
- had completed your program of study, were eligible to work off-campus without a permit, and
- did not work off-campus more than 20 hours a week during academic sessions.
Applicants who apply for a PGWP prior to the expiration of their study permit are eligible to begin working full time while their application is processing. Applicants may apply for a PGWP from overseas.

threads.answer:
Good day
QUESTION: What is the functional guidance from IRCC regarding truck driver applicants from overseas i.e. is the TFWP open to truck driver applicants from overseas or not? If yes, what is the general advise IRCC can give to employers and/or overseas truck driver applicants so that they can show that the MELT ground will/can be met or has been met?
RESPoNSE: Pargaph 200(3)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations states that an officer is prohibited from issuing a work permit if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the foreign national is unable to perform the work sought. If a Mandatory Entry Level Training (MELT) is required to drive a long-haul truck in a specific province then the officer must be satisifed that the foreign national has the MELT prior to the issuance of a work permit or that the foreign national will be able to obtain the MELT on arrival in Canada.
IRCC and ESDC are reviewing situations where there is mandatory training or certification requirements and will be providing more extensive instructions to officers in the future. However, at this time guidance is that applicants should be providing proof that they are registered in a MELT course (or when registration is expected), who will be paying for the training, will the foreign national be receiving wages while attending the training, and what the contingency plans are if the foreign worker fails the MELT course.

Moving to the next education level
If your study permit is still valid, you don't need to change or apply for a new permit if you’re moving between school levels. This could be:
- primary to high school
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
- high school to post-secondary

- any other move between school levels
If your study permit will expire, you need to apply to extend it.
If your permit has already expired, you must restore your status as a student at the same time as you apply to extend your study permit. You must apply to restore your status within 90 days of losing it. You can't continue or restart your studies until you have status as a student again and we’ve extended your study permit.
Post-secondary students changing schools
If you change post-secondary schools, the school you plan to change to must also be a DLI. Please check the DLI list and confirm your new school is a DLI before you commit to changing schools.
You must tell us each time you change post-secondary schools. Changing the post-secondary school on your account is a free service.
You don't need to apply to change your study permit if you are changing schools.
Post-secondary studies include:
- university community college, CEGEP, institute private university, career college, academy, school or training institution and ESL/FSL and other language training
Studying in Quebec
If you're moving to a school in Quebec, you must get a Québec Acceptance Certificate (CAQ).
You should contact the ministère de l'Immigration, de la Francisation et de l'Intégration (MIFI) if you're already studying in Quebec and want to change your:

In the situation where an outside of Canada applicant (principal applicant) is applying for a study permit and their planned program(s) of study is EAP (English for Academic Preparation) e.g. for one-term/4 months, followed by PSEC (assume PGWP eligible) program; is the dependent spouse be eligible to apply for an open work permit or would they need to apply as a visitor?
Response: Based on the information here, only spouses or common-law partners of certain foreign nationals who hold a study permit and study on a full-time basis in post-graduation work permit-eligible study programs and institutions may apply for an open work permit under the LMIA exemption category C42, as work designated by the Minister.
a) Assuming it's visitor only for the dependent spouse: Would the dependent spouse be able to enter Canada as a visitor and later apply for a work permit via C42? Response: a foreign national is eligible to apply as a visitor if they meet the requirements of The Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and are admissible. Additionally, the dependent spouse may apply for a work permit after entering Canada if their spouse holds a valid study permit and study on a full-time basis [R199].
i.If yes, can the dependent spouse apply sometime prior to the principal applicant student beginning PSEC (PGPW eligible) studies so the work permit is issued for the start of PSEC classes i.e. applying using the PSEC studies Letter of Acceptance prior to start of the PSEC classes; ii. Or would the dependent spouse need to show evidence of the principal applicant student's current enrollment in a PSEC program e.g. a Confirmation of Enrollment letter for the PSEC program? Response: evidence that the principal applicant foreign national is actively engaged in full-tirne studies in a post-graduation work perrnit-eligible study program and institution must be provided. Therefore, until they are able to provide all the required documents, the dependent spouse is not eligible.
b) In a scenario such as above (four months of EAP followed by PGWP eligible PSEC studies) and outside of Canada initial application: Is it possible for a work permit to be applied for and issued at the POE under C42 (given the Letter of Acceptance for upcoming PSEC studies) but perhaps with a border officer issuing a work permit with restrictions on work e.g. "May only work when spouse is enrolled full-time in PSEC (PGWP eligible) program” Response: applicants need to meet all the requirements mentioned to be eligible to apply.

a Canadian one-year post-secondary (or higher) educational credential, or a foreign educational credential and an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) report issued by an organization designated by IRCC
As per subsection 73(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, "Canadian educational credential" is defined as, “any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions." "One-year" does not refer to how many weeks or days the program is. The program can be one academic year, as long as it meets the requirements mentioned above.
Provincial and Territorial governments have the responsibility to register and certify educational institutions and programs in Canada, and the relevant Provincial or Territorial website (where the provider is located) would include this information. Hello,

Question: If an employer has a foreign worker on a work permit (LMIA exempt work permit), and during the course of the work permit, the foreign worker goes on a maternity leave and remains in Canada. If the foreign worker is not paid a salary during the maternity leave, per the employer's corporate policy, will the employer still be in compliance with the immigration regulations?
Is the employer required to disclose the leave to IRCC? If so, how would the employer do so?
Answer: The employer is required to pay the wages and provide the working conditions specified in the offer of employment. Working conditions may include non-wage related remuneration benefits and entitlements specifically detailed in the offer of employment, such as the following: location of employment statutory holidays, sick leave and vacation days hours of work (including overtime) transportation costs (where applicable) accommodations, conditions and costs (where applicable) extended health or medical insurance other non-taxable benefits
Employers are not legally required to inform IRCC of changes in working conditions. However, they must provide evidence of an acceptable justification [R203(1.1)] at the time of an inspection should there be differences between the working conditions offered and those found during the inspection.
Maternity leave without pay would be considered a change in working conditions. However, an example of where the employer may be justified is if the leave is in compliance with provisions of any collective agreement.
For more information on the employer's responsibilities after the hiring process, please see: International Mobility Program: after you hire a temporary worker

threads.subject: Study Permits: Applying from within Canada [R.215(1)(f)(i)] -- REP-2021-1626
threads.answer:
# Good day,
Under IRPR R215(1)(f)(i), the indication that the applicant must be a temporary resident and IS studying would infer that the applicant had already been found eligible to study (either under A30(2) or because they have been issued a study permit) and who is already studying at the pre-school, primary or secondary level. Therefore, clients who are temporary resident visitors, who are accompanying tourist parents who are not authorized to work or study, are not eligible to apply for a study permit from within Canada under this regulation.
We hope that this information is helpful to you.
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
De:
Envoyé: 21 septembre 2021 15:34
À : Objet : Study Permits: Applying from within Canada [R.215(1)(f)(i)]
Dear Sir/Madam,
We kindly seek your feedback and clarification with regards to the filing of a study permit for the first time from within Canada (Application IMM5709).
My interpretation of IRPR 215(1)(f)(i) is that a foreign national can apply for a study permit after entering Canada if they are a temporary resident who is studying at the preschool, primary or secondary level. I also interpret that "temporary resident" includes visitors, not just students or workers.
As noted in the Regulations and the Operational Instructions and Guidelines: “Study permits: Making an application" (see copies below), I understand that a Visitor in Canada who holds valid temporary resident status (i.e. Visitor Record) can apply for a Study Permit from inside Canada and change the terms and conditions of their stay.
For example, a 19-year-old applicant who entered Canada as a visitor and holds valid visitor status and was admitted into the final year (grade 12) of a secondary school program can apply to change the conditions of her stay from visitor to student, thus applying from within Canada. The applicant is in Canada visiting relatives and not accompanied by her parents.
Further, the Operational Instructions and Guidelines provide such examples for “Visitors in Canada" and “Applying from within Canada"; however we find that IRCC Edmonton is interpreting the instructions, guidelines and R.215(1)(f)(i) differently.
Your clarification whether this type of applicant is eligible to apply from within Canada (Application IMM5709) is appreciated. Thank you.
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (SOR (Statutory Orders and Regulations)/2002-227) APPLICATION AFTER ENTRY 215 (1) A foreign national may apply for a study permit after entering Canada if they
(a) hold a study permit;
(b) apply within the period beginning 90 days before the expiry of their authorization to engage in studies in Canada under subsection 30(2) of the Act, or paragraph 188(1)(a) of these Regulations, and ending 90 days after that expiry;
(c) hold a work permit;
(d) are subject to an unenforceable removal order;
(e) hold a temporary resident permit issued under subsection 24(1) of the Act that is valid for at least six months;
(f) are a temporary resident who
(i) is studying at the preschool, primary or secondary level, (ii) is a visiting or exchange student who is studying at a designated learning institution, or (iii) has completed a course or program of study that is a prerequisite to their enrolling at a designated learning institution; or
(g) are in a situation described in section 207.

The applicant must provide a letter of acceptance from the DLl at which they are enrolled or will be enrolled.

threads.subject: REP-2021-1696
threads.question:
Considering the foreign national is studying part-time in Canada on a valid study permit, will the full-time Canadian skilled work experience obtained during the period of their part-time studies in Canada while on valid Spousal Open Work Permit be counted towards the CEC program 1 year of full-time skilled work experience in Canada eligibility requirement?

Considering the foreign national is studying part-time in Canada on a valid study permit, will they be awarded Core/Human Capital AND Skilled Transferability CRS points for their Canadian full-time skilled work experience obtained during the period of their part-time studies while on valid Spousal Open Work Permit.
threads.answer:
Please note that points will be awarded under the EE CRS system if the client has a work permit and is not engaged in full time study. The educational institution must provide evidence that the client is studying part-time. Pursuant to paragraph 87.1(3)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) states, any period of employment during which the foreign national was engaged in full-time study shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience.
Foreign national would meet the CEC requirements as long as it's not unauthorized work or full time studies. Any periods of self-employment or unauthorized work will not be included in calculating the period of work experience. Pursuant to paragraph 87.1(3)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) states, any period of self-employment or unauthorized work shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience.
Please be advised that the onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements to facilitate a decision.

Ministerial Instruction section 2: Comprehensive Ranking System – Total number of points, stated that:
(2) The total number of points that may be assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System is 1200 points, allocated as follows:
- (a) for the core human capital factors
(i) a maximum of 500 points if the foreign national has no accompanying spouse or common-law partner, or (ii) a maximum of 460 points if the foreign national has an accompanying spouse or common-law partner;
(b) for accompanying spouse or common-law partner factors, a maximum of 40 points;
(c) for skill transferability factors, a maximum of 100 points; and
(d) for additional factors, a maximum of 600 points.
Please be advised that the assessment of an application is based on a case-by-case basis, considering the particular circumstances in conjunction with the supporting documentation available to the officer. The onus is always on the applicant to provide sufficient documentation to satisfy an officer that they meet the requirements. We trust that this information will assist you.

Thank you for contacting us with your inquiry. We recently clarified previous guidance on who is eligible to apply for a LMIA-exempt (C42) open work permit.
Spouses or common-law partners of certain foreign nationals who hold a study permit and study on a full-time basis at a post-graduation work permit-eligible study program and institution may apply for an open work permit under the LMIA exemption category C42, as work designated by the Minister. This LMIA exemption category is intended for spouses who are not, themselves, already study permit holders actively engaged in full-time studies.

a Canadian public post-secondary institution, such as a college trade or technical school university CEGEP in Quebec Oa private post-secondary institution in Quebec that operates under the same rules and regulations as a public post-secondary institution in Quebec 0 a private or public secondary or post-secondary institution in Quebec offering qualifying programs of 900 hours or longer leading to a diploma of vocational studies (DVS) or an attestation of vocational specialization (AVS) Oa Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees (for example, a bachelor's degree, master's degree, or doctorate), but only if the study permit holder is enrolled in a study program leading to a degree as authorized by the province, which may not include all study programs offered by the private institution.

threads.subject: Proof of settlement funds-Express Entry PNP applicants -- REP-2021-1937
threads.question:
Could you please advise if an applicant who receives an Invitation to Apply (ITA) under the Provincial Nominee Program
category is required to provide proof of settlement funds with their Express Entry application?
threads.answer:
Despite having received a Provincial nomination, Provincial Nominee Class applications that come through Express Entry must also meet the requirements of one of the three immigration programs managed through Express Entry (FSWC, FSTC, or CEC). Settlement funds are not included in the CRS. They do relate to the program requirements of FSWC and FSTC and maybe included in the MEC for Express Entry. Candidates who met the requirements of FSWC or the FSTC
(then were selected through PNP) are still required to meet the settlement funds requirement, unless they are currently authorized to work in Canada and have a qualifying offer of arranged employment from an employer in Canada.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
# Good Day,
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox. We appreciate your patience and apologize for the delay.
Question
1. When an employer creates an LMIA and job postings under this Program must they advertise the prevailing wage or the minimum wage is sufficient?
2. Must the employer pay the employee the prevailing wage during the 12 months of work experience?
3. Can the employer pay the employee minimum wage during the 12 month of work experience and then when the Job offer is created offer the prevailing wage?
4. Must the employer pay the prevailing wage during the processing of PR application? Response
1. When an employer creates an LMIA and job postings under this Program must they advertise the prevailing wage or the minimum wage is sufficient? Advertising requirements to obtain an LMIA are determined by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) and may vary depending on the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) stream the LMIA application is under (e.g. low-wage stream). For example, the Program requirements for low-wage positions indicate that the wage must be included in the job advertisement information. A wage range can be used for the purposes of complying with the advertisements; however, the minimum wage in the range must meet prevailing wage. Please see ESDC's website for further information on LMIA advertising requirements under other TFWP streams.
2. Must the employer pay the employee the prevailing wage during the 12 months of work experience? The prevailing wage is a requirement for the job offer in the AFP PR application, not the work experience. That said, for the temporary foreign worker program (TFWP) the employer is required by IRPR (s. 209.3) to pay the wage specified in the offer of employment (for the WP) and confirmed in the LMIA (as determined under the applicable TFWP stream), including during the applicant's 12 month work experience.
3. Can the employer pay the employee minimum wage during the 12 month of work experience and then when the Job offer is created offer the prevailing wage? The wage provided during the 12 months of work experience must comply with the Temporary Foreign Worker Program requirements, and the employer must continue to comply with their obligations under R209.3, including providing the
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
temporary foreign worker with wages that are substantially the same as-but not less favourable then-those set out in the offer (LMIA). However, when assessing the Application for Permanent Residence, the officer must be satisfied on balance that the job offer meets the requirements outlined in section 2(3)(c),(d), and (e) of the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Agri-food Immigration Class, including the requirement that it be genuine as per subsection 200(5) of the Regulations.
4. Must the employer pay the prevailing wage during the processing of PR application? If the employee holds an employer-specific work permit during the processing of the PR application, the employer is required to pay the temporary foreign worker with wages that are substantially the same as – but not less favourable than-those set out in the offer (LMIA) or they may face administrative penalties for violating their conditions under the employer compliance regime outline in R209.3.
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good Day,

Question: I am in the process of assessing an Express Entry candidate's potential Express Entry point score, and have the following question regarding his post-secondary education: The candidate attended a vocational training program with. It was a 6-month program that resulted in him earning his Private Pilot License. He then completed a one year commercial pilot program at the same institution and was issued a Commercial Pilot Licence. Could you kindly confirm if he is eligible for any CRS points under Express Entry? Would this be eligible as a one year
program from an "other institute"?
Answer: No, the applicant would not receive any CRS points for the training they received at In order to receive points for Canadian education, the credential must meet the definition of “Canadian education credential” as per Section 73(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) in that is must be issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions.
While is recognized by IRCC as a Designated Learning Institution (DLI), it is not a recognized public or private institution that has been given authority to grant degrees, diplomas, or other credentials by a public or private act of the provincial/territorial legislature or through a government-mandated quality assurance mechanism. You may check the Canadian Information Centre for International Credentials directory to see if an institution is recognized. Please note that CRS points will only be awarded for Canadian educational credentials that are granted by educational institutions that have the legal status of “recognized" or certain specific degrees, diplomas, or other credentials that an institution was "authorized" to grant. These institutions will have the legal status of "authorized."
We trust that this information will assist you.
Sincerely,
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Program Guidance Branch request).
I wanted to follow up on the 150 day issue as this is a topic of concern not only at the institutions across Canada, and the PDIs don't seem to fully clarify the issue.
out at
Thank you for the response to my inquiries (though I know I'm sending this reply only to the DLl list account, as per the
If I’ve interpreted it correctly, the 150 day rule pertains specifically to determining whether the student remained in compliance with their study permit (which is a consideration when determining PGWP eligibility). The PDI references that the leave should be less than 150 days but if the leave is longer, the student must either leave Canada or change their temporary status (presumably to visitor). That implies that leaving Canada within the 150 days keeps them in compliance. As such, being outside Canada should mean that the 150 day leave limit no longer applies.
This is an important issue as students that require leaves of absence may need more than 150 days. From experience, we know that students that have taken longer leaves have been able to successfully apply for a PGWP at the end of the degree with adequate explanation and documentation (eg. mandatory military service or extended medical issues). If
the 150 day rule only truly applies to those who remain in Canada during the break, then that should be made more clear.
We find students are feeling pressured into making decisions that are not in their best interests (or those of their families) because they want to keep their break in studies below 150 days. If they can remain compliant, and therefore maintain eligiblity for the PGWP, just by leaving Canada during the break in studies (which most of our students do anyway), that should be clear.
Further to that point, if a student takes a leave of longer than 150 days, but applies to change their status to visitor (as required), can they still be considered to be in compliance with the requirements of the study permit and therefore maintain eligiblity for the PGWP? Again, the PDI implies that, but it goes against the response that an authorized leave of greater than 150 days makes a student ineligible.
For what it's worth, this seems similar to IRCC's approach to students required by the pandemic to study remotely from outside Canada. IRCC has acknowledged the right of students to begin their studies online from outside Canada regardless of the status of their study permit application. This has been determined not to impact PGWP eligiblity as long as a study permit is approved at some point (acknowledging that the time spent studying outside Canada only counts towards PGWP eligibility if it was done after the application was submitted). Clearly this is a different set of rules for those that are outside Canada. Should there not be different rules regarding breaks in studies for those that leave Canada (or change their status)?
If this just gets left to the discretion of the officer processing the application, the PDls could still be clarified to not make the 150 days seem like a definitive rule (which it doesn't seem to be, in practice).
Best regards,
threads.answer:

RE: Clarifications -- REP-2021-1716
To clarify the 150 rule for study permit compliance, this applies to study permit conditions as mentioned in the PDI the student will not be eligible for PGWP if they exceed 150 days of authorized leave from their academic program. The 150 day rule is applicable to students inside and outside of Canada. Students are not required to inform IRCC if they are taking an authorized leave of 150 days from their studies; however, if requested proof is required if the student's leave is authorized and longer than 150 days. For more information on the 150 day rule for authorized leaves, please visit our website.
In the context of COVID 19, a temporary policy in regards to the period of stay outside of Canada for eligibility of PGWP has been implemented to better accommodate eligible international students who have completed distance learning in or outside Canada. All students who were enrolled in a PGWP-eligible program in progress in March 2020 or who started a program of study from spring 2020 up to and including the fall 2021 semester are not required to complete 50% of their program (or programs) of study in Canada. Up to 100% of their program can be completed online from outside Canada. Time spent studying outside of Canada can be counted towards the overall length of the post- graduation work permit until December 31, 2021.
I hope this information was helpful and clarified your inquiry.

In applying exemption code C16, officers should be satisfied that the foreign national's habitual language of daily use is French; however, the language of work does not have to be French.

Answer: Under Express Entry, candidates applying under the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) or Federal Skilled Trades (FST) are required to meet the settlement funds requirement, unless they are currently authorized to work in Canada and have a qualifying offer of arranged employment from an employer in Canada. Candidates invited to apply under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) do not have to demonstrate that they meet the settlement funds requirement.
The applicant should provide an official letter(s) from one or more financial institutions that lists all current bank and investment accounts as well as outstanding debts, such as credit card debts and loans. The letter(s) must be printed on the letterhead of the financial institution and must include the applicant's name, the contact information of the financial institution (address, telephone number and email address), the account numbers, the date each account was opened and the current balance of each account as well as the average balance for the past six months. There are no guidelines that say a candidate cannot include gifted money. However, we would recommend providing a letter of explanation along with any unusual banking transactions (including a large, gifted sum). The officer assessing the application may request other documentation so they can be satisfied that the applicant will meet the minimum settlement funds.
